I didn’t expect that quick review to be read by so many, and I definitely didn’t expect my typos to become a drinking game. I rewrote the piece, checked my sources, and realized I’d mixed up a couple of dates. Thanks for the patience. Here’s the cleaned-up version, with clearer headings, on why the Lanterns in the Crypt universe kept changing faces and why the latest web series might finally steady the ship.

Film vs. web rights: the short history no one asked for. In the late 2000s the original novelist signed away adaptation rights for a sum that would barely buy a mid-size car today. The initial platform holding the paperwork later split the pie: the first four novels’ film rights went to Aurora Pictures, the back four to Harbor Media. Web rights stayed in limbo, then were reassembled a few years later when TCloud entered the chat, bought the serial platform, and paid real money to scoop up streaming rights across the board.

That’s why movies and shows felt like cousins who don’t speak. Aurora teamed with a state studio and delivered a monster flick that wore the right clothes but forgot to bring a heart. The second attempt switched partners, doubled down on spectacle, and face-planted harder. Harbor, by contrast, got one theatrical title right by stacking the deck: three major studios and a director who loves pulp but respects people. Then … silence. Meanwhile, low-budget “internet films” with suspiciously familiar titles sprouted like mushrooms after rain—same keywords, none of the soul.

On the streaming side, TCloud could only make series, not movies. They cycled through production partners: one season with a prestige drama house that gave us legends-in-the-desert vibes and stately pacing; another with a scrappier crew that turned up the grime and the jokes. Casts changed. Directors changed. Audiences got tired of decoding family trees where every uncle had a different face. If we’re honest, that churn bled the brand.

Why the new run gives me hope. The current showrunner locked a core team and swore not to swap the trio every season. The scripts respect the arc—two entries are youth stories or ancestral tales where the main trio shouldn’t appear, so they won’t. Locations are real, not digital postcards. Practical creature work leads; CG fills the gaps. Most importantly, the emotional targets are consistent: loss, loyalty, and the cost of curiosity. If they stick the landing and resist “bigger equals better,” we might finally get the pulpy, propulsive, distinctly local adventure serial we’ve been promised since dial-up.

Will that fix the films? Probably not. Different rights, different incentives. But if the web series holds firm, it can be the spine, and everything else can hang from it without snapping. If it stumbles, chalk up another cautionary tale in the museum of squandered IPs we all visit too often.

Thanks for reading. If the images don’t load again, blame my CMS, not my heart.

My story with this actor starts in 2005, with a primetime melodrama called Clouds Over the Capital. I don’t remember the plot; I remember a pair of clear eyes and the sudden, ridiculous feeling of being fourteen and floored. Back then we didn’t have fandom jargon. There were no picks or stan lists—only someone you liked, quietly.

He disappeared after a handful of projects. Rumors filled the gap because the internet always does. Years later, I watched a New Year blockbuster and halfway through I realized the wry uncle who stole three scenes was the same boy from that old drama. Time had rounded his face and deepened the voice. I sighed, a little mournful and a little amused at myself for caring about cheekbones.

Then came a 2017 web series that dragged me into the uncle fan pit with both ankles. I had pressed play for the story and instead fell into a performance that didn’t beg for love, it earned it. He had shed the need to be pretty and replaced it with something harder to fake: timing, texture, and that invisible line between thought and action you can only feel when someone’s listening as they speak.

When this new adventure dropped on April 1, I watched with my partner. Twice I muttered, “He’s put on a bit, hasn’t he?” and got a very careful “mm” in return. It’s not an insult. It’s admiration for someone confident enough to let the character lead—even if it means the jawline doesn’t. Also, for the record, the banter between the lead and his loud, loyal friend is exactly the flavor I remember from the novels: patriotic quips, ragged courage, and a sense they’d sell each other for a cigarette but would actually torch the world to save the other.

If you’re worried about “role bleed” from his earlier aristocrat to this gruff salvager: don’t be. One uses silence to bully a room; the other uses it to weigh a choice. One keeps his back to the light; the other walks into it. Different men, different rhythms. The only overlap is the performer, and that’s the fun of it. Please, sir, maybe keep an eye on the late-night noodles, but also please keep out-acting your face. It’s working.

A few people asked for a nerdy breakdown of two set pieces in the finale of The Jade Labyrinth, so here goes—novel vs. show, and why the math and the myth both sort of check out.

1) The endless staircase. In the book, the trap is a design riff on a Penrose-like loop built into a natural cavern. The treads aren’t level, the widths change, and the walls are painted with light-absorbing pigment that flattens depth. Your brain insists you’re going straight when you’re actually carving lazy figure-eights—classic optical/kinesthetic miscue. The heroes break it by using spacing and discipline: three people fix equal distances, ignore the painted cues, and watch each other’s shoulders, not their own feet, until they spot a hidden landing.

The show rewrites it as an arithmetic puzzle. The team notices the staircase count and a crescent motif that hints at cycles; they key into a 384-step pattern, mapping to 64 hexagrams times six lines. The lead calls the current state “confinement” and looks for a transformation—one specific step where a single line flips state to change “confinement” to “release.” It’s pulpy numerology, sure, but internally consistent: if only one line moves, you resolve fate based on the original frame, not the target, so he jumps where the change originates rather than where it ends. Is it more cinematic than scientific? Absolutely. Does it work for the tension? Also yes.

2) The tomb’s nine-palace/ eight-gate room. Layout: a coffin in the center, eight walls around, each hiding a mechanism keyed to an element or image—water, fire, mountain, wind, etc. The walls are labeled to mislead you into chasing a so-called “life gate,” but the real solution is mapping the trigrams to the room properly, not just picking a lucky door.

How do you find orientation underground, with no sun and no compass you trust? The show borrows a classic mnemonic for the Lo Shu grid and overlays it on the coffin: “wear nine on the head, tread one underfoot; three on the left, seven on the right; two and four are shoulders; six and eight are feet.” If the coffin’s head points south, nine (fire/離) sits at the head, one (water/坎) at the foot, and so on. The lead treats the coffin as the ‘five’ at center and uses the rhyme to assign each wall its palace. Once he identifies the ‘water’ palace, he looks for an object that matches water’s symbolism—fish scales inlay, a damp draft, a carved wave—triggers it, and the mechanism cascades.

Bonus bit the show nods to: the sexagenary cycle. A character does back-of-the-napkin math from a reign title on a plaque to the team’s current year by hopscotching 60-year loops. You find a known anchor date, add multiples of sixty to get near your present, then adjust the stem and branch by one if you overshot. It’s a subtler flex than screaming and running, but it sells the idea that these people solve things with brains as well as boots.

You can prefer the book’s grounded illusions and still enjoy the series’ mythic flavor. What matters is the rules are clear enough that when someone leaps into the dark, you believe they knew where they’d land.

input.background: At the beginning of 2020, the novel coronavirus (COVID-19) outbreak occurred in Wuhan, rapidly spreading across the country and even globally, threatening human health and significantly impacting the social economy. - Date: The date of the epidemic data record (string type)
- New Confirmed: The number of new confirmed cases each day (integer type)
- Cumulative Confirmed: The total number of confirmed cases (integer type)
- Current Severe Cases: The number of current severe cases (integer type)
- Cumulative Deaths: The total number of deaths (integer type)
- Cumulative Recoveries: The total number of recoveries (integer type)
- Cumulative Close Contacts: The total number of close contacts (integer type)
- Currently Under Medical Observation: The number of close contacts currently under medical observation (integer type)
- New Close Contacts: The number of new close contacts each day (integer type)
input.question: The trend of daily new confirmed cases reflects the severity of the pandemic. What is the development trend?

input.background: In recent years, the development of the marriage and dating market has sparked a surge in matchmaking activities and dating websites. input.data_description_1: The data comes from the Speed Dating experiment conducted by the Chicago Booth School of Business, with the dataset named 'Speed Dating Data.pkl', which contains 8,378 rows and 195 columns of variables. Key variables include iid (participant ID), gender (0 for female, 1 for male), age, race, and dec (whether to choose to pursue further dating, with 0 for rejection and 1 for acceptance).

input.background: The Tokyo Olympics, as a globally anticipated sporting event, has attracted widespread attention. To explore the relationship between the content elements of short video releases and their dissemination effects, this study analyzes 579 short video data retrieved from the Douyin platform using "Tokyo Olympics" as the keyword before July 23, 2021. It examines how various factors on the content production side influence the level of discussion surrounding these short videos. This research aims to provide references for event organizers, self-media creators, and related communication agencies regarding content creation, topic selection, and dissemination strategies.
input.data_description_1: The data comes from the Douyin platform and includes 579 short video entries, containing the following variables: id0 (short video serial number), hot_or_not (whether it is trending), type_sv (topic type), nar_angle (narrative angle), zf_sv (attitude tendency), length_log (logarithm of short video length), title_sv (title text), media_type (publisher type), media_fans_log (logarithm of publisher's fan count), type_time_effe (timeliness), month (release month), month1 (whether released in July or August), love_sv (number of likes), love_sv_log (logarithm of the number of likes), com_sv (number of comments), com_sv_log (logarithm of the number of comments). Some continuous variables in the data have undergone logarithmic transformation to optimize their distribution characteristics.

input.background: The Tokyo Olympics, as a globally watched sporting event, has attracted widespread attention. To explore the relationship between the content elements of short video releases and their dissemination effects, this study analyzes 579 short video data presented on the Douyin platform prior to July 23, 2021, using "Tokyo Olympics" as the keyword. It examines how various factors on the content production side influence the level of discussion surrounding these short videos. This research aims to provide references for event organizers, self-media creators, and related communication agencies regarding content creation, topic selection, and dissemination strategies.
input.data_description_1: The data comes from the Douyin platform and includes 579 short video entries, containing the following variables: id0 (short video serial number), hot_or_not (whether it is a hot topic), type_sv (topic type), nar_angle (narrative angle), zf_sv (attitude tendency), length_log (logarithm of short video length), title_sv (title text), media_type (publisher type), media_fans_log (logarithm of publisher's fan count), type_time_effe (timeliness), month (release month), month1 (whether released in July or August), love_sv (number of likes), love_sv_log (logarithm of number of likes), com_sv (number of comments), com_sv_log (logarithm of number of comments). Some continuous variables in the data have undergone logarithmic transformation to optimize their distribution characteristics.

input.background: Weibo is a widely used social networking platform, and its convenience and openness have attracted a large number of users to express their opinions on the platform. The volume of new posts added daily is enormous, making it nearly impossible to manually verify the authenticity of each piece of information. This task aims to achieve automated identification or early detection of rumors by analyzing Weibo data, incorporating text, user, and dissemination characteristics.
input.data_description_1: The data was released by the NLP research group at the Chinese University of Hong Kong, covering 3.8 million Weibo posts and 2.74 million users from February 2012 to December 2015. The rumor data comes from the misinformation section of the Weibo Community Management Center, while the non-rumor data is sourced from content published by some authoritative Weibo accounts during the same period and has been manually reviewed. The data includes Weibo post IDs, text, images, timestamps, number of comments, number of shares, as well as user information such as nickname, gender, number of follows, number of fans, number of friends, and region.
input.question: What is the distribution of the number of posts on Weibo?

This case study aims to explore the factors influencing flight delays during the pandemic and to predict the rate of flight delays, helping airlines and passengers better manage the risks associated with flight delays.

input.background: With the development of internet technology, the food delivery industry has become an increasingly popular sector. Businesses aim to boost sales by optimizing pricing, delivery, and menus. This task is intended to help merchants identify the key factors affecting sales through the analysis of sales data from food delivery businesses in the Beijing area.
input.data_description_1:
The data is sourced from a web scraping of a food delivery platform in the Beijing area conducted in August 2017. It includes 32,043 records and 29 variables. The variables include basic information about the delivery merchants:

- delivery_mode (merchant delivery method)
- float_delivery_fee (delivery fee)
- float_minimum_order_amount (minimum order amount)
- is_new (whether it is a new store)
- is_premium (whether it is a brand store)
- order_lead_time (delivery time)
- recent_order_num (monthly sales volume)
- average_cost (average cost per order)
- 保 (whether it supports food delivery insurance)
- 票 (whether invoices can be issued)
- open_time (daily operating hours, in hours)
- open08 (whether open at 8 AM)
- open12 (whether open at 12 PM)
- open18 (whether open at 6 PM)
- open23 (whether open at 11 PM)
- shop_type (merchant category)

Rating information:

- compare_rating (comparative rating, score obtained by comparing with surrounding merchants)
- food_score (food rating)
- service_score (service rating)
- star_level (star level)

Location information:

- district (administrative division, includes all 16 administrative districts of Beijing)
- district0 (administrative division, where other districts outside the six core districts of Beijing are combined into a non-urban category)

Discount information:

- manjian_discount (full reduction discount rate)
- new_user (new user discount)
- other_activities (number of other activities, excluding full reduction and new user discounts)

Derived field information:

- log_recent_order_num (log of monthly sales volume: monthly sales volume plus 1, then take the logarithm)
- log_average_cost (log of average cost per order: average cost per order plus 1, then take the logarithm)
- log_float_delivery_fee (log of delivery fee: delivery fee plus 1, then take the logarithm)
- log_float_minimum_order_amount (log of minimum order fee)

To assist relevant companies in enhancing product quality and user experience, this task aims to analyze the relationship between the transaction volume of online travel products and various factors through data analysis, thereby providing data support for corporate decision-making.
input.data_description_1: The data comes from an online travel platform, and the dataset 'BearTrip.csv' contains 4,366 pieces of travel product information. The main variables include: transaction volume in the last three months (threemonth), customer satisfaction (satisfactory), travel agency rating (storerating), travel agency credit level (creditLevel), travel region (type), itinerary duration (tripschedule), number of attractions (num_spot), and price level (price.level), among others.
input.question: What factors have a significant impact on the sales volume of tourism products?

input.background: With the rapid development of the online education industry, MOOCs (Massive Open Online Courses) have become an important component of the education sector. In order to understand the factors influencing the revenue of online courses, this task will analyze data from 10,222 courses on a certain online course platform as of August 16, 2016, exploring how factors such as course content, number of participants, and course pricing affect revenue.

people.1: Aspiring CG practitioners who want to learn 3ds Max animation techniques and production basics.
people.2: Art and design students, as well as 3D enthusiasts exploring digital content creation.

intro.0: Learn 3ds Max through a structured path—mastering Max can be within reach for you too. Ideal for learners seeking a complete foundation, especially those aiming for interior visualization, architectural modeling, and production-ready drafting.
intro.1: This beginner-friendly animation course starts from zero and takes you to confident 3ds Max animation production. No dense jargon—just clear explanations of keyframes, interpolation, parent-child relationships, tangent controls, auto/manual keying, generic and specialized controllers, constraints, linking, reaction management, motion capture workflows, adjustment modes, space warps (force fields), particle systems, and MassFX dynamics, reinforced with many hands-on examples.
intro.2: In this series we begin with the 3ds Max interface and navigation. While Max is extremely powerful, this entry-level track focuses on the core tools so you can build a rock-solid base for future advanced techniques and pipelines. Official site: https://learn3d.example.com
intro.3: These brand-new material lessons combine 3ds Max procedural maps with V-Ray rendering, demonstrating practical methods for reproducing real-world surfaces. We cover native Max shading, V-Ray integration, 2D/3D textures, composite and blend maps, special map types, and how to pair them with materials for believable results—so you learn underlying principles, not just recipes.
intro.4: Drawing on years of production and teaching, this comprehensive guide to mechanical and character animation explains IK workflows (HI/HD and spline IK), interactive IK, Character Studio (Biped), CAT rigging, hair and fur, facial and lip-sync animation, skinning, cloth, and physics—offering a thorough, project-driven path for both mech rigs and human/creature and real-time characters.

people.1: Motivated individuals aiming to learn a CG workflow with a focus on 3ds Max character animation.
people.2: Students in art or design programs and 3D enthusiasts interested in modeling and rendering.
people.3: College learners, recent graduates, and professionals upgrading their 3ds Max skills for production use.
people.4: Learners wanting to deepen their knowledge of animation principles and rigging using 3ds Max.

intro.0: A structured 3ds Max study plan—master the software and you can, too. Suitable for: newcomers who want a systematic path in 3ds Max and those aiming for interior design, visualization, and architectural modeling roles.
intro.1: This set of lessons is the best choice for beginners to learn 3ds Max animation from zero, progressing to confident production. We avoid heavy jargon and make complex motion concepts approachable. Topics include: animation fundamentals (keyframes, interpolation, parent-child relationships, overshoot), auto and manual keying, general and specialized controllers, animation constraints, parameter wiring and reaction setups, motion capture workflows, adjustment modes, space warps and force fields, particle systems, and the MassFX dynamics toolset. Through numerous hands-on examples, you will learn faster and with less effort.
intro.2: In this course, we start with the 3ds Max interface and basic operations. While 3ds Max is extremely powerful, this curriculum focuses on the essentials for absolute beginners, laying a solid foundation for advanced techniques later on. Newsletter: cgstart101  Official site: www.mockstudiolearn.com
intro.3: This is the instructor's latest release, blending 3ds Max procedural maps with the V-Ray renderer and explaining practical methods to represent everyday materials. We cover pure 3ds Max material workflows as well as tips for combining them with V-Ray. If you want to break through in material creation, this course is an excellent choice. It details 2D maps, 3D maps, composite maps, special-purpose maps, and how they interact with material types. By the end, you will understand the core principles of texturing and be able to craft the exact looks you need, not just copy a few presets.
intro.4: Designed from years of teaching and production, this comprehensive program focuses on mechanical and character animation in 3ds Max. We thoroughly explain interactive IK, HI and HD solvers, spline IK, Character Studio biped systems, CAT rigs, hair and fur, facial and lip-sync animation, skeletal skinning, cloth, and rigid/soft-body dynamics. With rich case studies, it is a rare, complete guide to mechanical and character workflows and a new milestone following our rendering and materials series.

input.question: What is the impact of course grading on income, keeping other factors constant?

input.background: With the rapid development of the online education industry, MOOCs (Massive Open Online Courses) have become an important component of the education sector. To understand the factors influencing the revenue of online courses, this task will analyze the data of 10,222 courses from a certain online course platform as of August 16, 2016, exploring how factors such as course content, number of participants, and course pricing affect revenue.
input.data_description_1: The data comes from an online course platform and is divided into two main datasets: the course list (which includes information such as course category, name, instructor, number of participants, pricing, and revenue) and course information (which includes course ratings, target audience, and course description). The course list contains the following fields: s.ctg (sub-category of the course), b.ctg (main category of the course), url (course website), course.name (course name), teacher (instructor's name), size (number of participants), real.price (course pricing), orig.price (original price), revenue (course revenue). The course information includes the fields: url (course website), score (rating), people (target audience), intro (course description), detail (course schedule).

people.0: Suitable for learners seeking systematic 3ds Max training and a path into interior and architectural visualization.
people.1: Motivated individuals wanting to study a CG discipline and learn 3ds Max animation fundamentals.
people.2: Art and design students of various majors, plus 3D enthusiasts.
people.3: 3ds Max skill builders, university students, recent graduates, and professionals advancing their software proficiency.
people.4: Learners aiming to deepen their understanding of animation principles and production.

intro.0: Systematically learn 3ds Max; with the right practice you can master Max as well. Suitable: learners seeking a structured 3ds Max path and aiming for interior visualization, architectural modeling, or entry-level environment design roles.
intro.1: This series is an ideal starting point for newcomers to Max animation, taking you from zero to confident production. We avoid dense jargon and make complex topics approachable. Covered topics include: keyframe fundamentals, interpolation curves, parent-child relationships, overshoot and easing, automatic and manual keying, general and specialized controllers, animation constraints, linking and reaction setups, motion capture workflows, adjustment modes, space warps (force fields), particle systems, and MassFX dynamics. Through numerous practical demos, you will learn faster and more comfortably in a complete, up-to-date curriculum.
intro.2: In this course we start from the 3ds Max interface and navigation. Although 3ds Max is extremely powerful, this is an introductory program that builds a solid base for advanced workflows. You will learn core tools, scene organization, and best practices to prepare for modeling, animation, and rendering. Official page: www.example3dschool.com
intro.3: Our latest material-focused training combines 3ds Max procedural maps with V-Ray rendering, using many real-life case studies to demonstrate how to achieve believable surfaces. We explain both native 3ds Max material techniques and V-Ray shading tips. If you seek breakthroughs in material creation, this series is an excellent choice. Topics include 2D maps, 3D maps, composite maps, special-purpose maps, and how to integrate them with materials. By learning the underlying principles of texture mapping, you will be able to author any material rather than just follow recipes.
intro.4: Built on years of teaching and production experience, this comprehensive course covers mechanical and character animation in depth. We systematically explore interactive IK, HI and HD solvers, spline IK, Character Studio (Biped), CAT rigs, hair and fur, facial and lip-sync animation, bones and skinning, cloth, and physics-based dynamics. Packed with hands-on examples, it is a thorough and practical series following our rendering and material courses.

input.question: What is the relationship between the number of participants and the course revenue?

input.background: With the rapid development of the online education industry, MOOCs (Massive Open Online Courses) have become an important component of the education sector. To understand the factors affecting the revenue of online courses, this task will analyze data from 10,222 courses on a certain online course platform as of August 16, 2016, exploring how factors such as course content, number of participants, and course pricing impact revenue.
input.data_description_1: The data comes from an online course platform and is divided into two main datasets: the course list (which includes information such as course category, name, instructor, number of participants, pricing, and revenue) and course information (which includes course ratings, target audience, and course description). The course list contains the following fields: s.ctg (sub-category of the course), b.ctg (main category of the course), url (course website), course.name (course name), teacher (instructor's name), size (number of participants), real.price (course pricing), orig.price (original price), revenue (course revenue). The course information includes the fields: url (course website), score (rating), people (target audience), intro (course description), detail (course schedule).

people.0: Beginner designers seeking structured 3ds Max training for interior visualization roles.
people.1: Individuals motivated to study a CG discipline with emphasis on 3ds Max animation skills.
people.2: Students in art or design programs and 3D hobbyists interested in creative modeling.
people.3: Learners building 3ds Max proficiency, including university students and recent graduates.
people.4: Trainees aiming to deepen their knowledge of animation theory, rigging, and workflows.

intro.0: Learn 3ds Max step by step and build confidence. Ideal for newcomers aiming to work in interior visualization, architectural modeling, and related design tasks.
intro.1: A beginner-friendly path to animation in 3ds Max with clear explanations and hands-on practice. Explore keyframes, interpolation, parenting, extrapolation, auto/manual keying, general and specialized controllers, constraints, parameter wiring, reaction setups, motion capture, adjustment modes, space warps, particle systems, and rigid-body tools like MassFX through practical projects.
intro.2: This series begins with the 3ds Max interface and navigation, then moves into essential tools and workflow. It is an entry-level course that builds a solid base in scene organization, transforms, snapping, pivots, and modifier stacks to prepare you for advanced techniques later. Official page: https://example.com/learn-max-basics
intro.3: Guided by an experienced instructor, this course combines 3ds Max procedural maps with the V-Ray renderer to teach realistic material creation for everyday surfaces. Learn native 3ds Max shading methods and V-Ray integration, including 2D/3D textures, composite and utility maps, and strategies for pairing maps with materials to achieve believable results.
intro.4: Developed from real production workflows, this training focuses on mechanical rigs and character animation in 3ds Max. Topics include interactive IK, HI and HD solvers, spline IK, Character Studio biped, CAT rigging, hair and fur, facial and lip-sync setup, bones and skinning, cloth, and dynamics. A complete, project-driven program for animators in games and film.

input.background: In recent years, with the acceleration of urbanization and the development of industrialization, environmental pollution has become a global issue. Among various pollutants, PM2.5 is a particularly dangerous air pollutant, as its fine particles can easily be inhaled and deposited in the lungs, leading to health problems in the respiratory and cardiovascular systems, severely threatening people's health and lives. PM2.5 is not only related to the direct emissions of atmospheric pollutants, but the atmospheric pollutants such as SO2, NO2, CO, and O3 also undergo chemical and physical reactions with each other, resulting in the formation of new air pollutants and fine particles that further affect PM2.5 concentrations. Spatial modeling analysis based on urban air quality data can help us better understand the distribution patterns of PM2.5 concentrations and their influencing factors. Therefore, this case study collected air quality data from major cities across the country to explore the spatial distribution characteristics and influencing factors of PM2.5 concentrations, providing a basis for better addressing air pollution issues.
input.data_description_1: The case data "quarter.rda" contains two data frames, df_Q2 and df_Q4, which provide daily average air quality and meteorological indicator data for 158 cities in the second and fourth quarters of 2020, respectively. The dataset includes 15 fields: city, province of the city, daily average PM2.5 concentration (μg/m³), daily average SO2 concentration (μg/m³), daily average NO2 concentration (μg/m³), daily average CO concentration (μg/m³), daily average O3 concentration (μg/m³), daily average temperature (K), daily average boundary layer height (m), daily average K index (K), daily average surface air pressure (Pa), daily average precipitation (mm), daily average relative humidity (%), daily average horizontal wind speed (m/s), and daily average vertical wind speed (m/s).
input.question: What are the differences in the distribution of daily average PM2.5 concentrations in cities between the second and fourth quarters?

output.category: Relationship Between Discrete and Continuous Variables

input.background: With the rapid development of the live streaming industry, more and more companies are beginning to utilize live streaming platforms for product promotion and sales. This task is based on the live streaming data of a certain automotive company, and through data analysis, it aims to help the company understand the audience behavior and interaction in the live stream, thereby optimizing the live streaming strategy to enhance audience engagement and sales conversion rates.
input.data_description_1:
The data comes from a car company's 1,000 live broadcasts in November 2021, and the dataset includes 12 fields that mainly record audience interaction in the live stream. The variable descriptions are as follows:
1. zhibo_id: Unique ID for the live broadcast
2. time: Time label indicating the period of the live broadcast
3. danmu_total_num_lag: Total number of bullet comments in the next time period
4. danmu_user_num: Number of users posting bullet comments during the time period
5. danmu_effect_prop: Proportion of car-related bullet comments during the time period
6. danmu_price_prop: Proportion of price-related bullet comments during the time period
7. audio_effect_num: Number of car-related audio comments by the host during the time period
8. audio_price_num: Number of price-related audio comments by the host during the time period
9. audio_like_num: Number of like-related audio comments by the host during the time period
10. like_num: Number of likes in the live broadcast room during the time period
11. follow_num: Number of followers in the live broadcast room during the time period
12. gift_num: Number of gifts given during the time period.
input.question: What are the distribution characteristics of the average bullet comments in the live broadcast room?

input.data_description_1: The data comes from the cumulative revenue of 214 cinemas in Beijing for the first 11 months of 2019. input.background: A children’s apparel company is reviewing size coverage for a new line intended for 10-year-old boys. According to the growth reference currently used by the product team, boys’ heights in this age segment are modeled by a Normal distribution with a center of 138 centimeters and a spread parameter of 7 centimeters. Teams have also raised unrelated considerations such as color preference, regional sell-through, and seasonal timing, but for this sizing review management only wants to understand how many children fall under a specific height cutoff.
input.question: Using that Normal height profile, what proportion of 10-year-old boys would be shorter than 150 centimeters?

X_height.description: Heights of 10-year-old boys, following a Normal distribution with population mean μ=138 cm and population standard deviation σ=7 cm.

threshold.description: The cutoff value (150 cm) used in the answer to compute the proportion of the population below this height, directly substituted into the z-score formula z=(150−138)/7.

input.background: A care delivery team is doing a quick readout before deciding how to describe two alternative treatment paths in upcoming patient-facing materials. In a small pulse check, 10 people were each asked which of the two they would rather receive, and 7 indicated treatment A. Leadership has asked the team to judge this result against a neutral benchmark in which the broader patient population is evenly split between the two options, even though individual choices may still be shaped by messaging, prior experiences, and clinician framing.
input.question: If the wider market truly has no built-in lean toward either option, what is the chance that a 10-person check-in would produce 7 or more selections for treatment A?

n.description: Number of trials (patients) in the binomial distribution b(10, 0.5)

p.description: Assumed probability of a patient preferring treatment A under the null hypothesis of no preference

x.description: Observed number of patients who preferred treatment A, used as the threshold for computing Pr(X ≥ 7)

input.background: A performance review team is checking whether the decision rules used in a routine quality report are written clearly enough for approval. Before the report template is released, the team wants each draft statement screened for logical consistency and proper interpretation.
input.question: In the draft statement $H_0: \mu=100$ vs. $H_a: \mu \neq 110$, what is flawed about the way this comparison has been written?

input.background: A maternal health program is reviewing whether a routinely used planning benchmark for uncomplicated pregnancies is appropriate for a specific client segment. In broader community tracking, uncomplicated pregnancies are commonly expected to last about 39 weeks, with the usual spread around that benchmark being 2 weeks. A small internal review of 22 middle-class African American women produced an average recorded gestational length of 38.5 weeks. Program managers are aware that many factors can influence delivery timing in practice, and they are not yet asking for a full clinical explanation; they simply want to know whether this group appears to depart from the benchmark in either direction strongly enough to merit closer attention.
input.question: Using the benchmark of 39 weeks and the observed average of 38.5 weeks from 22 women, what standardized comparison value should be computed to assess whether this group differs materially from the expected gestational length in either direction?

gestation_length_African_American.description: Gestational length (in weeks) from a sample of 22 middle-class African American women, with sample mean x̄ = 38.5 weeks. Used in the answer to compute SE and the z test statistic.

gestation_length_general_population.description: Gestational length (in weeks) in the general population of uncomplicated pregnancies, with known population mean μ = 39 weeks and population standard deviation σ = 2 weeks. μ is used as the hypothesized value and σ is used to compute the standard error in the answer.

input.background: A regional healthcare system is preparing briefing material for an internal equity review after a group of 20 female hospital administrators reported that their average annual pay came to 80,900 and informally expressed concern that compensation for women may be trailing what is typical in the broader administrator market. For benchmarking purposes, the compensation office is using a published industry reference indicating that hospital administrators generally earn an average of μ = 85,100 with σ = 10,000. Leadership does not want a formal conclusion drafted yet; instead, they want a visual benchmark that shows where this group’s observed average would sit relative to the kind of fluctuation one might expect from a group of this size. Other factors such as tenure, institution type, and geography are being discussed elsewhere but are not part of this display.
input.question: Create a visual benchmark for the average pay figure that would arise from taking an SRS of n = 20 from a population with μ = 85,100 and σ = 10,000. Draw the curve for the distribution of group averages, label the horizontal axis at the center and at points that are ±1 and ±2 standard errors from μ, and place the observed average of x̄ = 80,900 at its appropriate location on that axis.

x_bar.description: The observed sample mean annual salary of 20 female hospital administrators, located on the horizontal axis of the sampling distribution.

n.description: Sample size of the female hospital administrators, used to compute the standard error.

mu.description: Published population mean salary of hospital administrators, used as the center of the sampling distribution under the null hypothesis.

sigma.description: Published population standard deviation of hospital administrator salaries, used to compute the standard error.

input.background: A regional healthcare employment committee is reviewing compensation concerns raised by a group of 20 female hospital administrators. Their average annual pay in this review came to 80,900. Several members believe their compensation may be trailing what is typical for the broader hospital administrator market and have informally attributed the gap to unequal treatment, although leadership notes that pay can also be shaped by organization size, tenure, local market conditions, and reporting scope. For benchmarking purposes, the committee is using a published reference indicating that hospital administrators generally earn an average of 85,100, with usual variation around 10,000.
input.question: Using the benchmark information and the group result above, quantify how unusual an average of 80,900 would be for a group of 20 female hospital administrators if they were being paid in line with the broader administrator market, and report the corresponding probability for the concern that their pay is lower than expected.

mu.description: Published population mean salary for hospital administrators.

sigma.description: Published population standard deviation of hospital administrator salaries.

input.background: A court administration team is preparing orientation material for new jurors on how verdict choices map to real-world case outcomes. In that training, the legal system’s starting point is that a defendant is to be treated as not having committed the offense unless the case presented in court is strong enough to overcome that starting position. The trainers want to emphasize that the two possible panel decisions interact with the two possible underlying realities in ways that do not carry the same institutional and ethical consequences. To make the discussion concrete, they use a simple 2×2 outcome grid contrasting the jury’s decision with what actually happened in the case, while noting that public safety, fairness to the accused, and confidence in the justice process are all affected by where a case lands in that grid.
input.question: For the following table, assign each of the labels to the appropriate cell of the 2×2 outcome grid: (a) Acquittal of an innocent person; (b) Conviction of an innocent person; (c) Acquittal of a guilty person; (d) Declaring a criminal guilty.

Decision_of_Jury.description: The jury's verdict, serving as the row variable of the 2×2 decision table (analogous to the decision to reject or fail to reject H0 in hypothesis testing).

Truth.description: The actual truth about whether the defendant committed the crime, serving as the column variable of the 2×2 decision table (analogous to whether H0 is actually true or false).

input.background: A court policy team is preparing onboarding material for new clerks on how formal decision frameworks are communicated in criminal proceedings. In the note, they emphasize that a trial begins from the position that the accused is to be treated as not guilty unless the evidence presented is strong enough to justify the opposite conclusion. Senior staff also point out that, when explaining courtroom decisions alongside other rule-based review settings, one particular mistake is viewed as especially serious because it imposes the cost of punishment on someone who should not have been sanctioned. Although jurors may discuss many practical concerns such as public pressure, case complexity, and the consequences of release, the training memo keeps the focus on the logic of the final verdict choice.
input.question: Under this decision framework, which verdict outcome matches the mistake of rejecting the starting position when that starting position was actually correct?

input.background: A public-sector legal training unit is developing decision-making guidance for new trial observers and wants to explain why case review begins from a default position that the accused should be treated as not responsible unless the case presented is strong enough to overturn that starting point. In internal workshops, instructors compare this courtroom logic with other formal decision settings where one begins from a standing position and then either keeps it or reverses it after reviewing the available record. They also note that some decision outcomes are more costly than others from an institutional risk perspective, especially when the system must balance the harm of punishing the wrong person against the harm of allowing an actually responsible person to leave without sanction.
input.question: Under this courtroom analogy, which verdict corresponds to the situation where the process fails to act against someone who in fact did commit the offense?

input.background: A regional maternal and newborn health team is preparing a summary benchmark for full-term infant birth weights to support planning, reporting, and communication with partner hospitals. Long-run operational tracking suggests that birth weights in this population typically vary by about 2 pounds. Leadership wants to understand what range should reasonably be reported for the underlying average birth weight under different record counts and observed average values, while recognizing that factors such as nutrition programs, local demographics, and seasonal delivery patterns may also be discussed in stakeholder meetings.
input.question: For the scenario where 81 full-term infant records are reviewed and the observed average birth weight is 6.1 pounds, what 95% range should be reported for the underlying average birth weight of full-term infants?

input.background: An internal reporting team is preparing a reference note for analysts who use Table C when setting a central operating band around a benchmark generated from a process with 22 degrees of freedom. The team wants the revised sheet to show the proper escalation boundaries for this exact setup.

input.background: A women’s health group is checking whether a calendar reference tied to the 29.5-day lunar cycle is a sensible benchmark for communication materials used in one small review. As part of the normal review cycle, a supervisor randomly pulls the case forms prepared by 2 workers for closer inspection. Internal concerns not yet known to the supervisor suggest that 3 of the workers have been repeatedly applying deductions that should not have been allowed. Leadership wants a simple way to quantify the exposure built into this audit process before discussing broader control issues.
input.question: Let event $A$ represent the situation in which the first worker whose forms are pulled in this random audit is one of the workers making illegal deductions. How should $P(A)$ be determined?

input.background: A county assistance office staffs 10 eligibility workers who process intake forms for food support applicants. From time to time, a supervisor conducts a routine file-quality check by pulling work associated with 2 different employees in sequence for review. Separately, there have been quiet internal concerns that 3 workers may have been consistently applying deduction adjustments that do not align with program rules, although the supervisor does not know which individuals are involved. The review is framed as a standard oversight exercise rather than a targeted inquiry, and staff performance on other administrative dimensions is not part of this question.
input.question: If the first worker selected in this sequential review turns out to be one of the 3 workers using those improper deductions, what is the probability that the second worker selected is also from that same group? Express this as P(B | A).

N_illegal.description: Number of workers who have regularly been giving illegal deductions. Used in the answer to determine the remaining number of illegal-deduction workers (3 − 1 = 2) after the first selected worker is known to be one of them.

input.background: A county benefits office is conducting a compliance review of front-line case processing. The unit has 10 welfare workers handling intake interviews for prospective food stamp recipients, and from time to time a supervisor pulls completed case files tied to 2 workers for a closer check. Internal concerns have surfaced because 3 of the workers have been consistently applying deduction practices that are not permitted under program rules. Although the review is framed as a routine quality-control step, leadership wants to understand the exposure associated with the current spot-check approach.
input.question: If the supervisor’s review happens to focus on 2 workers under this routine selection process, what is the chance that both of those workers are among the 3 who have been using the improper deductions?

total_workers.description: Total number of welfare workers employed by the agency, used as the population size in the probability calculation (denominator of P(A)=3/10).

illegal_workers.description: Number of workers who have regularly been giving illegal deductions, used as the count of 'success' items in the population (numerator of P(A)=3/10).

workers_selected.description: Number of workers randomly selected by the supervisor for auditing, defining the two-step selection process in the multiplicative rule.

input.background: A compliance team is reviewing a simple six-code random assignment mechanism used in a training simulation, where one and only one label from 1 through 6 is generated each time and each label is meant to appear with the same chance. For internal reporting, the team tracks two operational flags based on the observed label: Flag A is triggered when the result is an even number, and Flag B is triggered when the result is 4 or below. Leadership wants to understand not only how often each flag should appear on its own, but also whether the two flags behave as if one gives no added information about the other.
input.question: Under this assignment rule, what share of outcomes would trigger Flag A, what share would trigger Flag B, and what share would trigger both flags at the same time?

A.description: Event A: Observe an even number when tossing a fair die. The answer uses its constituent outcomes to compute P(A) = P(2) + P(4) + P(6) = 1/2 and P(A ∩ B).

B.description: Event B: Observe a number less than or equal to 4 when tossing a fair die. The answer uses its constituent outcomes to compute P(B) = P(1) + P(2) + P(3) + P(4) = 2/3 and P(A ∩ B).

input.background: A game studio is reviewing the rule logic for a simple six-sided bonus cube used in a promotional mini-game. The cube is balanced, and the payout team is checking whether two tagging rules overlap in a way that could create hidden dependence in downstream reward triggers. One rule, labeled A, flags any roll that lands on an even face. Another rule, labeled B, flags any roll that lands on a face with a value less than or equal to 4. Before the campaign goes live, the team wants to confirm whether seeing rule B triggered changes what should be expected for rule A, rather than treating the two labels as operationally unrelated.
input.question: If the cube roll has already been confirmed to meet rule B, what is the chance that it also meets rule A, and how does that compare with the overall chance of meeting rule A on any roll?

A.description: Event A: observing an even number when tossing a fair die. P(A) = 1/2.

B.description: Event B: observing a number less than or equal to 4 when tossing a fair die. P(B) = 2/3.

input.background: A defense-site operations team is reviewing field performance from an outdoor perimeter surveillance pilot that relies on automated video sensing and embedded processors to flag unauthorized entry attempts. In vendor discussions, the headline expectation has been that the platform catches 0.90 of intrusion events overall, but plant staff have repeatedly noted that real-world visibility and surface conditions may affect how that performance is distributed across different kinds of days. The system logs the prevailing weather whenever an intrusion attempt is later verified, and a set of controlled release exercises has already been summarized for management review. Among the cases in which the platform did register the intruder, the day was clear 75% of the time, cloudy 20% of the time, and raining 5% of the time. Among the cases in which the platform did not register the intruder, 60% of the days were clear, 30% cloudy, and 10% rainy. Although engineering has also raised issues such as camera angle, maintenance cycles, and site lighting, the current request is limited to turning these operational summaries into rainfall-specific event shares.
input.question: From the standpoint of incident reporting, what share of all controlled intrusion attempts fell into each of the following two situations: a rainy day on which the system registered the intruder, and a rainy day on which the system did not register the intruder?

P(D).description: Probability that the monitoring system detects an intruder. P(D^c) = 0.10 is derived as 1 − P(D) and also used in the answer.

P(Rainy|D).description: Conditional probability that the weather was rainy given the intruder was detected by the system.

P(Rainy|D^c).description: Conditional probability that the weather was rainy given the system failed to detect the intruder.

input.background: A remote perimeter-security prototype combining automated video capture and onboard processing is being trialed in outdoor conditions at a weapons munitions plant. Among the breach attempts that were successfully picked up by the system, the logged conditions were clear 75% of the time, cloudy 20% of the time, and raining 5% of the time. Among the breach attempts the system missed, 60% occurred on clear days, 30% on cloudy days, and 10% on rainy days. Plant management is less interested in the technical design details than in understanding how often each operating environment is actually represented in the test activity.

input.background: A defense facility is reviewing field performance of an automated perimeter-watch platform that combines video hardware with onboard processing to flag unauthorized entry. In routine briefings, the vendor cites an overall pickup rate of 0.90, but site engineers have cautioned operations staff that day-to-day conditions may affect how reliably the platform reacts. The system logs the weather whenever a breach attempt is successfully flagged, and a controlled set of trial runs has also been summarized for misses. From those trials, among the occasions when the platform did flag the intruder, conditions were clear 75% of the time, cloudy 20% of the time, and rainy 5% of the time. Among the occasions when the platform did not flag the intruder, 60% occurred on clear days, 30% on cloudy days, and 10% on rainy days. Although plant managers have also raised issues such as camera maintenance, lighting angles, and false-alarm burden, the immediate concern is how to describe performance specifically for wet-weather operations.
input.question: For security planning on rainy days, what chance should the plant assign to the platform successfully flagging an intruder when the weather is rainy?

P(Rainy|D).description: The conditional probability that the weather was rainy given the intruder was detected (5% of the time when detected).

P(Rainy|D').description: The conditional probability that the weather was rainy given the system failed to detect the intruder (10% of the days when not detected).

input.background: A rehabilitation technology team is reviewing how an intent-assist module should interpret user input for a powered wheelchair at a recurring decision point inside a therapy room. From that spot, users typically end up choosing one of three practical destinations: making a sharp left move to pass through a doorway, continuing ahead across the room, or drifting slightly right to stop at a table. For internal notation, these three destination choices are tracked as $D$ (door), $S$ (straight), and $T$ (table). Based on prior observed trips from the same location, the long-run mix of these choices has been estimated as $P(D)=.5$, $P(S)=.2$, and $P(T)=.3$. The chair is equipped with a robot-assisted joystick interface, and the engineering notes show that users do not always aim the stick in a way that cleanly matches the eventual path: when the user is actually trying to go through the door, the joystick is pointed straight $30\%$ of the time; when the user is trying to continue straight, the joystick is pointed straight $40\%$ of the time; and when the user is trying to stop at the table, the joystick is pointed straight $5\%$ of the time. The team wants a quick interpretation rule for this specific joystick signal before discussing broader issues such as room layout, training effects, and device calibration.
input.question: If, at this location, the joystick is observed to be pointed straight, how should the system reallocate its belief across the three possible intended destinations—door, straight ahead, and table—that is, what are $P(D \mid J)$, $P(S \mid J)$, and $P(T \mid J)$?

P(D).description: Prior probability that the wheelchair user intends to navigate through the door.

P(J|S).description: Probability of the joystick being pointed straight given the user intends to go straight.

P(J|T).description: Probability of the joystick being pointed straight given the user intends to stop at the table.

input.background: A rehabilitation technology team is reviewing how an assistive driving module should interpret user input in a recurring indoor travel situation. input.background: You are reviewing the economics of a small protection product in an insurer’s retail portfolio. input.question: For this single contract over the next policy year, what bottom-line amounts could the company end up with, and how likely is each of those outcomes?

premium.description: Annual premium charged for the $10,000 one-year term insurance policy; used directly as one possible gain value and to compute the other.

policy_amount.description: Face value of the one-year term insurance policy; used together with the premium to compute the company's loss upon the customer's death ($290 − $10,000 = −$9,710).

probability_of_death.description: Probability that the customer dies during the next year (from actuarial tables); used to assign probabilities to the gain values (0.001 for death, 0.999 = 1 − 0.001 for survival).

input.background: You are reviewing the economics of a small block of newly issued one-year protection contracts for the retail life business. Based on the company’s pricing reference for people with the same age, sex, health profile, and similar underwriting characteristics, the chance that a customer in this segment dies within the next 12 months is 0.001. Ignore operating expenses, commissions, investment income, and any broader portfolio effects; management only wants the contract-level financial picture for this single policy.

premium.description: Annual premium charged for the one-year term insurance policy ($290). Used directly in the expected gain calculation as the gain when the customer survives, and as part of computing the net loss when the customer dies.

policy_amount.description: Face value of the one-year term insurance policy ($10,000). Used together with the premium to derive the net loss of -$9,710 (= 290 − 10,000) in the event of the customer's death.

prob_death.description: Probability of the customer's death during the next year (0.001). Used directly in the expected gain calculation, and its complement (0.999) is also used as the probability of survival.

input.background: The USGA is reviewing whether four golf ball brands deliver meaningfully different carry performance under tightly controlled hitting conditions before making any broader statements about product comparability. To avoid the usual noise from player-to-player swing differences, the organization used Iron Byron, its robotic golfer, and had it strike 10 balls from each brand, with the order of shots mixed throughout the session. Distance was recorded for every shot, and the brand-specific results are listed in Table 9.3. Although equipment staff are also aware that factors such as ball construction, spin profile, launch behavior, and even market positioning often enter product discussions, this review is focused on whether the observed separation in recorded distances across the four brands is large enough to matter from a standards perspective.

After the first full cycle, HR analytics pulled a random review sample of 600 employees and summarized the realized mix of salary actions in Table 10.2. The commercial team no longer wants a purely straight-line adjustment based only on age and bidder turnout, because recent reviews suggest that value may accelerate or level off for older pieces and that the commercial lift from stronger bidding interest may not stay constant across the full range of lots. At the same time, partners note that hammer prices can also reflect styling, provenance, room momentum, catalog photography, and other deal-specific influences, so they want a practical formula grounded only in the fields already tracked in the historical file. Using the past sale records in Table 12.1, the team wants a fuller pricing rule that allows both age and bidder participation to have curvature and to work together rather than independently.
input.question: Using Table 12.1, write the fitted least-squares pricing equation for auction price $y$ when the valuation rule includes age $x_1$, number of bidders $x_2$, their combined effect, and the separate curvature terms for both $x_1$ and $x_2$.

x1.description: Age of the auction item (in years). Used as the first quantitative predictor in the complete second-order regression model.

x2.description: Number of bidders at the auction. Used as the second quantitative predictor in the complete second-order regression model.

y.description: Auction price of the item (in dollars). This is the response variable predicted by the complete second-order model involving x1, x2, their interaction, and their quadratic terms.

input.background: An antiques auction firm is refining how it explains price formation for grandfather clocks to consignors and category managers. The commercial team has been using age and bidder turnout from prior sales in Table 12.1 to support reserve discussions, but there is concern that a straight-line pricing story may be too simplistic once pieces become especially old or bidding activity becomes unusually light or heavy. Some staff also argue that presentation quality, catalog placement, and room mood matter, although those details were not captured consistently in the historical records. Management now wants to know whether the added complexity from allowing curvature in the effects of the two recorded business drivers is actually warranted before it is built into internal guidance.
input.question: Using Table 12.1, frame the benchmark claim and the competing claim needed to decide whether the age- and bidder-related curvature components provide meaningful added value for explaining auction price, $y$, beyond the simpler version that uses only the basic effects of those two inputs.

Age.description: Age of the antique item (x1), one of the two quantitative predictors whose quadratic term (x1²) is being tested in the hypotheses.

Number_of_Bidders.description: Number of bidders at the auction (x2), the second quantitative predictor whose quadratic term (x2²) is being tested in the hypotheses.

Auction_Price.description: Auction price in dollars (y), the response variable that the second-order regression model aims to predict using the quadratic terms of x1 and x2.

alpha.description: Significance level used for the nested regression F-test.

input.background: An antiques auction house is refining how it explains expected hammer prices to consignors using the historical transactions listed in Table 12.1. The commercial team already uses age and bidder turnout as the main measurable signals when discussing likely price performance, but some specialists argue that the pricing pattern may bend rather than move in a purely straight-line way as pieces get older or as bidding interest changes. Report the comparison result in the usual summary form, including the comparison statistic, the cutoff used for the decision, and the final business conclusion.

x1.description: Age of the antique item (in years), used as a quantitative independent variable in the second-order regression model.

x2.description: Number of bidders at the auction, used as a quantitative independent variable in the second-order regression model.

The analytics group has already run the usual internal pricing-style worksheet on the 25 brands and circulated part of the software output in Figure 12.50. Because these figures may be used in external health and compliance discussions, management is concerned about whether some of the inputs may be overlapping so heavily that the individual directional takeaways become hard to trust.
input.question: Review Figure 12.50 in the context of Table 12.9. Does the output suggest that tar, nicotine, and weight are overlapping enough that the separate contributions reported for these product attributes may be unstable or misleading when explaining carbon monoxide content, $y$?

Nicotine_x2.description: Nicotine content of each cigarette brand (in milligrams), used as predictor x2. The answer notes its negative estimated coefficient as a sign of multicollinearity.

Weight_x3.description: Weight of each cigarette brand (in grams), used as predictor x3. The answer notes its negative estimated coefficient as a sign of multicollinearity.

CarbonMonoxide_y.description: Carbon monoxide content of each cigarette brand (in milligrams), the response variable y in the multiple regression model.

alpha.description: Significance level used in the textbook interpretation of overall model utility.

input.background: A youth-advocacy briefing prepared for public and funding audiences cites several headline figures drawn from field outreach in selected local communities. One of the examples comes from the Bayside East Housing Project in Portland, Maine, where the organization summarizes the situation for 16- and 17-year-olds in a way intended to signal the scale of disengagement from school. Internally, however, staff notes indicate that the local check was based on only a very limited door-to-door count, and that the published message may be read far more broadly and definitively than the underlying field facts can comfortably support. For this item, the published figure was that 25% of the 16- and 17-year-olds in the Portland, Maine, Bayside East Housing Project were out of school; the field note behind that statement says that only eight children were contacted and two were found to be out of school.
input.question: If you were reviewing this Bayside East statement before it appeared in the report, what features of the way the result is presented would you flag as potentially giving readers a distorted impression of the local schooling situation?

sample_size.description: Total number of 16- and 17-year-old children surveyed in the Portland, Maine, Bayside East Housing Project.

children_out_of_school.description: Number of children found to be out of school among those surveyed.

reported_percentage.description: The percentage (25%) reported by CDF as the proportion of 16- and 17-year-olds out of school, critiqued in the answer as misleading due to the small sample size.

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A policy review team is revisiting messaging used in the government-backed report Children out of School in America, which discussed patterns tied to school discipline among school-age children in selected local areas. Leadership is concerned that some headline statements may sound more solid and broadly representative than the underlying field notes actually support. One example from census tract 22 in Columbia, South Carolina, summarized repeat suspensions among secondary-school students using percentage language. The underlying case review for that tract, however, shows that only three children in the entire area were found to fit the repeat-suspension description: one had been suspended twice, and two had been suspended three or more times. The team wants to assess whether the way this finding was presented could mislead readers about scale, stability, or practical meaning.
input.question: For reported result 2, review the statement that among secondary-school students in census tract 22 who had been suspended more than once, 33% had been suspended two times and 67% had been suspended three or more times. Based on the underlying fact pattern, what aspects of this presentation could give decision-makers a distorted impression?

children_suspended_twice.description: Number and reported percentage of children suspended exactly twice in census tract 22 in Columbia, South Carolina.

children_suspended_three_or_more.description: Number and reported percentage of children suspended three or more times in census tract 22 in Columbia, South Carolina.

total_sample_size.description: Total number of children found by CDF who had been suspended more than once in the entire census tract 22; the answer highlights this extremely small sample size as the key source of distortion.

input.background: A child-advocacy organization is preparing messaging for stakeholders about student discipline patterns in several communities and has been drawing from a broader field review of school-age youth. One statement circulated internally concerns the Portland Bayside East Housing Project and is being considered for use in external materials because it sounds straightforward and impactful. Program staff note, however, that neighborhood-level figures can sometimes read more dramatic than the underlying case notes suggest, especially when a statement is converted into a headline-style percentage for funders, partner agencies, or the press. In this instance, the write-up says that 50% of all the secondary-school children who had been suspended more than once had been suspended three or more times, while the supporting notes indicate that the survey actually found two secondary-school children in that area who had been suspended more than once, and one of them had been suspended three or more times.
input.question: If you were reviewing this Portland Bayside East Housing Project statement before it was used in a briefing or public-facing report, what features of the claim would you flag as potentially misleading or likely to give decision-makers the wrong impression?

suspended_children_count.description: Total number of secondary-school children who had been suspended more than once in the Portland Bayside East Housing Project.

suspended_three_or_more.description: Number of children (out of the two suspended) who had been suspended three or more times.

reported_percentage.description: The reported percentage (50%) of suspended children who had been suspended three or more times, derived from 1 out of 2 children.

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A small game studio is documenting the full set of possible display results for a very simple two-step feature in which two coins are tossed and the upward face of each coin is recorded in order. The product team wants a clean way to map every possible sequence a user could see before the feature is added to a rules sheet and internal QA checklist. Even though the mechanic is basic, they want the outcome paths laid out clearly so that no possible recorded sequence is overlooked during review.
input.question: How can a tree diagram be used to show every possible recorded result for this two-coin process, and what are all of the sample points for the experiment?

Coin1.description: Outcome of the first tossed coin, with two possible results: H (Heads) or T (Tails). Used as the first branching level in the tree diagram.

Coin2.description: Outcome of the second tossed coin, with two possible results: H (Heads) or T (Tails). Used as the second branching level in the tree diagram.

output.category: Probability Space Related (e.g., number of states)

Suppose one company is randomly drawn from the set of U.S. businesses that already use diversity training, and its single main stated reason is identified using the categories summarized in Table 3.2 and Table 3.3.
