input.background: A private investor is allocating funds across a small opportunity set of four ventures, with enough capital to back exactly two of them because each one calls for roughly the same commitment. In hindsight, the portfolio office knows that only two of the four will ultimately perform well, while the other two will not work out. Before making the commitment, the investor spends time reviewing founder materials, market chatter, and informal diligence notes in the hope of improving the pick list beyond what a blind choice would deliver, although not all of that work is necessarily actionable. For benchmarking purposes, the investor wants to understand the baseline odds associated with making the two picks without relying on any of the research at all.
input.question: If the two ventures were chosen purely as a blind benchmark from the four available opportunities, what is the chance that the resulting pair would include at least one of the two ventures that eventually turns out to be successful?

total_ventures.description: Total number of ventures available for investment

successful_ventures.description: Number of ventures that will eventually be successful (denoted S1 and S2 in the answer)

failing_ventures.description: Number of ventures that will eventually fail (denoted F1 and F2 in the answer)

ventures_selected.description: Number of ventures randomly selected for investment out of the total four

input.background: A corporate development team is designing a pilot portfolio and has decided that, for governance reasons, the same amount of capital would be committed to each initiative that makes the shortlist. The current pipeline contains 20 business ventures that have all cleared the initial screen. Leadership is not yet concerned with ranking, timing, or allocation differences across the chosen deals; at this stage, they only want to understand the full range of distinct five-venture shortlists that procurement and strategy could legally put forward for review. Other issues such as sector mix, founder quality, and post-investment support will be handled later.
input.question: Given that the pipeline contains 20 eligible ventures and the pilot portfolio must consist of 5 of them, how many different five-venture shortlists are possible?

N.description: Total number of business ventures available for selection.

n.description: Number of ventures to be selected as a sample.

output.category: Probability Space Related (e.g., number of states)

input.background: A game operations team is reviewing a simple six-sided promotional cube used in an in-store activity. The cube is assumed to be balanced so that each face from 1 through 6 is just as likely to appear on a throw. For one campaign rulebook, the team has flagged two trigger conditions for a single throw: A = landing on an even face, and B = landing on a face no greater than 3. Marketing wants to understand how often either trigger would activate and how often both descriptions would apply at the same time, before finalizing the customer-facing wording.
input.question: Based on one throw of this fair six-sided cube, determine the chance that condition A or condition B is triggered, and the chance that a result satisfies both A and B.

A.description: Event A: Toss an even number on a fair die.

B.description: Event B: Toss a number less than or equal to 3 on a fair die.

P_each_outcome.description: Probability of each outcome for a fair die, used in the calculation of P(A ∪ B) and P(A ∩ B).

input.background: A manufacturing operations team is reviewing how much confidence it should place in a screening flag before products are routed for rework or release. Historical line performance suggests that 5% of units coming off the assembly line are actually faulty. For the in-line diagnostic check currently used, when a unit truly has a fault, the system raises a fault indication 92% of the time; when a unit is in acceptable condition, the system clears it as good 96% of the time. Managers note that isolating flagged units is costly, while releasing questionable units can disrupt downstream fulfillment, so they want a clearer read on what a negative screen really means in business terms.
input.question: If the diagnostic test marks a unit as defective, what is the chance that the unit is in fact good?

P(A_c).description: Probability that the product is defective (5% failure rate from the assembly line).

P(B|A).description: Probability that the test indicates good given the product is actually good.

P(B_c|A_c).description: Probability that the test indicates defective given the product is actually defective.

input.background: A nuclear generating station is updating the operating note used by its control room and safety assurance teams for the ventilation air radioactivity protection chain. The current arrangement has five parallel monitoring channels that are built to the same design and are treated as operating separately at the channel level. The plant’s shutdown logic is intentionally conservative: once at least three channels indicate a hazardous air radioactivity condition, the reactor is taken offline automatically. Within each channel, there are three matching sensors, and the channel is treated as having detected the hazardous condition when at least two of those three sensors respond. Engineering records further state that an individual sensor may cease to function at a rate of 0.001 per day, while there is also a channel-level shared upset mechanism that can disable all sensors in the same channel at a rate of 0.0005 per day. Although operators also consider maintenance scheduling, alarm management, and regulatory reporting, this review is only concerned with how dependable the shutdown trigger remains over short operating horizons.
input.question: For planning and assurance purposes, determine how dependable the full shutdown protection arrangement remains after 10, 20, 30, and 40 days of operation, given the voting rules at both the sensor and channel levels.

num_channels.description: Number of identical and statistically independent channels in the monitoring system

channel_threshold.description: Minimum number of channels that must register dangerous radioactivity level for automatic reactor shutdown (k-out-of-n threshold for channels)

num_sensors_per_channel.description: Number of identical sensors in each channel

sensor_threshold.description: Minimum number of sensors that must register dangerous radioactivity level for the channel to register the dangerous level (k-out-of-n threshold for sensors)

sensor_failure_rate.description: Independent failure rate of each sensor in any channel, per day

common_cause_failure_rate.description: Common-cause failure rate of all sensors in a channel, per day

time_t.description: Time points in days at which the reliability calculation is requested.

input.background: An infrastructure team is reviewing the resilience of a power module used in a high-availability installation. The module contains 20 identical power supplies running in active service, and operations policy allows no more than one unit to be out at any time; once 2 of the 20 supplies are down, the module can no longer support service. Field engineers note that when all 20 supplies are healthy, each unit experiences an hourly breakdown tendency of \(\lambda_a\). If one unit has already dropped out, the remaining units carry a heavier burden and each then faces an hourly breakdown tendency of \(\lambda_b\), with \(\lambda_a \leq \lambda_b\). Maintenance can restore any failed supply, and each failed unit is brought back at an hourly repair pace of \(\mu\). Leadership is interested in the chance the module keeps running over a time window \((0,t)\), denoted by \(R(t)\), because this feeds into uptime commitments and spares planning.
input.question: Based on this operating setup, what is the expected length of time the power module will remain in service before it first reaches a service-stopping condition?

n_total.description: Total number of identical active power supplies in the system.

n_min.description: Minimum number of power supplies required for the system to function.

lambda_a.description: Constant failure rate per hour of each power supply when all 20 are operating.

lambda_b.description: Failure rate per hour of each remaining power supply when one power supply has already failed (λ_a ≤ λ_b).

mu.description: Constant repair rate per hour for a failed power supply.

input.background: An operations team is reviewing the resilience of a mission-critical platform that is supported by a bank of 20 identical live power modules. In normal service, the platform can tolerate the loss of only 1 module; once 2 modules are down at the same time, service is considered lost. Under full healthy operation, each module is observed to drop out at a steady rate of \(\lambda_a\) per hour. After the first module goes offline, the remaining active modules are understood to be under greater strain, and each then experiences a steady outage rate of \(\lambda_b\) per hour, with \(\lambda_a \leq \lambda_b\). Any module that goes down is returned to service by maintenance at a steady rate of \(\mu\) per hour. Leadership is interested in the likelihood that the platform can stay continuously available from start-up through a future time window \((0,t)\), while recognizing that field conditions, load redistribution, and maintenance response all matter to day-to-day continuity.
input.question: For planning and service-commitment purposes, using \(\lambda_a=0.0005\), \(\lambda_b=0.004\), and \(\mu=0.5\), what is the expected operating time before this platform first experiences a service-ending loss of power support?

lambda_a.description: Constant failure rate (per hour) of each power supply when all 20 are operating.

lambda_b.description: Constant failure rate (per hour) of each remaining power supply when one power supply has already failed.

mu.description: Constant repair rate (per hour) for a failed power supply.

n_total.description: Total number of identical active power supplies in the system.

n_min_required.description: Minimum number of power supplies required for the system to function (system fails when 2 fail).

input.background: An operations team is reviewing the resilience of a high-availability installation built around 15 interchangeable active power units. Service commitments require that the installation remain in acceptable operating condition as long as at least 14 of those units are available; once 2 of the 15 units are down, the installation is considered out of service. Under normal full-capacity operation, when all 15 units are running, each unit is known to drop out at a constant hourly rate of $\lambda_a$. If one unit has already gone down, the remaining units continue operating but each is then exposed to a constant hourly dropout rate of $\lambda_b$, with $\lambda_a \leq \lambda_b$. Any unit that goes down is sent through a recovery process that returns it to service at a constant hourly rate of $\mu$. Let $R(t)$ denote the chance that the installation stays serviceable for the entire interval $(0,t)$. Although field engineers may also discuss maintenance logistics, load balancing, and vendor response times, management wants the assessment based strictly on these operating rules.
input.question: (a) Based on this setup, what is the expected length of time the installation will remain in service before it first reaches an outage condition?

lambda_a.description: The constant failure rate (per hour) of each power supply when all 15 power supplies are operating.

lambda_b.description: The failure rate (per hour) of each of the 14 remaining power supplies when one power supply has already failed, where λ_a ≤ λ_b.

mu.description: The constant repair rate (per hour) for a failed power supply.

n_total.description: Total number of identical active power supplies in the system.

n_min_required.description: Minimum number of power supplies required for the system to function (system fails when 2 power supplies fail).

input.background: A high-availability operations platform is supported by 15 interchangeable live power modules running in parallel. Service can be maintained as long as at least 14 of the 15 modules remain available, so the platform is considered down once a second module is out of service. Under normal full-capacity operation, each module experiences an hourly outage tendency of $\lambda_a$. After the first module drops out, the remaining modules are assumed to operate under a less favorable stress condition, and each of them then carries an hourly outage tendency of $\lambda_b$, where $\lambda_a \leq \lambda_b$. Any module that is out of service is returned to operation through maintenance at a constant hourly restoration pace of $\mu$. Leadership is interested in the long-run service endurance of this architecture, understood as the average amount of time the platform can be expected to stay up before reaching a shutdown event. Ignore broader issues such as upstream grid events, scheduled maintenance windows, and demand-side curtailment; use only the operating assumptions stated here.
input.question: For this 15-module power design, if $\lambda_a=0.0003$, $\lambda_b=0.005$, and $\mu=0.6$, what is the expected operating time until the platform first becomes unavailable?

lambda_a.description: Constant failure rate per hour for each power supply when all 15 are operating.

lambda_b.description: Constant failure rate per hour for each remaining power supply when one has already failed.

mu.description: Constant repair rate per hour for a failed power supply.

n_total.description: Total number of identical active power supplies in the system.

n_min_required.description: Minimum number of power supplies required for the system to function (system fails when 2 fail).

input.background: A small firm is reviewing compensation records for six employees after a routine payroll benchmarking exercise. The annual gross income figures, recorded in units of $10^5$, are $$ 0.657,0.664,0.655,0.653,0.686,0.661 $$ Most of the entries fall in a very tight band, but the 0.686 figure stands noticeably above the rest. Management wants to know whether this higher value should be treated as a legitimate pay record within normal staff variation or flagged for special review before it is used in internal summaries and budgeting discussions.
input.question: Using the six income records, compute the screening ratio for the 0.686 entry and compare it with the decision cutoff associated with $\alpha=0.05$ for a group of size 6. Based on that comparison, should the 0.686 value be flagged as unusually high?

yearly_gross_income.description: Yearly gross income (in $10^5) of six workers, used to compute the outlier ratio (mean = 0.6627, standard deviation = 0.0121) and test whether the 0.686 value is an outlier.

input.background: A promotional team is assembling 4 giveaway items from a mixed stock of 20 identical units held in one bin. The inventory mix is 5 red, 7 green, 2 black, and 6 white. The items are picked blindly one after another for a single bundle, and once an item is taken it is not put back. Although packaging staff have mentioned other concerns such as visual balance and customer preference, management is currently interested only in how often a bundle ends up showing the full range of available colors.
input.question: If 4 items are selected from this bin under the process described above, what is the chance that the finished bundle contains no repeated color, meaning the 4 chosen items are all different in color?

input.background: A hardware provider is reviewing its support exposure for a newly deployed computer system. Engineering has characterized the operating-life pattern of a unit with the profile $$f(t)=\frac{1}{9,000} e^{-\frac{t}{9,000}}, t \geq 0$$, where $t$ is running time in hours. Commercial teams are less concerned with isolated early breakdowns than with units that survive the initial warranty window but still generate service events before the customer completes the first year of use, since those cases affect post-warranty parts planning, service staffing, and customer retention discussions.
input.question: Based on this operating-life profile, what share of systems should the company expect to break down after the warranty expires at six months (4380 h) but before the end of the first year (8760 h)?
input.data:
$$
R(t)=P(T>t) \quad t \geq 0 .
$$

failure_time_density_mean.description: Mean (θ) of the exponential failure time distribution, used as the parameter in the density function f(t) = (1/9000) * e^(-t/9000).

warranty_end_time.description: Lower bound of the time interval (six months = 4380 hours), representing the end of the warranty period.

first_year_end_time.description: Upper bound of the time interval (one year = 8760 hours), representing the end of the first year.

input.background: A reliability team is running a short qualification check on a new batch of 15 units before release. The trial window lasted 72 h for every unit that remained in operation. During the observation period, 5 units dropped out, with shutdowns recorded at 5, 15, 20, 50, and 68 h, while the other 10 units were still operating when the 72-h program ended. Engineering leadership wants a single steady in-service risk figure for planning spares, warranty messaging, and follow-up screening, even though other practical factors such as handling conditions and batch logistics may also matter.
input.question: Using these trial results, what constant hourly failure intensity should the team use as the baseline estimate for this product line?

failure_times.description: The times (in hours) at which each of the 5 failed units failed during the test period.

num_surviving_units.description: The number of units that survived (did not fail) through the entire 72-hour test period.

test_duration.description: The total duration of the test period in hours, used to calculate operating hours for surviving units.

num_failures.description: The total number of units that failed during the test period, used as the numerator in the failure rate calculation.

input.background: A manufacturer is conducting a planning review for one of its product lines using the last 10 monthly demand readings, recorded as $T_1, T_2, \ldots, T_{10}$. For the purpose of this review, finance and operations agree to treat these 10 monthly figures as separate outcomes generated under the same underlying demand pattern, so that no one month is taken to systematically influence another and each month is viewed as coming from the same demand environment. The business refers to the long-run average monthly demand as $\mu$, and the usual amount of variation around that level as $\sigma$. Although managers may later discuss promotions, customer timing, and channel effects, the current governance question is simply how much protection this assumption gives when the 10-month average is used in planning conversations.
input.question: If the team summarizes the 10 months by the average demand $\bar{T}=\frac{\sum_{i=1}^{10} T_i}{10}$, what guaranteed upper limit can be stated for the chance that this average is more than $3\sigma$ products away from the long-run average demand $\mu$?

monthly_demand_readings.description: The ten monthly demand observations used to form the average demand in the textbook answer.

deviation_threshold.description: The specified absolute-deviation threshold from the long-run mean used in the probability bound.

input.background: A lighting manufacturer is reviewing whether a routine packaging pull is consistent with normal line performance before releasing a shipment to a retail account. Historically, about 90% of bulbs coming off this production stream are saleable with no functional issues, although supervisors note that day-to-day outcomes can still fluctuate because of handling, machine calibration, and other shop-floor conditions. For one spot check, 20 lightbulbs are taken from the batch for a quick quality read, and operations wants to understand how likely it is to see a very strong result in that check.
input.question: If the expected saleable rate remains 90%, what is the chance that this 20-bulb spot check contains at least 18 good lightbulbs?

p_good.description: Probability that a lightbulb is good (90%).

n.description: Sample size, the number of lightbulbs in the random sample.

x_threshold.description: The threshold number of good lightbulbs for which the probability of obtaining at least this many is calculated.

input.background: A life insurer is preparing next year’s catastrophe servicing plan for one town where flood-related exposure is viewed as limited but not zero. The local portfolio currently contains 250 active flood cover contracts. Based on the firm’s internal risk view, the chance that any one contract gives rise to a flood claim during the coming year is being taken as 0.002, and for this planning exercise each contract is treated as operating separately from the others. Operations managers are less interested in the most likely count than in whether claims activity could move beyond the level that their routine workflow comfortably absorbs.
input.question: Using these assumptions for the town’s 250 active policies, what is the chance that flood claim notifications for the coming year end up above 4?

n.description: Number of active flood insurance policies in the town, used as the number of trials in the binomial distribution.

p.description: Estimated probability of a flood claim occurring for any single policy in the coming year.

threshold.description: The threshold number of claims; the problem asks for the probability of receiving more than this number of claims.

input.background: A reliability group is staging 10 identical units in a controlled life test, with all items energized simultaneously at time $t=0$. For planning purposes, engineering is using the usual exponential lifetime assumption for each unit, with a mean time to failure of $\mu=5$ h, and unit-to-unit operation is taken to be independent. The team is especially focused on what happens very early in the run, because first-hour losses drive staffing at the test bench, spare-part positioning, and the threshold for deciding whether an apparent cluster of early failures is still within normal expectations.
input.question: During the opening hour of the test, meaning over the interval $[0,1)$, what is the expected number of units that fail, and what is the corresponding variance of that failure count?

n.description: Number of identical units placed on test at time t=0.

MTTF.description: Mean time to failure (μ) for each unit's exponential life distribution, in hours.

time_interval.description: The time interval [0, 1) in hours during which failures are counted.

input.background: A reliability group is conducting an early-hours endurance check on 10 identical field-replaceable units, all energized at time 0. For planning purposes, the product is being treated under the standard constant failure-rate assumption used in service forecasting, with an average time to failure of 5 h for each unit. The units are regarded as operating independently, so one breakdown does not change the failure behavior of the others. The support team wants a simple expectation for how many incident tickets may arise in a narrow monitoring window rather than over the full test.
input.question: During the interval from 1 h after startup up to, but not including, 2 h, what is the expected number of unit failures, and what is the variance of that failure count?

n.description: Number of identical units placed on test at time t=0.

MTTF.description: Mean time to failure (μ) of each unit's exponential life distribution, in hours.

interval_start.description: Start time of the interval [1, 2) in hours.

interval_end.description: End time of the interval [1, 2) in hours.

input.background: A manufacturer that supplies air-cooling modules for computer systems is reviewing outbound quality risk for a routine customer order. Historical shop-floor tracking indicates that about 3% of units leave production with a defect, and for planning purposes each unit can be treated as behaving on its own rather than being affected by the condition of the others. Operations managers are not especially concerned about a small amount of normal fallout, but they do want to understand the chance that a 100-unit shipment will cross the level at which the receiving team is likely to flag the batch for extra attention. Other factors such as packaging, freight timing, and model mix are being discussed internally, but they are not part of this particular check.
input.question: For a shipment containing 100 cooling units, what is the chance that the number of defective units ends up above 2?

n.description: The number of cooling units in the shipment (sample size).

p_defective.description: The probability that any given cooling unit is defective.

threshold.description: The threshold number of defective units; the problem asks for the probability of more than this many defectives.

input.background: A founder at an early-stage company is running a tightly managed outbound sales day for a newly launched product. Based on past outreach, each prospect call is treated as having the same 20% chance of turning into a confirmed sale, and one call does not affect the next. The founder’s operating target for the day is 5 sales, and capacity allows for no more than 25 calls before the workday ends. Internally, the team is trying to understand whether the sales pace is on track early enough in the day to leave room for follow-up and admin work if the target is reached.
input.question: What is the chance that the founder secures the 5th sale exactly on the 15th call?

p.description: Probability of making a sale (success) on each call.

r.description: Number of successes (sales) needed to achieve the daily goal.

n.description: The specific trial number at which the fifth sale is achieved.

input.background: A company is running a controlled market trial for a new product. In any single customer exposure, the trial can end in exactly m distinct result categories, denoted by s1, …, sm, and the long-run share associated with those categories is p1, …, pm, respectively. The same exposure process is then carried out n times under the same operating conditions, with each run not affecting the others. Let Xi represent the total number of times category si is recorded over the full set of runs, for i = 1, 2, …, m. Teams may later discuss messaging, channel mix, and execution quality, but for this planning exercise the only concern is the pattern of category counts generated by the repeated trial.
input.question: Across the n independent runs, what rule describes the chance of observing any particular combination of counts X1, X2, …, Xm for the m result categories?

n.description: The number of independent repetitions of the experiment.

m.description: The number of possible outcomes of the experiment.

p.description: The probabilities corresponding to each of the m possible outcomes.

X.description: The count of each outcome type si observed across the n independent repetitions, where Xi is the number of outcomes of type si.

input.background: A laboratory that relies on X-ray equipment is reviewing its contingency arrangements for equipment downtime. Under the reliability assumption currently used in its maintenance planning, the number of X-ray machine breakdowns arising in a week is represented by a Poisson pattern with parameter \(\lambda=2\). The site engineering team can handle at most two failed machines within the week using internal resources; whenever the weekly breakdown count is higher than that, the additional repair work must be transferred to an outside specialist contractor. input.question: Based on the 25 recorded attempts, what value of $\hat{p}$ should be used as the best-supported estimate of the underlying success chance $p$, if it is chosen to make the observed 19 successes and 6 failures most plausible?

successes.description: Number of successes observed in the 25 Bernoulli trials.

failures.description: Number of failures observed in the 25 Bernoulli trials.

n.description: Total number of Bernoulli trials conducted.

input.background: A clinic is reviewing the expected short-term performance of a blood-pressure medication before discussing inventory and follow-up scheduling for a small treatment batch. In the next round, 10 patients with elevated blood pressures will receive the same therapy. Based on prior experience with this drug, each individual course is expected to bring a patient’s blood pressure down with likelihood 0.9. Administrators are mainly concerned with whether the overall rollout will look strong enough from an operations standpoint, although they also recognize that patient-specific factors, adherence, and timing of measurement can affect outcomes.
input.question: For this group of 10 treated patients, what is the chance that the medication lowers blood pressure for at least 8 of them?

n.description: Number of patients treated (sample size / number of trials in the binomial setting).

p.description: Probability that the drug successfully lowers blood pressure in an individual patient (probability of success per trial).

k.description: Threshold number of patients who respond successfully; the problem asks for P(X ≥ 8).

input.background: An operations team is reviewing the waiting-time profile of a service process using the grouped records shown in Table 3.3. Managers have been informally claiming that the pattern of times has the kind of steep early drop-off and long tail often seen in memoryless delay behavior, but the quality group wants that claim checked before it is used in planning discussions. The sample contains $N=60$ recorded cases, and for each interval the table already lists both the actual count observed and the count implied by the proposed benchmark pattern. Table A.3 is available as the company’s reference sheet for the final screening step. Although there may be many practical reasons for deviations in particular ranges, the current review is limited to the interval counts already provided.
input.question: Using the interval counts in Table 3.3 and the review cutoff $\alpha=0.1$, calculate the overall discrepancy index $S=\sum_{i=1}^{11} \frac{\left(f_i-E_i\right)^2}{E_i}$ to quantify how far the observed profile is from the proposed benchmark pattern.

f_i.description: Observed frequencies in each cell boundary from the sample data (N=60).

E_i.description: Expected frequencies in each cell boundary under the exponential distribution, computed as E_i = Q_i - Q_{i-1}.

input.background: A printed-circuit-board line is reviewing daily defect records to see whether the way bad soldering points appear on boards still matches the shop-floor assumption used in its quality handbook: flaws are treated as rare, separate mishaps occurring at a fairly steady pace across boards during a day. The grouped day-level results are listed in Table 3.4, where the team has already placed the actual board counts beside the counts implied by that operating assumption. Supervisors are not reopening broader issues such as operator mix, feeder calibration, board complexity, or inspection strictness at this stage; they only want to use the summary in Table 3.4 together with the reference cutoffs in Table A. 3 for a formal check.
input.question: Using the information in Table 3.4 and the review level $\alpha=0.1$, compute the discrepancy score $S$ from the observed frequencies and the corresponding expected frequencies in order to assess whether the daily defect counts remain in line with that rare-independent-occurrence assumption.

observed_frequency.description: Observed frequency (f_i) for each category of number of defective soldering points (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or more) on circuit boards, N=33.

expected_frequency.description: Expected frequency (E_i) under the Poisson distribution for each category of number of defective soldering points (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or more).

alpha.description: Significance level given for the chi-squared goodness-of-fit test.

input.background: A power equipment manufacturer is reviewing after-sales field records for a batch of electric generators and wants to know whether the observed run-life pattern is broadly consistent with the bell-shaped benchmark its reliability team has been using for planning. For this purpose, 100 recorded failure times (in hours) were grouped into the 8 operating-time bands shown in Table 3.5, alongside the corresponding benchmark counts the team would anticipate in each band. The current planning benchmark is based on fitted values of the center and spread, with $\mu=0.122$ and $\sigma=0.011$. Management is less interested in the raw hourly logs than in whether the grouped field experience departs materially from this reference pattern, since warranty provisioning, spare-parts staging, and service messaging may all be affected.
input.question: Using Table 3.5, compute the overall discrepancy score $S=\sum_{i=1}^8 \frac{\left(f_i-E_i\right)^2}{E_i}$ so the reliability team can compare the observed band counts with the benchmark profile.

f_i.description: Observed frequencies for each of the 8 intervals of failure times.

E_i.description: Expected frequencies for each of the 8 intervals under the assumed normal distribution.

input.background: A small business is reviewing front-desk staffing expectations for short operating windows during the day. Based on past switchboard records, inbound phone activity is treated as occurring unpredictably but at a fairly steady pace, averaging 0.5 calls per minute. Managers are less concerned with occasional spikes than with whether routine five-minute stretches remain manageable without adding backup coverage.
input.question: For a randomly selected five minute period, what is the chance that the business receives no more than three incoming calls?

call_rate.description: Rate of phone call arrivals, 0.5 calls per minute, used to compute the Poisson parameter λ for the given time period.

time_period.description: The length of the time period in minutes over which the probability is calculated.

threshold.description: The maximum number of calls (not more than 3) used as the upper bound in the cumulative Poisson probability calculation.

input.background: A manufacturing operations group is reviewing whether the pattern of defect counts across inspected cells aligns with the routine baseline used in internal quality reporting. The summary in Table 3.4 covers 33 cells and 56 total defectives, and the benchmark side of that table has already been prepared from the current operating assumption. To support an exception review, the team also assembled the side-by-side cumulative comparison shown in Table 3.6 and intends to compare the largest gap with the reference values in Table A.4 under a chosen tolerance level $\alpha$. Before any decision is communicated upward, supervisors want a clear explanation of how the cumulative proportions in Table 3.6 were produced from the defect-count categories and the benchmark pattern.
input.question: Using Table 3.4 together with the entries shown in Table 3.6, describe how to obtain each value of $F_n(x)$ and $F_0(x)$ for the categories 0, 1, 2, 3, and 4 or more defective items.

Number_of_defective.description: Number of defective items per observation (d), used as the discrete values at which F_n(x) and F_0(x) are evaluated.

Observed_frequency.description: Observed frequency (f_i) for each defective count category. Cumulated and divided by N=33 to compute the empirical CDF F_n(x).

lambda.description: Estimated Poisson parameter λ=1.7, used to compute the theoretical Poisson probabilities P(d) and hence the theoretical CDF F_0(x).

Fn_x.description: Cumulative observed relative frequency F_n(x) for each category of number of defectives (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or more), computed from the observed frequencies.

F0_x.description: Cumulative theoretical (Poisson) distribution F_0(x) for each category of number of defectives (0, 1, 2, 3, 4 or more).

input.background: A reliability review is being conducted for a system whose breakdown behavior has been described by the supplier as occurring at a steady pace of $\lambda=0.20$ failures per day. The engineering team has compiled 10 observed failure times, in days, and summarized in Table 3.8 how the accumulated share of observed failures compares with the accumulated share implied by that service claim at each recorded time point. The team will use this comparison as part of a routine 5\% quality-screening check before deciding whether the stated failure pattern is still a reasonable representation of field performance. Table A.4 provides the reference cutoffs used internally for this kind of review. Although maintenance conditions, operator handling, and shipment batches have also been discussed, the current check should rely only on the information already presented in Table 3.8 and Table A.4.
input.question: From Table 3.8, what is the single largest gap $D_n$ between the observed and claimed cumulative patterns, and from Table A.4, what cutoff $d_{n,\alpha}$ applies when there are 10 failure records and the review is conducted at the 5\% level?

input.background: A community mobility and recreation team collected feedback from 395 individuals while reviewing potential demand for bicycle-related programming and infrastructure. For planning purposes, respondents were grouped by age band and whether they indicated interest in riding a bicycle. The resulting summary is shown in Table 3.10, and Table 3.11 provides the reference counts used in the internal review. Although staff have also discussed issues such as weather, neighborhood access, and lifestyle differences, the current decision note is focused only on whether stated bicycle interest appears to shift across the age segments already reported.
input.question: Using Table 3.10 together with the review benchmark in Table 3.11, and applying the organization’s usual 5% decision standard, should the team treat willingness to ride a bicycle as varying by age group, or as broadly similar across the age categories?

Interest_Age_Contingency_Table.description: Observed counts from the contingency table cross-classifying interest in riding a bicycle (Variable A: Yes/No) by age group (Variable B: 15-20, 21-30, 31-40, 41-65). alpha.description: Significance threshold used for the independence decision.

input.background: A production team is reviewing the early performance consistency of a newly launched product before deciding what range of average field results should be communicated internally. From a pilot run of 25 units, the recorded average came out to be $\bar{X}=50$, and the observed variance was $\sigma^2=16$. For this review, the team has already pulled the reference value from Table A. 2 in Appendix A, namely $t_{\frac{\alpha}{2}, n-1}=t_{.975,24}=2.064$. Although engineers have also raised side issues such as packaging adjustments and supplier calibration, management wants the current assessment to rely only on these sample results and the cited table entry.
input.question: Using the available sample summary, what range should the team report as the likely band for the product’s underlying average level, expressed as the 95\% confidence limit for $\mu$?

X.description: The new product measurement variable, with sample mean X̄=50, variance σ²=16, and sample size n=25, used to construct the 95% confidence interval for the population mean μ.

input.background: A company’s quality team is reviewing mixed stock that has already been received into one shared inventory pool, so individual units are no longer being discussed supplier-by-supplier on the warehouse floor. Procurement notes show that the current pool is made up of shipments from four vendors: A accounts for 60% of units, B for 20%, C for 5%, and D for 15%. Historical incoming-quality records also suggest that the share of units later found to be faulty differs across sources: 5% for A, 3% for B, 2% for C, and 8% for D. Managers are less interested in the overall reject level here than in tracing likely source responsibility once a bad unit turns up, since supplier conversations and recovery actions depend on that attribution.
input.question: If one item is pulled from inventory and it turns out to be defective, what is the probability that this item came from supplier B?

inventory_percentage.description: Respective percentages of total inventory from suppliers A, B, C, and D, used as prior probabilities in Bayes' rule.

defect_rate.description: Defect rates for lots from suppliers A, B, C, and D, used as likelihoods in Bayes' rule.

input.background:
An operations review is being prepared for a process stream whose normal center point and routine consistency have not yet been documented. For an initial check, the team pulled 16 consecutive recorded readings from the line:
$$
\begin{array}{l|l|l|l}
\hline 16.16 & 9.33 & 12.96 & 11.49 \\

\hline 7.75 & 15.55 & 3.58 & 11.34 \\

\hline
\end{array}

input.question: Using these 16 recorded values, what is the arithmetic average for the batch, and what is the variance calculated from this same set of observations?

X.description: A random sample of size n=16 drawn from a normal distribution with unknown mean and standard deviation, used to compute the sample mean and sample variance.

input.background:

\hline

Management wants the note to reflect both the observed spread in this pilot run and the appropriate small-sample reference factor used in the company’s two-sided review template when the long-run level and spread are both unknown.

X.description: Random sample of size n=16 drawn from a normal distribution with unknown mean and standard deviation, used to compute the sample standard deviation S=3.313.

confidence_level.description: Confidence level used for the t-based interval in the textbook answer.

input.background:

The long-run center and natural variability of this characteristic have not yet been formally established, but the engineering team is comfortable treating readings from this source as coming from a single well-behaved process. To support an internal planning discussion, 16 routine observations were pulled from recent output records:

\end{array}
$$
Management is less interested in any single reading than in the likely range for the process’s underlying typical level, since that range will be used in downstream target-setting and stakeholder communication.
input.question: Based on these 16 observed values, what interval should the team report as a 95% range of plausible values for the process’s underlying average level, $\mu$?

The answer uses the sample mean (10.20), sample standard deviation (3.313), and sample size (16) computed from these values to construct the 95% confidence interval for μ.

input.background: A team is reviewing the launch performance of a standardized outreach program that was deployed to 100 eligible contacts. Of these, 25 produced the target response and 75 did not. input.background: A field support team is reviewing uptime commitments for a communications package made up of three separately sourced modules: a transmitting unit, a receiving unit, and a processing unit. Based on vendor service records, the transmitter is expected to experience issues at a steady rate of $\lambda_T=0.002$ per hour, the receiver at $\lambda_R=0.005$ per hour, and the processor at $\lambda_P=0.008$ per hour. The team is preparing guidance for a 25-hour continuous mission window and wants a quick sense of component-level dependability before discussing the package as a whole. Although procurement is also comparing maintenance burdens across all three modules, the immediate concern is whether the listening side of the system can reasonably be expected to stay available throughout the planned operating period.
input.question: For the 25-hour mission window, what is the chance that the receiving unit remains operational for the entire period?

lambda_R.description: Hourly failure rate of the receiving unit.

t.description: Mission duration in hours.

input.background: An operations team is reviewing the service continuity of a field-deployed communications setup that depends on three separate components working in their assigned roles: a transmitting unit, a receiving unit, and a processing unit. Based on supplier maintenance records, the transmitter is associated with a steady breakdown tendency of $\lambda_T=0.002$ per hour, the receiver with $\lambda_R=0.005$ per hour, and the processor with $\lambda_P=0.008$ per hour. The upcoming assignment is expected to last 25 h, and management wants a quick component-level readout before discussing the overall robustness of the full setup.
input.question: For the 25-hour assignment, what is the chance that the processing unit remains in working condition for the entire mission?

t.description: Mission duration in hours for which the reliability is calculated.

The setup depends on three separate pieces working continuously over the entire window: a transmitting unit, a receiving unit, and a processing unit. Based on service records, the transmitter experiences breakdowns at a steady rate of $\lambda_T=0.002$ per hour, the receiver at $\lambda_R=0.005$ per hour, and the processor at $\lambda_P=0.008$ per hour. For planning purposes, the team is treating these three sources of failure as unrelated to one another and is ignoring other practical issues such as operator error, power loss, and maintenance delays.
input.question: For this 25-hour mission, what is the probability that the full communication system remains operational for the entire assignment?

λ_T.description: Constant failure rate of the transmitting unit, per hour.

λ_R.description: Constant failure rate of the receiving unit, per hour.

λ_P.description: Constant failure rate of the processing unit, per hour.

input.background: An operations team is reviewing a three-unit backup configuration built so that service can continue as long as at least one unit is still functioning. Each of the 3 units is expected to perform successfully with reliability 0.95, and the overall service continuity for the arrangement has been summarized as $$R=1-(1-0.95)^3=0.9999$$. Although managers are satisfied with the headline continuity figure, maintenance planning also requires a clear rule for identifying the moment when the entire arrangement is considered to have gone out of service.
input.question: If the failure time of the ith unit is denoted by $T_i$, how should the failure time of the full three-unit backup arrangement be expressed?

lambda_1.description: Failure-rate input for component 1 in the parallel-system MTTF formula.

lambda_2.description: Failure-rate input for component 2 in the parallel-system MTTF formula.

lambda_3.description: Failure-rate input for component 3 in the parallel-system MTTF formula.

input.background: An operations team is reviewing the uptime profile of a service architecture built with redundant units so that the overall service can keep running as long as at least one unit remains available. In a simple illustration currently used in internal materials, the setup has 3 independent units, each with an availability level of 0.95 over the planning horizon, which gives an overall service availability of $$R=1-(1-0.95)^3=0.9999$$. Leadership now wants to move beyond that single-horizon snapshot and describe how the platform’s continuity behaves over elapsed operating time when each unit is assumed to wear out at its own steady pace, denoted by $\lambda_i$.
input.question: Under that time-based operating assumption, what expression should the team use for the service continuity curve of the redundant system as a function of time when the independent units each have a constant wear-out rate $\lambda_i$?

lambda_i.description: Constant failure rate of each independent component i in the parallel system, used as a parameter in the exponential failure time distribution.

t.description: Time variable representing the operating time in the reliability function R(t).

R(t).description: System reliability function of the parallel system, representing the probability that the system is operational at time t.

n.description: Number of independent components in the parallel system; in the specific background example n=3.

input.background: A reliability review is being prepared for an engineered setup that uses a parallel arrangement of $n$ identical units. The design intent is to preserve overall service as long as the configuration still has at least one unit operating. For planning purposes, the units are treated as independent in operation, and each one is assumed to deteriorate according to the same constant rate $\lambda$. The team wants a compact expression it can reference when discussing expected service continuity over an operating period of length $t$, without bringing in secondary issues such as inspections, repairs, or external disruptions.
input.question: Under these assumptions, what is the probability that the full parallel setup remains in service at time $t$, written in terms of $n$ and $\lambda$?

n.description: Number of identical and independent components in the parallel system.

lambda.description: Constant failure rate of each identical component.

t.description: Time variable over which system reliability is evaluated.

R(t).description: Reliability of the entire parallel system at time t.

input.background: An airline’s fleet risk team is reviewing a four-engine aircraft platform used on routes where dispatch continuity and safe recovery capability are both commercially important. The airframe carries four engines in total, with two mounted on each wing, and operating guidance indicates that the aircraft can still complete a safe landing provided at least three engines remain available through the mission window. For planning purposes, engineering has assigned the same mission-long success rate to each engine, $R_e=0.997$, and maintenance records are being treated as showing no carryover effect from one engine’s performance to another during the same mission. Although weather, crew action, and airport conditions also matter in real operations, management wants this review to isolate propulsion availability only.
input.question: Under these assumptions, what overall probability should operations report for the aircraft successfully getting through the mission with enough engine availability to make the landing?

R_e.description: Reliability of each individual engine for the duration of a mission.

n_engines.description: Total number of engines on the aircraft.

min_engines_required.description: Minimum number of functioning engines required for the aircraft to land successfully.

input.background: An operations team is reviewing a protected flow-control arrangement used in a long-duration installation. The setup has two identical valves, with one held in reserve and brought into service only if needed. For planning purposes, engineering treats each valve as having a steady loss rate of $\lambda=10^{-5}$ failures/hours over the period of interest. The transfer mechanism is highly dependable but not perfect: the probability $\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{s}}$ that switch $S$ successfully brings the standby valve online is 0.995. The team is preparing an annual service-risk summary and wants to ignore unrelated concerns such as inspection scheduling, staffing, and procurement delays.
input.question: Based on these assumptions, what is the probability that this protected valve arrangement is still able to perform its function through $\mathrm{t}=8760 \mathrm{~h}$, that is, over one full year?

lambda.description: Constant failure rate of each identical valve, in failures per hour.

p_s.description: Probability that the switch S will activate the standby valve.

t.description: Time in hours (one year) at which the system reliability is evaluated.

input.background: An operations team is reviewing the resilience of a fluid-control arrangement used in a continuous-service setting. The setup relies on two interchangeable valves arranged so that one unit operates first and the second is held in reserve until needed. Each valve has the same steady breakdown tendency of $\lambda=10^{-5}$ failures/hours, and when the first unit stops working, the transfer device $S$ is expected to bring the reserve valve online with probability $\mathrm{p}_{\mathrm{s}}=0.995$. Although maintenance crews note that field conditions, wear history, and inspection quality can all influence real-world performance, management wants a baseline lifecycle figure for this identical-valve configuration under the stated assumptions.
input.question: For this arrangement with identical valves, what average operating lifetime should be used for the system before the service is ultimately lost?

lambda.description: Constant failure rate of each identical valve, in failures per hour.

p_s.description: Probability that the switch S will successfully activate the standby valve.

input.background: An operations engineering team is reviewing the short-horizon service continuity of a mission-critical assembly built with three identical modules running in parallel. Under normal conditions, all three modules are active and the workload is divided evenly among them. If one module drops out, the remaining two continue carrying the demand by splitting the work between themselves; if another module is then lost, the last remaining module must carry the entire demand alone. The assembly is considered unavailable only when all three modules have stopped functioning. For this design review, the team is using the following field assumptions for how quickly an individual module tends to drop out under each operating state: when all three modules are active, the per-module rate is λ₀; when only two modules remain and each is carrying half of the total demand, the per-module rate is λₕ; and when only one module remains and is carrying the full demand, the rate is λf. Management is less interested in long technical derivations than in a practical statement about whether this architecture can stay online through the planned operating window.
input.question: For the three-module setup described above, what is the chance that the assembly is still operating at the 10-hour mark if λ₀=0.001/hour, λₕ=0.005/hour, and λf=0.05/hour?

t.description: Time point (in hours) at which the system reliability is evaluated.

λ₀.description: Constant failure rate (per hour) of a unit when all three units are operational.

λₕ.description: Constant failure rate (per hour) of each of the two surviving units sharing half of the total load.

λf.description: Constant failure rate (per hour) of a unit operating at full load.

input.background: An operations team is reviewing a three-module redundancy arrangement used to keep a critical service running. Under normal conditions, all three modules are active and the work is spread evenly across them. If one module drops out, the remaining two continue by splitting the demand between themselves; if only one module is left, it must carry the full burden alone. The service is considered down only when all three modules have ceased operating. Engineering notes indicate that the per-module breakdown pace is 0.001 while all three modules are running together, 0.005 for each remaining module after one module has already failed and the load is shared between two, and 0.05 for the last surviving module when it is operating alone at full burden. Management is less interested in the technical mechanics than in how long this configuration can typically be expected to keep the service available, recognizing that maintenance practices, environmental stress, and restart procedures may matter in practice but are outside the scope of this review.
input.question: Based on this three-module setup and the operating-rate assumptions above, what is the expected time until the service is no longer available?

λ₀.description: Constant failure rate of a unit when all three units are operational in the shared-load parallel system.

λₕ.description: Constant failure rate of each of the two surviving units sharing half of the total load.

λf.description: Constant failure rate of a unit at full load (single surviving unit carrying the entire load).

input.background: An operations team is reviewing the resilience of a protected power architecture used in a critical installation. The design uses eight identical active power-supply modules running in parallel, and service can continue as long as at least seven of the eight remain available. In other words, once two of the eight modules are out at the same time, the installation is considered down. While all eight modules are healthy, each module experiences a constant hourly loss tendency of λa. After the first module drops out, the remaining modules may be under greater stress, so each of those units is then taken to have a constant hourly loss tendency of λb, with λa ≤ λb. Any module that is out of service can be returned to operation at a constant hourly restoration rate μ. Leadership is interested in the chance that the installation stays continuously available over the interval (0, t), denoted by R(t), and ultimately in the average time until service is first lost. For internal tracking, the engineering note reduces the operating situation to three condition levels: Condition 0: all 8 modules available; Condition 1: 7 modules available; Condition 2: more than 1 module unavailable and the installation cannot operate. At startup, the system begins fully healthy, so P0(0)=1 and P1(0)=P2(0)=0.
input.question: Using that three-condition representation, set up the time-based balance equations that describe how the installation moves among Condition 0, Condition 1, and Condition 2.

λa.description: Constant failure rate per hour for each power supply when all eight are operating.

λb.description: Failure rate per hour for each remaining power supply when one has already failed (λa ≤ λb).

μ.description: Constant repair rate per hour for a failed power supply.

number_of_power_supplies.description: Total number of identical active power supplies in the system, used to determine transition rates (8λa from State 0, 7λb from State 1).

input.background: An operations team is reviewing a planned upkeep program for a critical asset that is pulled from service and returned to a like-new condition on a regular schedule. The reset happens every T units of operating time, so the asset effectively starts over at T, 2T, and so on. From a business standpoint, the asset is considered continuously available through calendar time t only when it gets through each completed service window before t without breaking down and then also remains running during the unfinished portion of the current window. For a newly restored asset, engineering has characterized the run-length pattern by f(t) = lambda^2 t e^(-lambda t) for t > 0 with lambda > 0. Management wants a compact way to describe how this scheduled service policy changes in-service performance over time.
input.question: Under this fixed-interval restoration program, what formula should be used for the probability that the asset is still operating at calendar time t when service is performed every T time units, and what is the corresponding expected calendar time until the first breakdown under the program?

f(t).description: Failure time probability density function of the system, used to derive the reliability function R(t) and subsequently the system reliability under PM and MTTFF.

T.description: The fixed time interval at which the system is periodically restored to 'as good as new'. Used throughout the answer to define PM cycles and compute R_M(t) and MTTFF.

input.background: A game studio is reviewing a simple promotional mechanic used in a tabletop-style app. In one play, a fair six-sided die is rolled twice. The product team tracks three rule triggers for the same play sequence: A: the first roll shows an odd number; B: the second roll shows an even number; C: the two rolls add up to seven. Although the mechanic is intentionally simple, the team wants to know whether these checkpoints can be discussed separately in player-facing documentation or whether the way they occur together creates hidden dependence.
input.question: Based on this two-roll setup, determine whether the three triggers A, B, and C can truly be treated as unrelated to one another. If not, demonstrate why that business assumption fails.

A.description: Event that the first toss is odd; probability P{A} = 1/2, used in checking independence.

B.description: Event that the second toss is even; probability P{B} = 1/2, used in checking independence.

C.description: Event that the total number of spots equals seven; probability P{C} = 1/6, used in checking independence.

A_intersect_B_intersect_C.description: Joint probability of events A, B, and C occurring simultaneously; P{A ∩ B ∩ C} = 1/12, compared with P{A}·P{B}·P{C} to check independence.

input.background: A production supervisor is reviewing a mixed lot of 120 finished pieces before release to downstream handling. Based on the latest sizing check, 40 pieces fall above the allowable range, 20 fall below it, and the remaining 60 are within specification. For a quick spot-check, two pieces are taken sequentially from the lot and the first piece is not returned before the second is selected. Operations is interested in how often this kind of two-pick check would end up pulling items with matching status, even though other factors such as surface finish and packaging priority are not being considered here.
input.question: For this two-piece spot-check, what is the chance that the two selected units end up in the same size-status group?

total_units.description: Total number of units in the batch.

oversized_units.description: Number of oversized units in the batch.

undersized_units.description: Number of undersized units in the batch.

conforming_units.description: Number of units conforming to specification in the batch.

sample_size.description: Number of units drawn at random without replacement.

input.background: A technical operations team is planning a readiness campaign for a special device before a high-visibility deployment window. Based on prior engineering assessments, any single launch attempt has a 0.5 chance of working as intended, and one attempt does not affect the outcome of the next. Managers are less concerned with the result of any one try than with how many attempts should be budgeted so that the overall campaign is very unlikely to end without at least one working launch. Other issues such as crew scheduling, reset time, and reporting procedures are being handled separately.
input.question: For planning purposes, what is the smallest number of launch attempts the team should allow so that the chance of getting at least one successful launch is no less than 0.99?

p_success.description: The probability of a successful launching of the special device in a single trial.

p_target.description: The target minimum probability of at least one successful launching over n trials.

output.category: Minimum Sample Size Required to Achieve a Specified Probability

input.background: A simple trial process is being reviewed in which the same fair coin is flipped repeatedly and the sequence is stopped as soon as the first heads result appears. For this quick check, no further complications are being introduced beyond the standard assumption that the coin is fair and each flip proceeds in the usual way.
input.question: Under this setup, what is the chance that the process is concluded on or before the sixth toss?

p.description: Probability of heads on a single toss of the fair coin.

n.description: Maximum number of tosses (the experiment must end on or before this toss).

input.background:
A local consumer-goods retailer is reviewing a household lifestyle snapshot from a community outreach survey covering 1000 families. The commercial team is using the results to get a rough sense of how often certain durable purchases appear together when planning neighborhood promotions, although they recognize that income, housing type, and family size may also shape ownership patterns. The survey summary below records whether families reported having a television set and whether they reported having a car:
$$
\begin{array}{lll} 
& \text { TV } & \text { No TV } \\
\text { Car } & 115 & 245 \\
\text { No Car } & 380 & 260
\end{array}
$$
input.question: Based on this community snapshot, what share of families would the retailer treat as households that already have both a TV set and a car?

TV_Car.description: Number of families that have both a TV set and a car.

Total_families.description: Total number of families surveyed in the community.

input.background:
A local retailer is reviewing household access to two durable consumer goods in a community before planning bundled promotions and outreach priorities. As part of a market scan, 1000 families were checked for whether they currently have a television set, a car, both, or neither. The field summary is:
$$
\begin{array}{lll} 
& \text { TV } & \text { No TV } \\
\text { Car } & 115 & 245 \\
\text { No Car } & 380 & 260
\end{array}
$$
Management is less interested in the split across every cell than in the overall share of households already touched by at least one of these two product categories, since that affects channel reach, financing offers, and future cross-sell strategy.
input.question: Based on this community snapshot, what portion of families should the retailer treat as already having at least one of the two items—a television set, a car, or both?

Car_TV.description: Number of families that have both a car and a TV set.

Car_NoTV.description: Number of families that have a car but no TV set.

NoCar_TV.description: Number of families that have a TV set but no car.

Total_families.description: Total number of families surveyed in the community.

input.background: A marketing team is testing a simple three-step customer-engagement mechanic built around a balanced two-sided token, where each side is equally likely to appear. In one trial run, the token is flipped three times in sequence to determine whether a participant qualifies for a small reward tier. Operations staff already know that the first flip came up on the head side, and they want to assess the participant’s remaining path to qualification before documenting the rule in the campaign notes.
input.question: Given that the first flip was a head, what is the chance that the three-flip sequence ends with heads showing on at least two of the three flips overall?

head_probability.description: Probability of heads on each fair toss.

condition_first_toss.description: Condition that the first toss is a head.

threshold_heads.description: Minimum total number of heads in the event of interest.

input.background: A founder at an early-stage start-up is personally handling outbound sales and is tracking performance in terms that investors and the commercial team can easily understand. For this product, each customer call is treated as a fresh opportunity, and past call results are not assumed to affect the next one. Historically, the founder closes a deal on 20% of calls. Because of time and staffing limits, no more than 25 calls can be placed in a day, and the operating target for the day is to bring in 5 completed sales. The team is less interested in raw call volume by itself than in whether the day’s target tends to be reached relatively early or only after a long stretch of outreach.
input.question: From a planning perspective, what is the chance that the founder reaches the 5-sale daily target sometime between the 15th and the 20th call, inclusive?

p.description: Probability of making a sale on each call (probability of success per trial).

r.description: Number of sales (successes) needed to achieve the daily goal, defining the 5th success in the negative binomial distribution.

lower_bound.description: Lower bound of the number of trials in the probability calculation P(15 ≤ Y ≤ 20).

upper_bound.description: Upper bound of the number of trials in the probability calculation P(15 ≤ Y ≤ 20).

input.background: A youth program is organising 200 participants into two activity cohorts of the same size for operational reasons. The intake is perfectly balanced overall, with 100 boys and 100 girls enrolled. Assignment to the two cohorts is to be made without any special adjustment for gender, even though coordinators would ideally like both cohorts to end up with the same internal mix. Apart from that balance concern, there is no difference between the two cohorts in capacity or schedule.
input.question: If the 200 participants are split into two cohorts of equal size under this setup, what is the chance that both cohorts end up with an exact 50-50 split of boys and girls?

boys_count.description: Total number of boys in the group, used in the combination calculation C(100,50).

girls_count.description: Total number of girls in the group, used in the combination calculation C(100,50).

total_count.description: Total number of children (boys + girls = 200), used in the combination calculation C(200,100).

group_size.description: Size of each of the two equal groups (200/2 = 100), used as the selection size in C(200,100) and the equal split target (50 boys and 50 girls per group).

input.background: A document services vendor is reviewing the uptime expectations it communicates for one of its fax units used in small-office settings. Based on field experience for this model, the service team states that a machine of this type has a 0.80 chance of getting through 720 hours of operation without any breakdown. Although technicians note that actual usage patterns, paper quality, and maintenance habits can vary from customer to customer, management wants a single underlying pace of malfunction for planning service parts, support commitments, and replacement expectations.
input.question: Using this service expectation, what underlying breakdown pace, denoted by $\lambda$, is implied for the fax machine?

survival_time.description: The time period (in hours) during which the fax machine survives without failure.

survival_probability.description: The probability that the fax machine survives the given time period without failure.

input.background: A regional operations team is reviewing service continuity expectations for an older fax unit that is still used for document transmission in a few back-office workflows. Engineering notes describe its breakdown pattern as steady over time rather than varying by age, usage stage, or recent uptime. Based on historical reliability records, the unit is expected to remain in service for 720 hours without interruption with probability 0.80. Managers are less concerned with the absolute age of the device than with the risk over the next stretch of use once it has already made it through part of the work cycle.
input.question: If the fax machine is confirmed to still be operating after 600 hours, what is the chance that it will continue operating through 800 hours?

survival_time_T.description: The random variable representing the time (in hours) until the fax machine fails, following an exponential distribution with constant failure rate λ.

survival_probability_720.description: The probability that the machine survives for 720 hours without failure, P(T > 720) = 0.80, used to determine λ.

conditioning_time.description: The time (in hours) at which the machine is known to still be functioning, used as the conditioning event T > 600.

target_time.description: The time (in hours) for which we want to determine the probability of the machine still functioning, i.e., P(T > 800 | T > 600).

input.background: An operations team is reviewing the field reliability profile of a fax unit that is being used in a steady, round-the-clock document workflow. Based on historical service experience, the unit is treated as having the same breakdown tendency throughout its life rather than becoming noticeably more or less fragile over time. Internal planning notes indicate that the chance the machine is still running without any failure after 720 hours of use is 0.80. Although technicians know that paper quality, cleaning habits, and office environment can also affect performance, management wants a simple risk estimate tied to the current uptime milestone.
input.question: If the machine has already remained operational through 720 hours, what is the chance that it breaks down at some point before reaching 900 hours of use?

survival_probability_720.description: The probability that the fax machine survives for 720 hours without failure, used to determine the constant failure rate λ.

t1.description: The time (in hours) at which the machine is known to be functioning (conditioning event T ≥ 720).

t2.description: The time (in hours) by which the probability of failure is to be computed (T ≤ 900).

input.background: The failure rate for a hydraulic component is given as $$h(t)=\frac{t}{t+1} \quad t>0$$ where $t$ is in years.
input.question: Determine the reliability function $R(t)$.

h(t).description: The failure rate (hazard function) for the hydraulic component, given as h(t) = t/(t+1) for t > 0, used to derive the reliability function R(t).

input.background: A manufacturer of heavy equipment is reviewing the service-life profile of one hydraulic component used in field operations. Engineering notes describe the component’s year-by-year breakdown tendency through the function $$h(t)=\frac{t}{t+1} \quad t>0$$ where $t$ measures time in years since installation. Operations managers are less concerned with the full formula itself than with turning it into a single planning number for warranty budgeting, spare-parts positioning, and long-run maintenance scheduling. Assume the component is observed from new and that this relationship appropriately represents how its risk evolves over time.
input.question: Based on this service-life profile, what is the component’s expected operating life before failure, expressed as its MTTF?

h(t).description: The failure rate (hazard rate) function for the hydraulic component, defined as h(t) = t/(t+1) for t > 0, used to compute the MTTF.

input.background: A vehicle manufacturer is reviewing the service-risk assumptions behind its 18-month new-car guarantee. Finance and after-sales teams have aligned on a commercial rule that the program remains acceptable only if customer returns tied to in-service breakdowns stay at or below 5% during the covered period. For planning purposes, the reliability team is working under the simplifying view that the month-to-month breakdown tendency does not build up or ease off over time, even though actual field experience can also be affected by driver behavior, climate, and maintenance habits.
input.question: Under that planning assumption, what is the highest ongoing breakdown pace the manufacturer can allow while still supporting the 18-month guarantee target?

guarantee_period.description: Known survival time and guarantee period, in months.

max_return_rate.description: Maximum failure probability during the 18-month guarantee.

input.background: A classroom teacher is putting together a small 6-student project team from a roster of 22 children. The class currently includes 10 girls and 12 boys. Because the activity is meant to move quickly, the teacher plans to pull names without using any balancing rule or adjustment afterward. Some parents have informally commented that, with numbers this close, the team will probably come out evenly split anyway, while the teacher notes that classroom chemistry, participation styles, and seating arrangements are not part of the selection process.
input.question: If the 6 places are filled purely by chance from this class, should the teacher treat an even mix of 3 girls and 3 boys as a likely outcome?

girls_count.description: Number of girls in the class, used to compute the combination C(10,3).

boys_count.description: Number of boys in the class, used to compute the combination C(12,3).

girls_selected.description: Number of girls to be chosen in the scenario of interest (3 girls and 3 boys).

boys_selected.description: Number of boys to be chosen in the scenario of interest (3 girls and 3 boys).

input.background: A vehicle manufacturer has structured its after-sales policy around an 18-month guarantee, with the commercial expectation that the share of newly sold cars coming back because of breakdown-related issues should not exceed 5% during that period. Internal engineering teams also describe the pattern of breakdown risk over a car’s life as remaining steady rather than ramping up or easing off over time. As the company reviews longer-horizon service exposure, managers want to understand what this means for cars that have already made it through the guarantee window without trouble.
input.question: For a newly sold car that is still operating normally at 18 months, what is the chance that it will experience its first failure at some point within three years of sale?

T.value: Time to failure of a car, with constant failure rate (exponential distribution)
T.description: Random variable representing the time to failure of a new car, following an exponential distribution (constant failure rate).

guarantee_period.description: The guarantee period of 18 months (1.5 years), used both as the conditioning threshold (T ≥ 1.5) and to determine the failure rate from the return rate assumption.

max_return_rate.description: The assumed maximum proportion of new cars returned within the guarantee period, i.e., P(T ≤ 1.5) = 0.05, used to determine the failure rate λ.

time_horizon.description: The time horizon of 3 years, used in the event T ≤ 3 for computing the conditional probability of failure.

input.background: A network equipment supplier is reviewing the early-service reliability of a communication system component before a deployment batch is released. Engineering has established that the operating life of a unit, measured in hours, follows the profile $$f(t)=\frac{2 e^t}{\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{t}}+1\right)^2} \quad \mathrm{t}>0.$$ For a qualification run, $n=30$ units are switched on together at time $\mathrm{t}=0$, and each unit’s performance is assumed not to affect any other unit. Although field teams are also concerned with installation practices and maintenance scheduling, management is currently focused only on how many units are likely to drop out very early in operation.
input.question: For this 30-unit startup batch, what is the chance that at least 2 units stop working within the first hour? Also report the average number of first-hour failures the team should plan for, and how much fluctuation around that count should be expected.

f_t.description: Probability density function of the lifetime (in hours) of a communication system unit, used to compute the probability of failure within the first hour.

input.background:
An operations team is reviewing field reliability for a communication device whose in-service runtime, measured in hours, follows the profile
$$f(t)=\frac{2 e^t}{\left(\mathrm{e}^{\mathrm{t}}+1\right)^2} \quad \mathrm{t}>0.$$
