For one scheduled assessment, $n=30$ units are switched on together at $\mathrm{t}=0$, and each unit runs without affecting the others. Although the team is mainly interested in how many devices remain active through the early part of the trial, management specifically wants a clear interpretation of the risk window immediately after a unit has already made it through the initial hour of operation.
input.question: For a unit that is still operating after the first hour of testing, what is the chance that it stops working at some point during the second hour?

T.description: Lifetime of a communication system (in hours) with the given probability density function, used to compute the CDF values F(1) and F(2) in the conditional probability calculation.

t1.description: The conditioning time point (1 hour), representing the time the unit has already survived; used to evaluate F(1) in the conditional probability formula.

t2.description: The event time point (2 hours), representing the upper bound of the failure interval; used to evaluate F(2) in the conditional probability formula.

input.background: A board governance team is documenting how a search committee could order a slate of $n$ finalists for a chief executive appointment. For process review purposes, they want to understand the full set of possible ordered shortlists that could emerge before any interviews, references, or strategic preferences are applied. One point of interest in the internal discussion is Mr. Best, who is identified as the fifth candidate on the roster. The team is considering a purely neutral scenario in which every complete ordering of the $n$ candidates is treated the same way.
input.question: Under that fully neutral ordering process, what is the chance that Mr. Best ends up listed in second place?

n.description: The total number of candidates for the corporate chief executive position, used to calculate the total number of possible rankings (n!) and the number of favorable rankings ((n-1)!).

Mr_Best_placement.description: The specific placement (second place) of the fifth candidate, Mr. Best, whose probability of occurring under random ranking is being calculated.

input.background: An organization is putting together a small working group from its current volunteer pool for a special initiative. The available pool consists of 7 women and 4 men. Leadership has not fixed the final team size in advance because the scope may be adjusted after seeing who can be included, but they do want the group composition to reflect a perfectly balanced split between the two gender categories. Other considerations such as seniority, department, and scheduling are being set aside for this first-pass planning exercise.
input.question: Given those staffing constraints, how many distinct working-group lineups could the organization assemble if the group must include at least one person and must contain the same number of women and men?

women_count.description: The number of women in the set from which the committee is chosen.

men_count.description: The number of men in the set from which the committee is chosen.

output.category: Probability Space Related (e.g., number of states)

input.background: A small organization is putting together a 4-person working group for a short-term initiative. The available internal pool contains 7 women and 4 men. One of the men, Mr. Good, has already been identified as a required participant because of his role in the project. Apart from that requirement, the remaining seats may be filled from the rest of the available people, even though managers have also been informally discussing balance, availability, and visibility across teams.
input.question: Given these staffing rules, in how many different ways can the organization finalize the 4-person working group if Mr. Good must be included?

num_women.description: The number of women in the set from which the committee is chosen.

num_men.description: The number of men in the set from which the committee is chosen.

committee_size.description: The required number of people on the committee.

num_fixed_members.description: The number of fixed members (Mr. Good) who must be on the committee.

output.category: Probability Space Related (e.g., number of states)

input.background: A homeroom teacher is putting together a small project team for an upcoming classroom activity and wants the selection to be made in a way that no one can claim was planned around a particular mix. The class roster currently includes 10 girls and 12 boys, and 6 children will be pulled from the class list for the assignment. Although parents and staff sometimes read a lot into the final makeup of these groups, the teacher wants to understand how ordinary a specific outcome would be if the choice really comes down to chance alone.
input.question: If 6 children are drawn from this class in that way, how plausible is the outcome in which the project team ends up with 2 girls and 4 boys?

girls_count.description: Number of girls in the class, used in the hypergeometric probability calculation as the size of the success group.

boys_count.description: Number of boys in the class, used in the hypergeometric probability calculation as the size of the non-success group.

sample_size.description: Number of children selected at random by the teacher for group projects (the sample drawn without replacement).

girls_selected.description: Number of girls in the specific combination being evaluated (2 girls chosen out of 10).

boys_selected.description: Number of boys in the specific combination being evaluated (4 boys chosen out of 12).

input.background: A civic organization is putting together a 4-person planning panel for an upcoming community initiative. The candidate pool currently includes 7 women and 4 men. To avoid possible conflicts in scheduling and household obligations, the organizers have decided that the married pair Mr. and Mrs. Good should not be assigned to serve together on this panel, even though each remains individually eligible. The group also wants the panel composition to reflect a balanced representation by sex for this particular assignment.
input.question: Under these staffing rules, how many distinct 4-person panels can the organization assemble if the panel must include exactly 2 women and 2 men, while ensuring that Mr. and Mrs. Good are not both selected?

women_count.description: Total number of women in the set from which the committee is chosen.

men_count.description: Total number of men in the set from which the committee is chosen.

women_on_committee.description: Number of women required on the committee.

men_on_committee.description: Number of men required on the committee.

constraint_Mr_Mrs_Good.value: Mr. and Mrs. Good cannot both be on the committee
constraint_Mr_Mrs_Good.description: Constraint that the married couple (one from women, one from men) cannot both serve on the committee simultaneously.

output.category: Probability Space Related (e.g., number of states)

input.background: A manufacturer of industrial equipment is preparing warranty and service planning assumptions for a line of electric motors. For this product family, the operating life of a motor, measured in years and denoted by t>0, is summarized by the profile f(t)=0.25 t e^{-0.5 t}. Operations managers are mainly concerned with early in-service breakdowns because those cases drive replacement inventory, field technician scheduling, and customer support costs.
input.question: Based on this lifecycle profile, what share of motors should the company expect to fail before completing their first year in operation?

t.description: Lifetime of an electric motor in years; the answer integrates the pdf from 0 to t=1 to find the probability of failure during the first year.

f(t).description: Probability density function of the electric motor's lifetime, used to compute the cumulative distribution function F(1).

input.background: A manufacturer of electric drive units is preparing warranty messaging for a motor line and is reviewing the service-life pattern already established for the product. Based on historical engineering records, the operating lifetime (t) of one such motor, measured in years, follows the profile (f(t)=0.25,t e^{-0.5 t}) for (t>0). Commercial teams are mainly concerned with how often a unit remains in use beyond a minimum ownership horizon, even though field performance can also be affected by installation conditions and maintenance practices.
input.question: Using this lifetime profile, what share of motors would be expected to remain operational for at least 3 years?

t.description: The specific time point (in years) at which the reliability/survival probability is evaluated; here t = 3 years representing the minimum desired lifetime of the electric motor.

f(t).description: The probability density function (pdf) of the lifetime of the electric motor, used to compute the survival probability R(t) = P(T ≥ 3) by integrating from t=3 to infinity.

input.background: A manufacturer of electric motors is setting the service commitment for a new product line. Engineering has provided the expected operating-life profile for a motor: its lifetime t, measured in years, follows the density function f(t)=0.25 t e^{-0.5 t} for t>0. The sales team is pushing for a stronger market-facing promise, while the warranty group wants to keep the share of units needing attention during the covered period very low. Although field performance can also be influenced by installation practices and customer usage, the decision is to be based on this stated lifetime pattern.
input.question: Using this operating-life profile, what is the longest warranty period, in days, that the company can announce if it wants no more than 3% of motors to require warranty service during the covered period?

T.value: Lifetime of an electric motor (in years), with pdf f(t) = 0.25 t e^{-0.5 t}, t > 0
T.description: The random variable representing the lifetime of an electric motor, whose probability density function is f(t) = 0.25 t e^{-0.5 t} for t > 0. The answer integrates this pdf to find the warranty period.

warranty_failure_probability.description: The maximum proportion of motors allowed to require warranty services (3%), used as the threshold probability in solving for the warranty period.

input.background:
A property insurer is reviewing exposure from a small cluster of wind-related homeowner losses. For this line of business, individual claim severities are treated as unrelated across homes and follow the established severity pattern

$$
f(x)= \begin{cases}3 x^{-4} & \text { for } x>1 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
$$

where $x$ denotes a single claim amount measured in thousands. Assume that, for the situation being reviewed, exactly 3 claims are expected to be filed. The reinsurance team is less interested in the overall average payout across the three files than in the one case most likely to drive attention, since large isolated losses often dominate internal escalation, reserve discussion, and vendor involvement.
input.question: Based on this claim pattern, what benchmark amount should the insurer use for the expected size of the largest claim among the 3 wind-damage claims?

claim_density.description: Common probability density function of each individual claim amount (in thousands), used to derive the distribution of the order statistics.

n.description: Number of independent claims made, determining the order statistic (maximum) to be computed.

input.background:
A fuel retailer receives one gasoline delivery each week and wants to set on-site storage so routine operations are not disrupted before the next replenishment arrives. Let the station’s weekly gasoline drawdown, measured in thousands of gallons, be denoted by $x$. Based on past operating patterns, the usage profile is represented by
$$f(x)= \begin{cases}5(1-x)^4 & 0<x<1 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}$$
Management notes that actual pump demand can vary from week to week because of traffic flow, weather, nearby road activity, and local promotions, but for this planning exercise the above relationship is to be used.
input.question: How large should the gasoline tank capacity be so that the chance of the station running out of supply before the next weekly delivery is no greater than 0.01?

X.description: Weekly volume of sales in thousands of gallons, a random variable with the given probability density function f(x) = 5(1-x)^4 for 0 < x < 1.

probability_threshold.description: The maximum allowable probability that the supplies are completely used up in a given week.

input.background:
A neighborhood filling station receives one gasoline delivery each week and is reviewing its replenishment outlook for routine planning. Internal records suggest that weekly demand, measured in thousands of gallons, does not stay fixed from week to week but follows the pattern summarized by
$$f(x)= \begin{cases}5(1-x)^4 & 0<x<1 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}$$
Management is less concerned with unusually high or low single-week outcomes than with the typical weekly draw that should be used for budgeting, delivery coordination, and discussions with the supplier.
input.question: Based on this demand pattern, what weekly sales volume should the station use as its average planning figure, in thousands of gallons? Show how you obtain it.

X.description: Weekly volume of sales in thousands of gallons, a random variable with the given probability density function f(x) = 5(1-x)^4 on (0,1). The expected value E(X) is computed from this distribution.

input.background: An automotive parts supplier is reviewing the service promise it gives fleet customers for a battery line used in vehicles that operate for long continuous periods. Engineering notes indicate that, over the operating window of interest, the battery can be treated as having a steady breakdown pace of 0.0001 failures per hour. The commercial team is less interested in the technical label and more interested in what this means for whether a unit can stay in service through a meaningful usage milestone, especially since real-world replacement decisions may also be influenced by labor scheduling, downtime costs, and warranty messaging.
input.question: Based on that reliability assumption, what share of batteries should the supplier expect to remain in service beyond 5,000 h?

failure_rate.description: Constant failure rate parameter λ of the exponential distribution, in failures per hour.

time_threshold.description: The time threshold (in hours) for which the probability of the battery lasting more than this duration is calculated.

input.background: A facilities team is sourcing replacement components for a lamp model that uses bulbs from the same reliability class. For a quick service-risk check, they are looking at two bulbs currently on hand rather than the broader inventory. Let $X$ denote the operating life of the first bulb and $Y$ denote the operating life of the second bulb. Engineering notes indicate that the two bulbs do not affect one another in use, and that each bulb’s time-to-burnout follows the standard wear pattern for this supplier category with a constant failure intensity of $\lambda=0.001$ per hour. Although procurement has also raised issues about packaging, storage shelves, and vendor lead times, this review is concerned only with the operating-life behavior of these two bulbs.
input.question: From a maintenance planning perspective, what is the chance that both bulbs will be exhausted no later than 1000 h of operation?

X.description: Lifetime (in hours) of the first light bulb, exponentially distributed with λ=0.001 per hour.

Y.description: Lifetime (in hours) of the second light bulb, exponentially distributed with λ=0.001 per hour, independent of X.

t.description: The time threshold (1000 hours) used to evaluate the probability that each bulb lasts at most this many hours.

input.background: A facilities team is planning replacement logistics for a lamp that uses two spare bulbs one after the other rather than at the same time. Let $X$ represent the service life of the first bulb placed into use and let $Y$ represent the service life of the second bulb that is installed after the first one burns out. The supplier states that the two bulbs come from the same production standard, each operates with a steady burnout tendency corresponding to $\lambda=0.001$ per hour, and the performance of one bulb does not affect the other. Although purchasing staff have also raised issues such as packaging, storage conditions, and vendor lead times, this review is limited to the operating-life assumptions just described.
input.question: For maintenance planning, what is the chance that the pair of bulbs will provide no more than 2000 h of combined operating time before both need to be replaced?

X.description: Lifetime of the first light bulb (in hours), exponentially distributed with λ=0.001.

Y.description: Lifetime of the second light bulb (in hours), exponentially distributed with λ=0.001. Independent of X.

total_lifetime_threshold.description: The threshold (in hours) for the total lifetime of the two bulbs, used to compute P(X+Y ≤ 2000).

input.background:
A property insurer is reviewing how small-loss exposure behaves within a short run of wind-related homeowner claims, because frontline reserving teams often want a benchmark for the least costly file in a small cluster of events. For this line of business, each individual claim amount, measured in thousands, follows the severity pattern

$$
f(x)= \begin{cases}3 x^{-4} & \text{for } x \geq 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}
$$

Assume the claims arise separately from one another and that exactly 3 such wind-damage claims are reported. Although adjusters may also discuss roof type, neighborhood exposure, and contractor availability, management wants this calculation based only on the claim-size pattern above.
input.question: Across these 3 reported wind-damage claims, what benchmark amount, in thousands, should the insurer use for the smallest claim on average?

X.description: Claim amount (in thousands) for wind damage to insured homes, following the given probability density function f(x) = 3x^{-4} for x >= 1.

n.description: Number of independent claims (sample size), used to determine the distribution of the minimum order statistic.

input.background:
A property insurer is reviewing catastrophe exposure for a small batch of wind-related home losses expected to arrive from the same event window. For planning purposes, each individual claim amount, measured in thousands, is treated as arising independently from the portfolio’s established severity pattern:

$$
f(x)= \begin{cases}3 x^{-4} & \text { for } x \geq 1 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise }\end{cases}
$$

Operations is particularly interested in the lower end of the incoming claims set, since even the least severe file in a cluster still affects adjuster routing, reserve communication, and vendor assignment. Assume that 5 such claims are submitted.
input.question: For this group of 5 claims, what average amount, in thousands, should the insurer expect for the smallest claim in the batch?

X.description: Claim amount (in thousands) for wind damage to insured homes, following a Pareto-type distribution with PDF f(x) = 3x^{-4} for x ≥ 1.

n.description: Number of independent claims to be made, used to determine the distribution of the minimum order statistic.

input.background: A field support team is reviewing a simple backup arrangement in which one primary unit is deployed together with one spare, and the combined setup remains operational for a service duration denoted by $X$ months before both support options are exhausted. Based on prior engineering assumptions, the pattern governing this operating duration is described for $x>0$ by $f(x)=C\,x e^{-x/2}$, with $C$ as a fixed scaling constant, and no operating time is recorded for $x\le 0$. Although managers may also care about replacement logistics and warranty messaging, the immediate concern is whether this configuration can credibly cover a short early-use window.
input.question: For planning purposes, what is the chance that this primary-plus-spare setup stays in service for at least 5 months?

X.value: Continuous random variable with density f(x) = C * x * e^(-x/2) for x > 0
X.description: The random amount of time (in months) that the system functions, with the given density function f(x) = C * x * e^(-x/2) for x > 0.

threshold.description: The threshold value (5 months) used to compute the probability P(X ≥ 5).

input.background: A property insurer is reviewing a very small set of homeowner loss files tied to wind events from a fairly uniform book of business. Internal pricing guidance says that each individual claim amount x, recorded in thousands, follows the cost pattern f(x) = 3e^(-3x) for x > 0, and that one file does not affect another. Suppose 4 such claims are expected to come in. The claims team is particularly interested in the smallest file in the group because very low-severity cases can influence routing, automation, and adjuster workload.
input.question: Using this portfolio assumption, what average claim amount should the insurer plan for as the smallest of the 4 wind-damage claims?

claim_amount.description: Claim amounts for wind damage to insured homes, independent random variables following an exponential distribution with PDF f(x) = 3e^(-3x) for x > 0.

n.description: Number of claims (sample size), used to compute the expected value of the smallest (minimum order statistic) of the four claims.

input.background: An innovation unit is planning the budget for a simulation-driven initiative that will keep moving through repeated runs until the first run meets the required acceptance standard. Each run is treated as operationally independent of the others. The direct execution cost is $25,000 per run, and whenever a run fails to qualify, an additional $5,000 must be spent to reset and prepare the workflow for the next attempt. Finance wants a planning figure that reflects the average overall spend for this kind of effort rather than a single-scenario estimate. If Y represents the number of runs needed before the first acceptable outcome is achieved, the total project cost is given by C(Y) = $25,000 Y + $5,000(Y-1).
input.question: Using this operating setup, what expected total project cost should be used for budgeting purposes?

Y.value: The number of trials required to obtain a successful experiment (geometric random variable with parameter p)
Y.description: The number of trials required to obtain a successful result. Follows a geometric distribution with success probability p. Used to compute the expected cost via C(Y) = 25000Y + 5000(Y-1).

cost_per_trial.description: The cost of performing each experiment trial, $25,000, used in the cost function C(Y).

setup_cost_per_failure.description: The cost to set up for the next trial after a failure, $5,000, used in the cost function C(Y).

input.background: A manufacturing team is reviewing the assembly playbook for a product that must pass through six distinct shop-floor tasks before release. None of these tasks is inherently tied to a fixed upstream or downstream step, so supervisors are considering whether the routing instructions can be made more flexible across shifts. Aside from standard concerns such as labor balancing, workstation congestion, and handoff clarity, the immediate issue is to understand the full range of valid processing orders available when all six tasks are required exactly once.
input.question: If the product must complete all six operations and the operations may be arranged in any order, how many distinct production sequences are available?

N.description: The number of operations that can be performed in any sequence to produce the product.

output.category: Probability Space Related (e.g., number of states)

input.background: An automotive service network is reviewing warranty messaging for a battery line whose field performance is treated internally as having a steady-hourly breakdown tendency of 0.0001 per operating hour. Product managers are less interested in average customer anecdotes than in what should be communicated once a unit has already been in use for a meaningful period. In practice, battery replacements are also affected by driving habits, climate, storage conditions, and service patterns, but for this planning exercise the team wants to rely only on the stated durability assumption.
input.question: Under that assumption, if a battery has already remained in service for 3,000 h, what is the chance that it will still be operating beyond 5,000 h?

λ.description: Constant failure rate parameter of the exponential distribution, in failures per hour.

t_survived.description: The number of hours the battery has already survived (given condition), used in the memoryless property calculation.

t_target.description: Original target lifetime in hours whose exceedance probability is requested.

input.background: A program manager is reviewing the spending exposure for a technical validation effort that keeps cycling until it finally delivers one acceptable run. Each run is treated as a fresh attempt, and operations has indicated that executing a run uses $25,000 in direct project funds. Whenever a run does not work, an additional $5,000 is needed to reconfigure equipment and prepare the next attempt. Finance has been tracking total spend with the rule $C(Y)=\$25{,}000Y+\$5{,}000(Y-1)$, where $Y$ is the number of runs needed before the first acceptable outcome is achieved. The team is less concerned with the average invoice than with whether the project might overrun its approved cap, especially since other portfolio items are competing for the same cash allocation.
input.question: If the chance that any single run produces an acceptable outcome is 0.25 and the project cannot exceed $500,000 without triggering an escalation, what is the chance that the total cost of this validation effort ends up above $500,000?

p_success.description: The probability of success on a single trial.

budget_max.description: The maximum budget available for the experimental work, in dollars.

trial_cost.description: The cost of performing each trial, in dollars.

setup_cost.description: The cost to set up for the next trial after a failure, in dollars.

input.background: A manufacturing operations team is reviewing a quick screening checkpoint used on units coming off an assembly line before they move downstream. Historically, about 5% of output has turned out to have a quality issue. The screening step is not perfect: when a unit truly has a problem, the checkpoint flags it 92% of the time; when a unit is actually fine, it clears that unit as fine 96% of the time. Supervisors are less interested in the engineering details of the device than in what signal volume the checkpoint will generate in routine production, since extra flags trigger handling, paperwork, and possible reinspection.
input.question: Based on these operating characteristics, what is the overall chance that a randomly selected unit from the line will be flagged by the checkpoint as defective?

P_defective.description: Prior probability that a randomly selected product is defective.

P_test_defective_given_defective.description: Probability that the test flags a product as defective given that it is defective.

P_test_good_given_good.description: Probability that the test indicates good given that the product is good.

input.background:
A delivery organization is reviewing the turnaround profile for a certain type of project so that operations leaders can quote a single benchmark timeline for planning and client communication. Historical process behavior has already been summarized through the following cumulative completion profile for the project duration $X$:

$$
F(x)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } x<0 \\
\frac{x^3}{3} & \text { for } 0 \leq x<1 \\
1-\frac{1}{2}\left(\frac{7}{3}-x\right)\left(\frac{7}{4}-\frac{3}{4} x\right) & \text { for } 1 \leq x<\frac{7}{3} \\
1 & \text { for } x \geq \frac{7}{3}\end{cases}
$$

While managers know that individual jobs may still be sped up or delayed by staffing, approvals, and handoff quality, they want to base the discussion on this existing service profile rather than on anecdotal cases.
input.question: Using this completion profile, what single average project duration should the team treat as the typical completion time for planning purposes?

X.description: Completion time for a project, a continuous random variable with a piecewise cumulative distribution function (CDF). The expected value E(X) is computed from this CDF.

input.background: A property insurer is reviewing its catastrophe pricing notes for residential wind-loss cases. For this line of business, each paid claim is treated as arising separately but following the same portfolio-level loss pattern, with claim size measured in thousands and represented by the density function \(f(x)=0.5x^2e^{-x}\) for \(x>0\). The finance team is less concerned with any single household event than with the typical payout level that should be built into planning assumptions, even though actual files can vary widely depending on roof condition, debris exposure, and neighborhood construction characteristics.
input.question: Based on this portfolio loss pattern, what average claim amount should the insurer expect for a wind-damage claim?

X.value: Claim amounts (in thousands) following density f(x) = 0.5 x^2 e^{-x} for x > 0
X.description: Claim amounts for wind damage to insured homes, measured in thousands of dollars, with density function f(x) = 0.5 x^2 e^{-x} for x > 0. The expected value E[X] = ∫₀^∞ x · 0.5 x^2 e^{-x} dx = 3 is computed directly from this distribution.

input.background:
A corporate operations team is trying to set more realistic room-release expectations for a recurring management session. The agenda is built around a nominal slot of $b$ minutes, but in practice the discussion almost never wraps up before $a$ minutes, while it cannot run past $L$ minutes because another group is booked into the same room immediately afterward. To support scheduling, the team uses the following completion profile for the actual meeting length $X$:

$$
F(x)= \begin{cases}0 & \text { for } 0 \leq x \leq a \\ \beta\left(\frac{x-a}{b-a}\right)^2 & \text { for } a \leq x \leq b \\ \left(\frac{1-\beta}{L-b}\right) x+\frac{\beta L-b}{L-b} & \text { for } b \leq x \leq L \\ 1 & \text { for } L \leq x<\infty\end{cases}
$$

where $0<\beta<1$. The facilities manager is less interested in edge cases than in the typical amount of time the room should be treated as occupied when planning adjacent bookings and support staff coverage.
input.question: If $a=40$, $b=50$, $L=60$, and $\beta=0.8$, what average meeting duration should the operations team use for planning purposes?

a.description: Minimum possible duration of the meeting (in minutes), the lower bound before which the meeting will not end.

b.description: Scheduled length of the management meeting (in minutes), marking the transition point in the CDF.

L.description: Maximum possible duration of the meeting (in minutes), the upper bound beyond which the meeting cannot last.

beta.description: Parameter β in the CDF, representing the cumulative probability at x = b.

X.description: Random variable representing the duration (lifetime) of the meeting, whose expected value E(X) is to be computed.

input.background: A reliability team is reviewing a piece of equipment during routine bench checks before wider deployment. Based on past experience, each check has a 0.2 chance of the unit failing that check. The checks are carried out one after another, and the result of one check does not change what happens on the next. Although engineers may also look at wear, operator notes, and environmental conditions, management currently wants a quick read on how soon a breakdown signal is likely to appear during this sequence of checks.
input.question: For planning purposes, what is the chance that the first failure shows up before the fourth test is completed?

p_failure.description: The probability of failure of the equipment on each test.

n_tests_threshold.description: The threshold number of tests; we seek the probability that the first failure occurs in fewer than this many tests.

input.background: A power utility is stress-testing its restoration playbook for a relay section containing $N$ relays. In the scenario under review, the time required to return any one tripped relay to service is assumed to follow the standard exponential pattern used in reliability planning, with constant rate parameter $\lambda=19/\mathrm{h}$. Following one disturbance event, ten relays are taken out at exactly the same time, and only one repairman is available to clear them. Dispatch supervisors are trying to understand whether this staffing level is likely to leave customers without service longer than internal response expectations, regardless of the original cause of the trip.
input.question: For this restoration scenario, what is the probability that the power outage lasts more than $\frac{3}{4}\mathrm{~h}$?

N_tripped.description: Number of relays that have tripped simultaneously.

lambda.description: Constant failure rate parameter (per hour) of the exponential distribution for repair time of each relay.

t.description: Time threshold (3/4 hour) for which the probability of power failure lasting longer is calculated.

n_repairman.description: Number of repairmen available to perform repairs.

input.background: A field service team is reviewing a modular device built from $k$ interchangeable units that is expected to stay in operation through a scheduled run of length $t$. For planning purposes, each unit is treated as having the same chance $p$ of getting through that run without trouble, and issues in one unit do not affect the others. Once the run ends, the device is taken offline and a technician checks which units did not make it through the cycle and swaps those out. Each swap requires $s$ units of time. Operations managers are trying to understand whether a very short turnaround target is realistic, since setup, paperwork, and other shop-floor considerations are often discussed even though the bottleneck here is the actual replacement work.
input.question: Based on this service setup, what is the chance, denoted by $P$, that the device can be put back into working condition within the $2s$ time window immediately after the stoppage?

k.description: Number of units in the instrument.

p.description: Reliability (probability of failure-free performance) of each unit during time t.

s.description: Time required by the technician to replace one failed unit. The available repair window is 2s, so at most 2 units can be replaced.

input.background: A minting facility uses two approved production settings for a commemorative token used in an internal acceptance check. Under the standard setting, the token yields a front-face result half the time, while under an alternative setting it shows the front face 55 percent of the time. A quality lead has been handed one token from these two possible streams, but its production setting was not recorded. To decide how to label the token for downstream review, he plans a fixed verification run of 1000 flips. If the front face appears 525 times or more, he will classify the token as having come from the alternative setting; otherwise, he will treat it as a standard token. The team prefers a quick large-sample approximation rather than an exact count-based calculation.
input.question: Assuming the token actually came from the standard setting, what is the chance that this screening rule causes the quality lead to assign it to the alternative setting by mistake?

n.description: Number of coin tosses performed in the statistical test.

p_fair.description: Probability of heads for the fair coin (assumed true probability under the null hypothesis).

threshold.description: Decision threshold: if heads ≥ 525, conclude biased coin; otherwise conclude fair coin.

input.background: An assembly plant is reviewing whether a supplier’s incoming carton can move straight into production under its routine receiving screen. The shipment contains 100 items, and the supplier has stated that the off-spec share does not exceed 2%. For this intake check, the quality lead instructs staff to pull 10 items at random from the carton without putting any back during the check. The carton is cleared for use if the inspection team finds no more than 1 item that fails the requirement. If the supplier’s stated upper-limit condition is exactly met, that means 2 of the 100 items in the carton are defective. The plant is mainly interested in the chance that a shipment meeting that edge-case condition still passes the receiving screen.
input.question: Under this receiving rule, what is the chance that the quality manager signs off on the lot for production use?

N.description: Total number of items in the lot (population size).

K.description: Number of defective items in the lot, derived from the claim that 2% of 100 items are defective.

n.description: Sample size drawn from the lot without replacement.

acceptance_threshold.description: Maximum number of defective items allowed in the sample for the lot to be accepted (at most 1).

input.background: An airport ground-transport operator is reviewing its booking policy for a premium limousine service used on a single departure run. The vehicle has only 4 usable passenger seats, but to reduce the chance of leaving with empty capacity, the reservations desk is allowed to confirm as many as 6 bookings for that run. Based on past operating records, about 30% of customers who secure a booking do not actually arrive for pickup, and each customer’s arrival behavior is treated as unrelated to the others. Management wants to understand the service risk created by this overbooking practice before deciding whether the current rule should remain in place.
input.question: Suppose all 6 reservation slots are filled for one trip. What is the chance that pickup demand exceeds the 4-seat limit, so that at least one customer holding a valid reservation cannot be taken on that limousine run?

limousine_capacity.description: Maximum number of passengers the airport limousine can accommodate on any one trip.

num_reservations.description: Number of reservations made for the trip, serving as the number of Bernoulli trials (n) in the binomial model.

no_show_probability.description: Probability that a person with a reservation does not appear for the trip (30%). The complement (0.70) is the probability of showing up, used as the success probability in the binomial calculation.

input.background: A reliability team is reviewing a small batch of components believed to wear out within a fairly even service window rather than clustering around any particular day. Internally, the team describes this window using two business quantities: a central service-life target, denoted by $c$, and an allowance on either side of that target, denoted by $d$, so that actual failure times are expected to fall between $c-d$ and $c+d$. Both of these planning quantities are currently unknown. The observed failure times for the batch were 20, 23, 25, 26, 28, 29, 31, 33, 34, and 35 days. Management wants to calibrate the service window from these records for future warranty and stocking discussions.
input.question: Using the observed failure times and the assumption that failures are spread evenly across an unknown interval from $c-d$ to $c+d$, what values of $c$ and $d$ should be chosen to make the recorded batch most consistent with that service-window assumption?

failure_time.description: Failure time data (in days) assumed to follow a uniform distribution on [c-d, c+d]. The answer uses the max and min of these values to compute the MLEs of c and d.

input.background: A product reliability group is examining a set of lifetimes for identical units that seem to fail within a fairly sharp service window rather than showing a central concentration. To support maintenance guidance, the team wants to summarize that window by a center point, denoted by $c$, and a distance from the center to either edge, denoted by $d$, so that any failure would fall between $c-d$ and $c+d$. The exact values are not known in advance, with $-\infty<c<\infty$ and $d>0$. The recorded failure times are 20, 23, 25, 26, 28, 29, 31, 33, 34, and 35 days, and the current working assumption is that failures are spread evenly over the interval $[c-d,c+d]$.
input.question: Based on the observed failure times of 20, 23, 25, 26, 28, 29, 31, 33, 34, and 35 days, which values of the center $c$ and half-width $d$ are most defensible under this assumption?

failure_time.description: Failure time data (in days) assumed to follow a uniform distribution on [c-d, c+d], used to estimate parameters c and d via maximum likelihood estimation.

input.background: A neighborhood printing shop is reviewing walk-in activity over a five-day stretch in the same month because the owner is deciding whether front-desk coverage and machine readiness were balanced across the week. The recorded counts of customers entering the service area on those five consecutive days were 48, 60, 78, 56, and 73. Staff have suggested that the differences may simply reflect normal day-to-day fluctuation, while the owner is concerned that at least one day may have been meaningfully busier or quieter than the others due to scheduling, local business traffic, or timing of nearby school and office orders.
input.question: Using these five daily entry counts, assess at the 5% decision threshold whether the shop should treat customer inflow as being essentially evenly spread across the five consecutive days, or conclude that the pattern across days was not balanced.

customers_per_day.description: The observed number of customers who entered the printing shop on each of the five consecutive days, used in the Chi-square goodness-of-fit test.

alpha.description: Significance threshold used to decide whether the daily counts are equal.

input.background:
A gaming products team is reviewing a quality-control check on a six-sided die intended for use in a promotional tabletop kit. As part of the check, the die was thrown 120 times under the same operating routine, and the tally for each face was logged as follows:
$$
\begin{array}{l|l|l|l|l|l|l}
\hline \text { Face } & 1 & 2 & 3 & 4 & 5 & 6 \\
\hline \mathrm{n}_{\mathrm{i}} & 15 & 21 & 20 & 15 & 26 & 23 \\
\hline
\end{array}
$$
The supplier notes that small run-to-run fluctuations can occur because of handling, surface bounce, and ordinary chance, while the operations team wants to know whether these counts are still consistent with a balanced product rather than a face-preference issue.
input.question: Using the recorded face counts, decide whether this die should still be treated as behaving like a properly balanced six-sided die, or whether the observed pattern is strong enough to raise concern under the company’s 5% decision standard.

Face.description: The six faces of the die, serving as categories for the Chi-square goodness-of-fit test.

Observed_Frequency.description: The observed frequencies (n_i) for each face of the die over 120 rolls, used in the Chi-square goodness-of-fit test.

input.background: A production manager is reviewing whether the line’s quality mix this year still looks in line with the historical operating pattern used for planning. Last year’s benchmark mix for finished components was 3% scrapped, 6% sent for rework, and 91% released as acceptable. In a recent review of 500 units produced this year, inspectors classified 20 units as scrap and 25 units as rework, with the remainder falling into the acceptable category. There has also been discussion on the floor about tooling wear, operator rotation, and a tighter delivery schedule, but no one wants to overreact to normal fluctuation without a formal check against the legacy benchmark.
input.question: Based on the 500-unit inspection and using last year’s mix as the reference point, is this year’s outcome close enough to the historical pattern to be treated as consistent for reporting purposes at the 5% decision threshold?

observed_counts.description: Observed counts from this year's inspection of 500 units: 20 scrapped, 25 reworked, and 455 acceptable (500 - 20 - 25).

expected_proportions.description: Expected proportions from last year's manufacturing process: 3% scrapped, 6% reworked, 91% acceptable, used to compute expected counts for the Chi-square test.

n.description: Total number of units inspected this year, used to compute expected counts.

input.background: A process-improvement team is reviewing an internal quality summary for a recurring measurement operation. In the broader discussion, analysts have also been comparing how uneven results appear across batches, whether the pattern of readings leans to one side, how extreme values behave, and what the middle observation would represent once records are lined up. For the current checkpoint, however, the operations manager wants a quick translation of the typical within-group spread into the more familiar process-variability scale used in reporting. The team’s worksheet refers to Table A.5 for the factor tied to subgroup size, and the observed average within-sample range is \( \bar{w}=25.7 \). Each subgroup contains \( n=4 \) observations.
input.question: Using Table A.5 and the reported average range \( \bar{w}=25.7 \) for subgroups of size \( n=4 \), what estimate should the team use for the underlying process standard deviation \( \sigma \)?

mean_range.description: The mean range (w̄) given in the problem, used to estimate the standard deviation.

n.description: The sample size (number in sample), used to look up the corresponding d_n value from Table A.5.

d_n.description: The range value d_n corresponding to n=4 from Table A.5, used as the divisor to estimate the standard deviation.

input.background: A product-reliability team is reviewing normalized early-life breakdown timing for a component used in a compact device platform. For each unit that fails during the observation window, the recorded timing is scaled to a fraction between 0 and 1, giving values \(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_n\). The units are being treated as separate cases, and the engineering group is using a one-parameter timing profile in which the relative behavior of failure timing over \(0<t<1\) is described by \(f(t)=(1+\lambda)t^{\lambda}\). Although field staff have also mentioned installation variation and customer usage intensity, management wants the current calibration to rely only on this timing rule and the observed failure records.
input.question: Based on the observed failure timings \(t_1,t_2,\ldots,t_n\) and the rule \(f(t)=(1+\lambda)t^{\lambda}\) for \(0<t<1\), what value of \(\lambda\) should be chosen as the best-fitting estimate for this failure-timing profile?

t.description: Failure times, independent observations from the population with PDF f(t) = (1+λ)t^λ for 0<t<1. The answer uses ln(ti) in the formula for the MLE.

n.description: Sample size, i.e., the number of failure time observations. Used directly in the MLE formula λ̂ = -1 - n / Σ(ln(ti)).

input.background: An operations engineering group is assessing the early-life reliability profile of a specialized component line. For this product, any unit that breaks down does so within the first hour after startup, and the elapsed shutdown time is represented on a 0 to 1 hour scale. Based on an existing technical assumption, the timing pattern for these breakdowns follows the rule \(f(t)=(1+\lambda)t^{\lambda}\) for \(0<t<1\). The records from different units are to be treated as separate observations. Management is less interested in descriptive summaries than in locking down the single tuning constant \(\lambda\) so future planning, warranty messaging, and bench-test expectations are aligned with the observed run behavior.
input.question: For the observed shutdown times 0.2, 0.3, 0.35, 0.45, 0.5, 0.6, 0.7, 0.75, 0.8, and 0.95 hours, what value of \(\lambda\) makes the stated breakdown-time rule most consistent with these field-test records?

failure_times.description: Independent failure time observations (in hours) from a population with pdf f(t) = (1+λ)t^λ for 0<t<1, used to compute the MLE of λ.

input.background: An operations team is reviewing the completion times for a recurring service task. Internally, they believe each recorded duration is made up of two parts: a fixed baseline amount of time that must elapse before any task can possibly finish, and then an additional waiting component whose chance of continuing falls off steadily as the overrun gets larger. Both the baseline floor and the scale of that extra waiting are currently unknown. A small set of seven independently recorded task times has been pulled for a quick calibration exercise: 5.3, 3.2, 2.4, 3.8, 4.2, 3.4, and 2.9.
input.question: Using these 7 observed task times, what values should the team use for the hidden minimum completion-time threshold and the size of the extra waiting component so that the observed records are most consistent with the assumed timing pattern?

X.description: Independent random variables X1 through X7, observations from the shifted exponential distribution f(x, α, β), used to compute the MLEs of α and β.

n.description: Sample size, the number of independent observations.

input.background: A neighborhood printing shop is reviewing front-counter traffic as part of a short operational check during one stretch of a month. Over five consecutive business days, the counts of customers entering the service area were 48, 60, 78, 56, and 73. Managers have noted that day-to-day demand can be influenced by walk-in errands, school deadlines, local business orders, weather, and promotional spillover from nearby stores, but for staffing and counter preparation they want to know whether this five-day run looks broadly even or whether one or more days appear to be drawing meaningfully different customer volume.
input.question: Based on these five consecutive daily counts, assess at the shop’s standard 5% decision threshold whether customer arrivals can reasonably be treated as being spread evenly across the five days, or whether the observed differences are too large to attribute to ordinary fluctuation alone.

customers_per_day.description: The observed number of customers who entered the printing shop on each of five consecutive days, used in the Chi-square goodness-of-fit test.

alpha.description: Significance level used for the five-day uniformity test.

input.background:
A project operations group is reviewing how engineers actually divide their assigned hours on one flagship initiative. Let $X$ represent the share of an engineer’s allotted time devoted to that project. Based on an internal workload pattern used by the planning team, these shares are assumed to follow

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}
(\theta+1) x^\theta & \text { for } 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\
0 & \text { otherwise }
\end{array} .\right.
$$

with $\theta>-1$. Although managers also mention meeting load, client interruptions, and reporting cycles, the current review is limited to the time-allocation shares themselves. A check of 10 randomly selected engineers produced

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_1=0.92, x_2=0.79, x_3=0.90, x_4=0.65, x_5=0.86 \\
& x_6=0.47, x_7=0.73, x_8=0.97, x_9=0.94, x_{10}=0.77
\end{aligned}
$$
input.question: Using this workload pattern and the 10 observed time shares, determine a data-based value for $\theta$ by matching the model’s average behavior to the sample’s average behavior, and then calculate the resulting value for these engineers.

X.description: Proportion of allotted time that each of 10 randomly selected engineers spends working on a certain project. This is the random sample used to compute the method of moments estimate of θ.

input.background:
A technology firm is reviewing how consistently engineers devote their assigned project hours to one particular initiative. Let $X$ represent the share of an engineer’s allotted time that ends up being spent on that project. For workforce planning purposes, leadership is using the following rule to describe how these time shares tend to appear across staff:

$$
f(x)=\left\{\begin{array}{cl}
(\theta+1) x^\theta & \text { for } 0 \leq x \leq 1 \\
0 & \text { otherwise }
\end{array} .\right.
$$

where $\theta>-1$. A spot check of 10 engineers produced the following recorded shares of allotted time:

$$
\begin{aligned}
& x_1=0.92, x_2=0.79, x_3=0.90, x_4=0.65, x_5=0.86 \\
& x_6=0.47, x_7=0.73, x_8=0.97, x_9=0.94, x_{10}=0.77
\end{aligned}
$$

Managers note that billing cycles, meeting load, and cross-team support can all affect day-to-day allocations, but they want the current review to rely only on the rule above and these 10 observations.
input.question: Using the operating rule above and the 10 recorded time-share values, determine the value of $\theta$ that best aligns with the observed engineer behavior, and then calculate its numerical estimate for this sample.

X.description: Proportion of allotted time that each of 10 randomly selected engineers spends working on a certain project. Used to compute the maximum likelihood estimate of θ.

input.background: A city transit operations team is reviewing rider experience on a lightly managed rail line where, for planning purposes, passenger arrival relative to the next train is being treated as evenly spread between no wait at all and some unknown longest possible wait within the current schedule design. The team collected seven spot observations from routine field checks rather than from a full operational audit. The recorded rider waits were 4.5, 5.3, 1.2, 7.4, 3.6, 4.8, and 2.9 minutes. Although platform crowding, time of day, and weather may also affect perceptions of service quality, management wants a quick benchmark for the outer limit of this waiting window under the simplifying assumption above.
input.question: Using these seven observed waits and the average-implied calibration from the even-spread waiting-window assumption, what value should be used for the unknown upper bound of rider waiting time, $\theta$?

waiting_times.description: Observed waiting times (x_1 through x_7) from a random sample of a uniform distribution on [0, θ], used to estimate θ via the method of moments.

input.background: A transit operations team is trying to characterize the outer limit of passenger platform wait exposure for a particular rail service under a simplified service-window assumption: on ordinary days, a rider’s arrival within the cycle is treated as equally likely anywhere from immediate boarding up to some unknown upper bound. To support a quick internal benchmark, one rider’s observed waits from several comparable trips were recorded as 4.5, 5.3, 1.2, 7.4, 3.6, 4.8, and 2.9 minutes. Although day-to-day conditions such as crowding, station access time, and minor dispatch variation may affect how staff discuss the experience operationally, the review is to rely only on these observed waits and the stated service-window assumption.
input.question: Based on those observed waiting times, what single value should the team use as the most defensible estimate of the unknown upper limit θ for the wait-time window?

waiting_times.description: Observed waiting times for a train, drawn as a random sample from a uniform distribution on [0, θ]. The maximum likelihood estimate of θ is the maximum of these observations.

input.background: A reliability team is conducting a short qualification run for a newly sourced batch of identical units before approving a broader rollout. Under the life-behavior assumption being used for this product line, an individual unit’s operating life is described by \(f(x)=\lambda e^{-\lambda x}\) for \(x\geq 0,\;\lambda>0\). At time \(x=0\), 20 units are started simultaneously. Because the test area is left unattended overnight, no one records the exact failure times as they occur. When the quality manager returns 24 hours later, only a simple status check is available: 15 of the 20 units are still running, so 5 have failed by that point. The manager then ends the run and files the result for supplier review.
input.question: Using only this 24-hour checkpoint result, what value of \(\lambda\) is most consistent with the observed run, where \(y=15\) of the 20 units are still operating after 24 hours?

n.description: Total number of identical units put on test at time x=0.

y.description: Number of units still in operation (surviving) after 24 hours out of the 20 units tested.

x.description: The observation time (in hours) at which the manager returns and records the number of surviving units.

input.background: A production team is reviewing a shipment under a stop/go incoming-quality procedure in which units are checked one at a time and each result is recorded in sequence. In the record, g means a good item and b means a defective item. The inspection history obtained is: ggbggbgggbgbggbbbggg. Management wants the decision rule calibrated around two benchmark defect levels for the supplier: 0.10 as the expected nonproblem level and 0.20 as the clearly unsatisfactory level. The operating requirements for the rule are that when the true defective share is 0.10, the chance of turning away the shipment should be 0.05, and when the true defective share is 0.20, the chance of waving the shipment through should be 0.20. The review is to be carried out using the step-by-step inspection plan already specified for this purpose.
input.question: Using that step-by-step acceptance procedure, what decision should be made for the lot after processing the observed sequence ggbggbgggbgbggbbbggg: release the lot or reject it?

observations.description: Sequential observations drawn one at a time, where 'g' denotes a good item and 'b' denotes a defective item.

p0.description: Proportion of defective items under the null hypothesis H0.

p1.description: Proportion of defective items under the alternative hypothesis H1.

alpha.description: Probability of rejecting H0 when it is true (Type I error probability).

beta.description: Probability of accepting H0 when H1 is true (Type II error probability).

input.background: A small premium-gift pack is being assembled from a display case that currently holds exactly four distinct pieces: one white, one black, one red, and one green sphere, all identical in size. Operations is reviewing how many different fulfilment sequences the team might need to account for when preparing a three-item bundle, since in some handling workflows the pickup sequence itself is treated as part of the recorded process rather than just the final set of items. The exercise concerns only these four available pieces and the selection of three of them.
input.question: If the packing log distinguishes the first, second, and third sphere taken, how many different three-sphere draw sequences are possible?

n.description: Total number of spheres in the urn (white, black, red, green), used as the total set size in the permutation calculation P(n, r).

r.description: Number of spheres drawn from the urn, used as the selection size in the permutation calculation P(n, r).

output.category: Probability Space Related (e.g., number of states)

input.background: A supplier quality team is reviewing incoming units from a lot one at a time, recording each inspection result in the exact order observed as: b g b g b g, where b marks a defective unit and g marks a good unit. The vendor’s standing target assumes a defect share of 0.10, while a materially worse condition of concern is a defect share of 0.25. Management wants to use an inspection rule that keeps the chance of wrongly turning away an acceptable lot to 0.05, while also keeping the chance of mistakenly clearing a poor lot at 0.10. The team is expected to make a release decision as evidence accumulates rather than waiting for a large fixed batch review.
input.question: Applying the agreed step-by-step lot disposition rule to the inspection record b g b g b g, should the lot be accepted or rejected?

observations.description: Sequentially drawn observations where 'b' denotes a defective item and 'g' denotes a good item, used in the sequential testing plan to determine acceptance or rejection of the lot.

p0.description: Proportion of defective items under the null hypothesis H0.

p1.description: Proportion of defective items under the alternative hypothesis H1.

alpha.description: Probability of rejecting H0 when it is true (Type I error probability), used to determine the sequential test boundaries.

beta.description: Probability of accepting H0 when H1 is true (Type II error probability), used to determine the sequential test boundaries.

input.background: A facility manager is reviewing how long customers typically occupy a service station and is using an internal duration profile for positive waiting/handling times of the form $f(x)=0.5 \lambda^3 x^2 e^{-\lambda x}$ for $x>0, \lambda>0$. Although day-to-day conditions such as staffing, queue mix, and customer needs may vary, the manager wants to anchor the discussion on a small set of recent observations rather than anecdotal impressions. For five customers, the recorded service times were $x_1=20, x_2=16, x_3=15, x_4=18, x_5=25$.
input.question: Based on this service-time profile and the five observed customer durations, what value should be used for the operational rate setting $\lambda$ when it is calibrated by matching the model’s average service duration to the average seen in these records?

X.description: Random sample of service times (in some unit) for 5 customers, used to compute the sample mean for the method of moments estimator of λ.

input.background: An operations lead is reviewing customer processing times at a service counter where the company already uses the duration pattern f(x)=0.5 \lambda^3 x^2 e^{-\lambda x} for x>0, \lambda>0 as its standard representation of how visits unfold. The practical goal is to calibrate the current setting of \lambda so the site can be aligned with internal planning assumptions and compared with other locations, even though day-to-day conditions may also reflect staffing, queue mix, and time-of-day effects. A quick check on 5 customers recorded service times of x_1=20, x_2=16, x_3=15, x_4=18, x_5=25.
input.question: Using these 5 observed service times and the company’s stated duration pattern, what value of \lambda should be used as the best estimate for the current service environment?

X.description: Random sample of service times at the facility for 5 customers, used to estimate the parameter λ via maximum likelihood estimation.

input.background: An engineering team is reviewing service continuity for a high-voltage platform built around one power supply and two mechanically tuned magnetron transmitters, A and B. Under normal operating conditions, the two transmitters split the intended frequency coverage, each handling one-half of the target range. If either transmitter drops out, the remaining unit is expected to stretch to cover the full range, which changes the operating burden on that surviving transmitter. The platform is considered mission-capable only when the power supply is available and at least one transmitter remains usable. While both transmitters are up, their operating behavior is treated as separate. However, the review must also account for the fact that a hidden fault in either transmitter can bring down the overall platform even before operations staff recognize the issue. For planning purposes, transmitter A is known to deteriorate at rate λ_A while transmitter B is still available, and at rate λ_A' once B has already been lost. In the same way, transmitter B deteriorates at rate λ_B while transmitter A is available, and at rate λ_B' after A has been lost. The power supply and fault-coverage mechanism are characterized by constant rates λ_P and λ_C, respectively. Program management wants a compact expression that can be used later in lifecycle and readiness discussions, even though other practical issues such as maintenance access, operator response, and environmental stress are being discussed separately.
input.question: Based on this operating logic, derive the time-based expression R(t) giving the chance that the high-voltage load-sharing system is still able to perform its required function at time t when the two transmitters influence each other’s effective exposure after one of them is lost.

λ_A.description: Constant failure rate of transmitter A when transmitter B is operating.

λ_B.description: Constant failure rate of transmitter B when transmitter A is operating.

λ_A'.description: Constant failure rate of transmitter A when transmitter B has failed.

λ_B'.description: Constant failure rate of transmitter B when transmitter A has failed.

λ_P.description: Constant failure rate of the power supply.

λ_C.description: Constant failure rate of fault coverage (undetected fault).

t.description: Time variable over which the reliability function R(t) is evaluated.

input.background: A defense-electronics maintenance team is reviewing the service endurance of a high-voltage RF subsystem built around one shared power unit and two mechanically tuned magnetron transmitters, labeled A and B. In routine deployment, the two transmitters split the assigned tuning band, so each normally carries only one-half of the intended frequency span. Field engineers note, however, that this balanced arrangement changes immediately after the loss of one transmitter: the surviving unit must then shoulder the full band, and its wear profile is no longer the same as under normal dual-operation conditions. The overall platform can continue its mission only while the power unit remains available and at least one transmitter is still usable. When both transmitters are healthy, their breakdown behavior is treated as separate. A further operational complication is that a hidden malfunction in either transmitter can bring down the whole subsystem because the problem is not successfully isolated in time. Internal reliability notation records the applicable constant loss intensities as follows: transmitter A experiences rate \(\lambda_A\) while B is still in service and rate \(\lambda_A'\) once B has dropped out; transmitter B analogously experiences rate \(\lambda_B\) while A is still in service and rate \(\lambda_B'\) once A has dropped out. The shared power unit and the fault-coverage mechanism are tracked by constant rates \(\lambda_P\) and \(\lambda_C\), respectively. Management wants a compact lifetime expression for this architecture before deciding whether additional redundancy is commercially justified.
input.question: Using this operating logic and the notation above, derive the expected run length until the high-voltage load-sharing subsystem is no longer able to deliver service, taking into account that the surviving transmitter faces a different loss behavior after its counterpart fails and that an uncontained transmitter fault also ends the mission.

λ_A.description: Constant failure rate of transmitter A when transmitter B is operating.

λ_B.description: Constant failure rate of transmitter B when transmitter A is operating.

λ_A'.description: Constant failure rate of transmitter A when transmitter B has failed (dependent/load-sharing rate).

λ_B'.description: Constant failure rate of transmitter B when transmitter A has failed (dependent/load-sharing rate).

λ_P.description: Constant failure rate of the power supply.

λ_C.description: Constant failure rate of fault coverage (undetected fault causing system failure).

input.background: At a nuclear facility, the engineering assurance team is reviewing the long-run cooling readiness of System XYZ for a 100,000 h operating horizon. The configuration uses five water pumps in parallel support of the reactor cooling process. Based on vendor history and maintenance records, each pump is treated as having the same 0.995 chance of remaining available across that interval, and the performance of one pump is taken not to affect the others. Operations has noted that the cooling arrangement is considered acceptable as long as no more than one of the five pumps is unavailable, since the reactor can continue to be supported when at least four pumps are still working. This review is being prepared for a broader resilience memo that also mentions inspection practices and contingency procedures, although those items are outside the immediate calculation.
input.question: Under these assumptions, what overall service readiness should be reported for System XYZ over 100,000 h?

n.description: Total number of water pumps in System XYZ.

p.description: Reliability of each individual pump over a period of 100,000 hours.

k.description: Minimum number of pumps that must function for the system to operate (k-out-of-n requirement).

input.background: An operations group is assessing post-cycle recovery performance for a piece of equipment assembled from $k$ replaceable units. Over a planned run of length $t$, each unit remains serviceable with probability $p$. Once that run ends, the equipment is taken out of service, inspected, and every unit that did not make it through the run is replaced before the equipment can be released back into use. The technician’s replacement time is standardized at $s$ for each unit changed. From a scheduling perspective, the main concern is whether the maintenance turnaround after shutdown is short enough to avoid disrupting the next deployment.
input.question: Based on this setup, what is the probability that the equipment will be ready to operate again within the $2s$ period immediately following the stop?

k.description: Number of units in the instrument.

p.description: Reliability (probability of not failing) of each unit during time t.

s.description: Time needed by the technician to replace one failed unit; the problem asks for readiness within time 2s after stop.

input.background: An engineering team is reviewing the run-readiness of a modular system built from two supplier classes of components. The assembly contains $m$ units from class I and $n$ units from class II. Over a planned operating window of length $t$, each class I unit is expected to remain functioning with likelihood $p_1$, while each class II unit remains functioning with likelihood $p_2$. Individual unit outcomes over that window are treated as unrelated to one another. Due to design redundancy rules, the system is considered serviceable during the full window only if at least two class I units and at least two class II units are still working at the same time. Managers are not concerned here with repair logistics, replacement cost, or which specific units survive, only whether the assembled system clears the minimum support requirement.
input.question: Based on these operating rules, what is the overall chance that the assembled device remains serviceable for the entire assigned time $t$?

m.description: Number of type I units in the device.

n.description: Number of type II units in the device.

p1.description: Reliability (probability of operating for assigned time t) of each type I unit.

p2.description: Reliability (probability of operating for assigned time t) of each type II unit.

input.background: An engineering team is reviewing a two-tier support assembly that must remain functional throughout a planned service window of length $t$. The assembly is built with $m$ modules from supplier class I and $n$ modules from supplier class II. Based on prior field experience, any single class I module has a probability $p_1$ of still being up for the full window, and any single class II module has a probability $p_2$ of doing the same. Each module’s outcome over the window is treated as unaffected by the others. Operational policy is strict: the assembly is considered available only if at least two class I modules and at least two class II modules are still running at the same time by the end of the window. Although technicians sometimes discuss load-sharing, maintenance quality, and installation conditions, for this review management wants to use only the stated component profile.
input.question: For the current configuration with $m=5$, $p_1=0.9$, $n=7$, and $p_2=0.8$, what is the overall chance that the assembly remains available for the full service window?

m.description: Number of type I units in the device.

p1.description: Reliability for assigned time t of each type I unit.

n.description: Number of type II units in the device.

p2.description: Reliability for assigned time t of each type II unit.

input.background: An operations team is reviewing a service unit built with three identical modules. At any given moment, the service only needs two modules running to keep customer-facing functions available, while the third module waits in reserve and is brought in only if needed. The handoff logic and fault detection are treated as flawless, so there is no loss during monitoring or changeover. When a module is actively carrying load, its breakdown pace is $\lambda$; when it is sitting in reserve, it is assumed not to deteriorate at all. The modules are treated as behaving independently of one another.
input.question: For an operating horizon of length $t$, what expression should the team use for the chance that this service arrangement is still up and meeting its requirement?

lambda.description: Active component failure rate per hour used by the textbook answer.

t.description: Time horizon in hours used by the textbook answer.

input.background: An operations team is reviewing a protection setup built around three interchangeable units. Day-to-day service can be maintained as long as any two units are running, while the third unit is kept on standby at the start and only brought in if needed. The engineering note for this configuration assumes the handover logic always detects a loss immediately and places the standby unit into service without error or delay. While a unit is actively running, its breakdown pace is taken to be $\lambda$ per hour, and the standby unit is treated as not wearing out before it is called upon. The team wants a concise view of how dependable this arrangement is under those assumptions before using it in a service commitment discussion.
input.question: Under this setup, when $\lambda=0.005$ per hour, what is the chance the arrangement is still able to deliver service through $t=10 \mathrm{~h}$, and what is the expected operating time before the setup can no longer meet the requirement?

lambda.description: Active failure rate of each component, given as 0.005 per hour.

t.description: Time duration in hours at which reliability is evaluated.

input.background: A cooling system for a reactor has four identical cooling loops. Each cooling loop has two identical pumps connected in parallel. The cooling system requires that at least 3 of the 4 cooling loops operate successfully. The reliability of a pump over the life span of the plant is $R_p=0.75$.
input.question: Calculate the reliability of the cooling system.

R_p.description: Reliability of a single pump over the life span of the plant.

num_cooling_loops.description: Total number of identical cooling loops in the cooling system.

min_loops_required.description: Minimum number of cooling loops that must operate successfully for the system to function (k-out-of-n requirement).

pumps_per_loop.description: Number of identical pumps connected in parallel within each cooling loop.

input.background: A fleet planning team is reviewing dispatch-readiness assumptions for a four-engine aircraft configuration, with two power units mounted on each wing. For the flight segment under discussion, operations engineering treats each engine as having a 0.98 chance of remaining available through the entire mission window. For this quick planning exercise, a problem affecting one engine is not assumed to change the status of the others. The aircraft is considered capable of completing the mission and getting on the ground safely as long as at least any two engines are still available. The team wants a single top-line figure that can be used in internal risk and service planning discussions.
input.question: Based on these operating assumptions, what overall chance should the airline assign to the aircraft successfully getting through the mission?

R_e.description: Reliability of each individual engine for the duration of a flight mission.

num_engines.description: Total number of engines on the aircraft (two on each wing).

min_engines_required.description: Minimum number of engines required for the aircraft to land successfully.

input.background: A small organization is setting up a temporary working group for an upcoming initiative. There are 10 eligible people available to be considered, and management wants the group to consist of exactly 3 people. The order in which names are discussed or listed is not meant to change the makeup of the group, although there may be informal debate about seniority, availability, and fit.
input.question: Based on these staffing rules, how many distinct 3-person working groups can be created from the 10 eligible people?

total_people.description: Total number of people from whom the committee is to be formed.

committee_size.description: Number of people to be chosen to form the committee.

output.category: Probability Space Related (e.g., number of states)

input.background: A flight-operations risk team is reviewing dispatch guidance for a four-engine aircraft configured with two engines on each wing. In principle, crews can complete a mission and recover the aircraft even when not all powerplants remain available, but the company’s handling notes also stress balance and controllability considerations across the two wings. For a single mission, each engine is assumed to remain available with probability $\mathrm{R}_{\mathrm{e}}=0.98$, and the loss of one engine does not affect the others. Management wants a simple mission-level success figure for this configuration to support internal planning and resilience reporting.
input.question: Under the operating requirement that the aircraft must finish the mission with at least one working engine on each wing, what overall mission success rate should be reported?

Re.description: Reliability of each individual engine for the duration of a flight mission.

num_engines_per_wing.description: Number of engines on each wing of the aircraft.

min_functioning_engines_per_wing.description: Minimum number of functioning engines required on each wing for a successful mission (at least one per wing).

input.background: A product team is using a normalized one-dimensional engagement score, denoted by $X$, that can only fall between 0 and 1. Internal calibration notes indicate that the way values are distributed across this scale follows the rule $$f(x)=\begin{cases}2x & 0\leq \mathrm{x}\leq 1 \\ 0 & \text{otherwise.}\end{cases}$$ In operational terms, this means higher scores within the admissible range occur more heavily than lower ones, while anything outside the 0 to 1 band is not feasible. Leadership wants a complete lookup rule for threshold-based reporting so teams can quickly tell what share of cases fall at or below any chosen cutoff on the scorecard.
