input.question: Based on the calibration rule above, write the full threshold-to-share function for $X$; that is, for any value on the scale, determine the proportion of observations that would be at or below that level.

X.description: Random variable X with the given probability density function, used to derive its cumulative distribution function.

input.background: An internal scoring system produces a continuous index $X$ that can take values only between 0 and 1. Operationally, higher scores occur more often than lower ones, following the rule $$f(x)= \begin{cases}2 x & 0 \leq \mathrm{x} \leq 1 \\ 0 & \text { otherwise. }\end{cases}$$ Product managers want a single benchmark that splits the long-run score distribution into two equal halves. Although teams sometimes discuss other cutoff rules for reporting, this review is concerned only with the point that leaves the same share of cases on each side.
input.question: Determine the score level $m$ that serves as this halfway benchmark for $X$, that is, the point below which 50% of outcomes fall and above which the remaining 50% fall.

X.description: Random variable X with the given probability density function f(x) = 2x on [0,1], used to find its median by solving F(m) = 1/2.

target_cumulative_probability.description: Target cumulative probability defining the halfway benchmark, used as F(m) = 1/2.

input.background: A nuclear generating station is reviewing the dependability of the ventilation radioactivity warning arrangement used to support shutdown decisions. The architecture is deliberately layered: there are five identical monitoring channels serving the air-handling system, and plant procedures treat the overall warning as actionable once at least three channels indicate that the airborne reading has reached a dangerous level. Within any one channel, there are three identical sensors, and the channel itself is treated as having detected the dangerous condition when at least two of those three sensors respond accordingly. Engineering records state that each individual sensor has a failure rate of 0.001 per day, while a shared within-channel cause that can disable all sensors in that channel occurs at a rate of 0.0005 per day. Management wants a channel-level view for different operating durations so maintenance planning and protection reviews are not based only on component specifications.
input.question: For different elapsed times $t$, determine the reliability of a single monitoring channel under this decision logic.

sensor_failure_rate.description: Failure rate of each individual sensor per day (lambda = 0.001/day).

common_cause_failure_rate.description: Common-cause failure rate of all sensors in a channel per day (lambda_c = 0.0005/day).

num_sensors_per_channel.description: Number of identical sensors in each channel.

sensor_voting_threshold.description: Minimum number of sensors that must register dangerous radioactivity for the channel to register it (2-out-of-3 voting logic).

input.background: A maternal-fetal medicine team is reviewing results from a small third-trimester medication study involving 65 pregnant women who had already been identified as having elevated concern for pregnancy-induced hypertension. Participants were assigned to receive either 100 mg of aspirin daily or a matching placebo as part of routine trial follow-up. Of the 34 women who received aspirin, 4 went on to develop hypertension before delivery, whereas 11 of the 31 women in the placebo arm did so. Investigators want a concise summary that can be used in discussions about whether the aspirin regimen appears to lower the occurrence of this complication, while recognizing that bedside decisions will still depend on broader clinical judgment and not this study alone.
input.question: Based on these study results, by how many percentage points did the share of women who developed hypertension differ between the aspirin arm and the placebo arm, and what 95% comparison range should be reported for that gap?

Hypertension_Aspirin.description: Hypertension outcome in the aspirin group (number of women developing hypertension out of total in aspirin group). This variable and Hypertension_Placebo represent the same outcome measure (hypertension status) for the same sample of 65 women, split by treatment group.

Hypertension_Placebo.description: Hypertension outcome in the placebo group (number of women developing hypertension out of total in placebo group). This variable and Hypertension_Aspirin represent the same outcome measure (hypertension status) for the same sample of 65 women, split by treatment group.

input.background: A Los Angeles County health team reviewed whether job-related sound conditions might be linked to later diagnoses of acoustic neuromas among men aged 25-69. The review was limited to county residents in that age range. Investigators initially identified 118 men with the condition, although 28 could not be interviewed for practical reasons. For 86 men who remained in the review, the team also located and interviewed one nearby comparison subject of the same race and within five years of age so that each diagnosed man could be considered alongside a broadly similar community counterpart. The interview process was handled in the same way for both members of each pair and covered prior life and work circumstances, with particular attention to whether the person had worked in a loud-noise environment. Across all completed interviews, 58 of the men with acoustic neuroma and 46 of the comparison men said they had been exposed to loud noise at work. Looking pair by pair, there were 20 matched pairs in which the diagnosed man reported such exposure while his comparison subject did not, and 8 pairs in which the comparison subject reported such exposure while the diagnosed man did not. The clinical team is preparing a concise conclusion for colleagues and wants the matched structure of the fieldwork respected rather than treating everyone as unrelated respondents.
input.question: Using the completed matched interviews, determine whether workplace exposure to loud noise appears more common among the men with acoustic neuroma than among their matched comparison subjects, and summarize the strength of that evidence in a way suitable for a medical audience.

paired_data.description: 2x2 table of matched case-control pairs classified by exposure to loud noise at work. The discordant pairs (20 with case exposed/control unexposed, 8 with control exposed/case unexposed) are the key quantities used in McNemar's test.

exposure_cases.description: Number of cases exposed and unexposed to loud noise at work. Used to compute the proportion of exposed cases (58/86 = 0.674).

exposure_controls.description: Number of controls exposed and unexposed to loud noise at work. Used to compute the proportion of exposed controls (46/86 = 0.535).

input.background: An occupational health review in Los Angeles County is revisiting records on a rare hearing-related tumour among men aged 25–69. The original fieldwork located 118 potentially eligible men, although 28 could not be completed because of issues such as nonresponse or other practical barriers. For 86 completed patient records, the team also obtained a comparison interview from a nearby resident of the same race and within five years of age, and both sides were asked the same life-history questions. One issue of interest for employer liability discussions is whether a history of loud workplace noise shows up more often on the tumour side than on the matched comparison side. Across all completed interviews, 58 patient records and 46 comparison records indicated loud noise at work. Looking specifically at the matched pairs, there were 20 pairs in which only the patient reported loud workplace noise and 8 pairs in which only the comparison person reported it. Management is less interested in the broader interview narrative—such as commuting, neighborhood conditions, or other personal experiences—than in a single summary number that captures how strongly the workplace noise history is tilted toward the tumour group within these matched pairings.
input.question: Using the completed matched pairs, what single comparative exposure measure should be reported for the link between acoustic neuroma and loud noise at work?

discordant_pairs_case_exposed_control_no.description: Number of discordant case-control pairs where the case was exposed to loud noise at work but the matched control was not.

discordant_pairs_control_exposed_case_no.description: Number of discordant case-control pairs where the matched control was exposed to loud noise at work but the case was not.

confidence_level.description: Confidence level for the matched-pair odds-ratio interval.

input.background: A clinical review team is revisiting records from 29 paediatric and adult patients with severe lactic acidosis who received intravenous dichloroacetate at 50 mg/kg body weight. For each case, the file captures the short-term change after treatment in arterial lactate, bicarbonate, and pH, along with the length of time the patient was known to remain alive, as listed in the table below. Physicians hope these early chemistry shifts might help them tell which patients are doing better, although bedside decisions were also influenced by age, underlying illness, and intensity of supportive care. One record is unusual: the last listed survival duration reflects that the patient was still alive at last follow-up rather than a completed outcome.
input.question: The authors tried to judge whether larger or smaller post-treatment changes in these arterial measures tended to go with longer or shorter survival by comparing the ordered patient records. From a results-review standpoint, is that approach defensible when one patient's survival duration is only known to exceed 24456 hours because the patient was still alive?

Survival_time.description: Survival time in hours for each patient after administration of dichloroacetate. Patient 29's value is censored (still alive). The answer discusses the validity of using Spearman's rank correlation with this variable, noting the censored observation receives the highest rank.

Lactate.description: Change in arterial lactate level for each patient. One of the metabolic variables examined for association with survival time using Spearman's rank correlation.

Bicarbonate.description: Change in arterial bicarbonate level for each patient. One of the metabolic variables examined for association with survival time using Spearman's rank correlation.

pH.description: Change in arterial pH level for each patient. One of the metabolic variables examined for association with survival time using Spearman's rank correlation.

output.category: Evaluation of Reliability of Statistical Results

input.background: A nutrition and weight-management team is reviewing historical observations reported by Owen et al. input.background:
A transplant program is reviewing follow-up results for 37 bone marrow transplant recipients first discussed in Exercise 12.3. The original review linked several patient and donor characteristics with the appearance of acute graft-versus-host disease (GvHD), and the service later used diagnosis, recipient age and sex, donor age and sex, donor pregnancy history, the MECLR/MLR index, and GvHD status in an internal time-to-outcome risk review for post-transplant survival. After trimming the list down to the factors that still carried material signal, the summary retained the following entries:

Variable | Regression coefficient | Standard error
GvHD (0=No, 1=Yes) | 2.306 | 0.5898
CML (0=No, 1=Yes) | -2.508 | 0.8095

Clinicians note that bedside decisions are never driven by any one number alone, since conditioning regimen, infection control, supportive care intensity, and case complexity can also shape outcomes. Even so, leadership wants a concise risk message for acute GvHD that can be included in a survival briefing for non-technical stakeholders.
input.question: Using the figures reported for GvHD, what range should the team present, under its usual 95% assurance convention, for the multiplicative change in a patient's ongoing risk of death when acute GvHD is present versus absent?

GvHD_coefficient.description: Regression coefficient for GvHD from the backward stepwise Cox regression model.

GvHD_SE.description: Standard error of the regression coefficient for GvHD from the Cox regression model.

input.background:
A transplant program is reviewing a small historical cohort of 37 bone marrow recipients to understand which case features appear most closely tied to post-transplant survival. An earlier internal exercise assembled information on acute graft-versus-host disease occurrence together with diagnosis, recipient age and sex, donor age and sex, donor pregnancy history, and the MECLR/MLR index. After a screening process that trimmed the list to the factors thought to matter most, the final decision-support summary reported the following effects for time-to-outcome tracking:

Variable | Regression coefficient | Standard error
GvHD (0=No, 1=Yes) | 2.306 | 0.5898
CML (0=No, 1=Yes) | -2.508 | 0.8095

Clinical leadership is interested in whether these retained signals are strong enough to inform how confidently such a summary could be used in discussions, especially since not every patient experienced the outcome of interest and the review was based on a fairly limited case pool.
input.question: From a governance and decision-support standpoint, how much confidence should the transplant team place in this survival summary, given that it was built from 37 patients with 18 deaths?

sample_size.description: Total number of patients in the bone marrow transplant study.

number_of_deaths.description: Number of death events among the 37 patients, which determines the power of the Cox regression analysis.

output.category: Evaluation of Reliability of Statistical Results

input.background: A hospital transfusion service is considering whether it can shift from a radioactive red-cell labelling workflow to a non-radioactive alternative for routine red cell volume work, partly because of handling burden, staff training, and operational convenience. For 19 patients, both approaches were applied at essentially the same time, and the paired readings are listed in the table. In the published write-up by Cavill et al. (1988), the authors relied on a matched-pair significance check and reported $\mathrm{P}>0.05$, after which they stated that the side-by-side use of the two approaches 'showed no consistent clinically significant difference between the two'. Management wants to know whether that conclusion really supports treating the two measurement routes as practically interchangeable in service use, especially since clinicians care about how closely individual patient readings line up, not just whether one method is systematically higher on average.
input.question: Review the authors’ approach and the way they framed their conclusion. Based on the paired patient results in the table and the statement tied to $\mathrm{P}>0.05$, does their analysis justify the claim that the two measurement approaches show no consistent clinically significant difference and can be regarded as giving sufficiently similar patient-level results for operational decision-making?

51Cr_volume.description: Red cell volume (ml) measured using the radioactive 51Cr cell label for each of the 19 patients. Paired with Biotin volume measurements on the same patients.

Biotin_volume.description: Red cell volume (ml) measured using the non-radioactive biotin cell label for each of the 19 patients. Paired with 51Cr volume measurements on the same patients.

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A regional hospital network is reviewing contingency planning for its transfusion inventory ahead of a high-demand period. Historical intake patterns suggest that, for any single unrelated donor, the chance that a collected unit turns out to be blood group B is 0.08. Operations staff are discussing what kinds of shortfalls might realistically occur when 1 pint is collected from each of 100 unrelated donors, especially in scenarios where the inbound mix is less favorable than expected. Although the broader conversation has included concerns about storage, routing, and cross-site balancing, leadership wants a clear read on one very specific edge case within this 100-donor collection run.
input.question: In that 100-donor collection run, what is the chance that the system receives no group B blood at all—that is, 0 pints of group B?

p_blood_group_B.description: The probability of a single donor being blood group B.

n_donors.description: The number of unrelated blood donors (sample size), each providing one pint of blood.

k_pints_group_B.description: The number of pints of group B blood for which the probability is being calculated (0 pints in this case).

input.background: A hospital haematology service was reviewing whether a newer non-radioactive tagging workflow could be discussed internally as giving practically similar red cell volume readings to the long-used ${ }^{51} \mathrm{Cr}$ process. For 19 people already sent to the service for red cell volume assessment, both readings were taken at the same visit, and the paired results are listed in the tables below (Cavill et al., 1988). The published write-up emphasized that a routine side-by-side comparison produced no clear overall separation between the two reading streams and therefore suggested there was no consistent clinically meaningful gap. At the same time, some clinicians noted that these cases did not come from a broad wellness screening pool but from the service’s usual referral pathway, where patients are often sent precisely because a measurement is needed for a clinical reason.
input.question: When judging how far this side-by-side exercise can support the claim that the two approaches show no consistent clinically important difference, why does it matter that all 19 individuals had already been referred for red cell volume measurement?

51Cr_volume.description: Red cell volume (ml) measured using radioactive 51Cr cell labels for each of the 19 patients.

Biotin_volume.description: Red cell volume (ml) measured using non-radioactive biotin cell labels for each of the 19 patients.

output.category: Evaluation of Reliability of Statistical Results

input.background: A hospital transfusion and haematology team is reviewing whether a newer non-radioactive workflow based on biotin-labelled cells could be used alongside, or potentially in place of, the long-established ${ }^{51}\mathrm{Cr}$ process for red cell volume assessment. Table records paired readings taken on the same 19 patients under both laboratory workflows. The original write-up noted that, at an overall level, the two approaches did not appear to diverge in a way that would alter routine clinical decisions. Even so, method adoption has practical implications for isotope handling, scheduling, and patient communication, so laboratory leadership is looking beyond the headline conclusion. During case review, staff noticed that a few patients showed much wider gaps between the two readings than the rest. There is also a pre-analytic concern specific to the biotin-based workflow: prior egg consumption may interfere with the reading, and the case notes indicate that at least one of the patients with a large mismatch had eaten eggs for breakfast.
input.question: When deciding how much confidence to place in the side-by-side comparison of the two workflows, should the review explicitly reflect the additional breakfast information for the patients with the largest discrepancies, especially subjects 1 and 18?

51Cr_volume.description: Red cell volume measured using the radioactive (51Cr) cell label for each of the 19 patients. Used together with Biotin volume to compute between-method differences and limits of agreement.

Biotin_volume.description: Red cell volume measured using the non-radioactive (biotin) cell label for each of the 19 patients. Used together with 51Cr volume to compute between-method differences and limits of agreement.

Patient.description: Patient identifier used to identify specific subjects (particularly patients 1 and 18) for potential exclusion based on egg consumption affecting the biotin method.

input.background: A clinical development team is revisiting a small legacy pharmacology review from Furst and Paulus (1975) to understand whether exposure to clonixin appears to differ between patients with rheumatoid arthritis and otherwise normal volunteers after the same oral dose regimen of three 250 mg tablets. Blood samples were taken over the first 8 hours after dosing, and the available records summarize post-dose serum clonixin readings for 12 participants in the rheumatoid arthritis group and 12 in the comparison group. The baseline pre-dose readings were not included in the original write-up, but for this review the team is willing to treat the starting level at time 0 as absent. Although clinicians have noted that meal timing, symptom burden, concurrent care, and ordinary person-to-person variability may all affect how quickly a drug rises and falls, management wants a concise side-by-side assessment of overall exposure and the highest observed concentration reached in each group based only on the values provided.
input.question: Using the measurements provided and taking the time-0 clonixin level to be 0.0, determine whether the rheumatoid arthritis group and the control group differ in (i) the highest serum clonixin level reached and (ii) the total 0-to-8-hour exposure reflected by the concentration-time profile.

time.description: Time points (in hours) after clonixin administration at which serum levels were measured. The 0-hour value is assumed to be 0.0 as stated in the question.

clonixin_levels_RA.description: Serum clonixin levels (μg/ml) over time for the 12 patients with rheumatoid arthritis. These are the same subjects as in clonixin_levels_RA, grouped under the rheumatoid arthritis condition.

clonixin_levels_control.description: Serum clonixin levels (μg/ml) over time for the 12 normal control subjects. These are the same subjects as in clonixin_levels_control, grouped under the control condition.

input.background: A regional blood service is reviewing an added screening step for donor intake. Prior external reviews of a lie-detection device suggest that, in operating terms, it correctly flags deceptive responses 0.76 of the time and clears truthful responses 0.63 of the time. Management is considering using this device alongside the routine intake question about drug use before accepting donations. For this operational discussion, staff are asked to work under the simplifying assumption that people who do not use drugs answer that question honestly. The broader policy debate also includes cost, queue times, and public perception, but the immediate concern is the safety mix of donations that would still get through the process.
input.question: Suppose 5% of potential donors are drug users and one third of those donors deny it when asked. Under the proposed intake process, what share of the blood donations ultimately accepted would come from drug users?

sensitivity.description: Sensitivity of the polygraph (lie-detector), i.e., the probability of correctly detecting a liar. The answer uses 1 - sensitivity = 0.24 as the probability that a lying drug user passes the test.

specificity.description: Specificity of the polygraph, i.e., the probability that a non-drug user (truth-teller) passes the test. Used directly in the denominator and numerator of the final proportion calculation.

drug_user_prevalence.description: Proportion of potential donors who use drugs (5%). Used in the calculation of the proportion of blood donations from drug users.

proportion_lying.description: Proportion of drug users who lie about their drug use (one third ≈ 0.33). Two thirds admit and are excluded; the remaining third undergo polygraph testing.

input.background: In many front-line child health settings, especially where laboratory support is limited, clinicians need a quick bedside rule to help decide which young patients with cough or breathing-related complaints are more likely to have chest involvement and should be considered for antibiotic treatment, versus those whose illness is more likely confined to the upper airways. Program managers are reviewing whether breathing speed alone could serve as a practical triage signal. The distribution of children already classified as having lower respiratory tract infection (LRI) or upper respiratory tract infection (URI) across the breathing-rate bands shown in the table is available for this review, although staff are also aware that age, nutrition, and timing of presentation can affect how any simple rule performs in practice.

For each threshold, set up the corresponding two-group summary showing how children would be sorted into lower versus higher breathing-rate groups against the actual LRI/URI status. input.background: Frontline child-health programs in resource-constrained settings often have to decide quickly which infants arriving with cough or breathing-related illness should be treated as likely chest infection cases needing antibiotics and which can be managed as having an illness confined to the upper airways. Because laboratory support and imaging are frequently unavailable or delayed, programme managers are interested in whether a simple bedside sign could be turned into a practical triage rule. The records summarized in the table compare breathing-rate bands for infants ultimately classified as having lower respiratory tract infection (LRI) versus upper respiratory tract infection (URI). For planning purposes, officials note that across all infants presenting with acute respiratory infection in the wider population, only 3% are expected to have LRI. The aim is to identify a breathing-rate trigger that is useful both for flagging the few true chest infections and for reassuring staff when that trigger is not met, while recognizing that overtreatment and missed treatment both carry costs.

input.background: A frontline child-health programme operating in resource-constrained clinics is reviewing whether one very quick bedside sign can support first-pass treatment decisions for infants arriving with acute cough or breathing complaints. The service challenge is operational rather than academic: clinicians need a practical rule to help separate children whose chest involvement is serious enough to justify antibiotics from those more likely to have infection limited to the upper airways, especially when laboratory support and senior review may not be immediately available. Table 1 summarises how children already classified as having lower respiratory tract infection (LRI) or upper respiratory tract infection (URI) were distributed across respiratory-rate bands. Programme managers are aware that breathing rate can be influenced by crying, fever, waiting-room delays, and handling during assessment, but they still want to understand the consequences of using a simple threshold in routine triage.
input.question: Suppose the clinic adopts a rule that any infant breathing at more than 50 breaths per minute is managed as if they have LRI and is therefore given antibiotics immediately. Based on Table 1, among all infants who would receive antibiotics under this rule, what share would be receiving them without actually having LRI? Also, among infants who truly have LRI, what share would be missed by this rule and therefore not receive antibiotics?

\hline 41-50 & 10 (7\%) & 46 (30\%) \\

input.background: A clinical services team is reviewing the enrollment profile from a low back pain study before giving too much weight to any later differences in patient progress. Table 3.5 summarizes the three care pathways used in the study—Short-wave diathermy, Osteopathy, and Placebo—and shows how the incoming patient mix looked at the point of presentation. Although the trial was intended to compare management options, physicians have noted that recovery expectations in this population can already differ depending on who entered each arm: age, sex mix, how long symptoms had been present, initial pain burden on the visual analogue scale, and whether spinal changes were seen on radiology may all shape what happens afterward. There is also some concern that unequal group sizes and ordinary referral patterns could make the groups look balanced on paper in some respects but not in others.
input.question: Using Table 3.5, how comfortable should the study team be that the three treatment groups started from a sufficiently similar clinical position, and what do any differences in baseline characteristics imply for interpreting later group differences in patient prognosis?

Before discussing treatment performance, they want an operational read on whether the three groups started from roughly the same position in terms of headcount, mix of men and women, age profile, how long symptoms had already been present, initial pain burden measured on the visual analogue scale, and the presence of radiological spinal abnormalities. The study team is also aware that some opening differences may matter more than others if they are closely tied to the way improvement will later be tracked.

input.background: A cardiology service was reviewing an older post-admission care initiative reported by Ahlmark and Saetre (1976), in which patients entering hospital after myocardial infarction were allocated on admission either to a beta-blocker pathway involving alprenolol or to usual care. The project was run openly, so ward teams were aware of which pathway each patient had been assigned to. Although the treatment plan was determined at admission, medication itself did not begin until two weeks later. During that interval, 60% of the original 393 patients were removed from further participation, most commonly because the patient died, the infarction diagnosis was not ultimately confirmed, or the beta-blocker was considered unsuitable. This left 162 patients who actually went on to treatment, of whom 69 received alprenolol and 93 received the control regimen. Administrators are trying to understand whether the resulting treated groups can be read at face value, given that real hospital workflows, evolving diagnoses, and bedside judgment often affect who remains eligible long enough to start the planned regimen.
input.question: From a study-quality and decision-process perspective, what features of this hospital trial could help explain why the number of patients withdrawn before treatment began may not have been the same in the alprenolol and control groups?

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A dermatology team carried out a small open, ward-based exploratory review involving 13 people with chronic skin disorders whose nighttime discomfort remained a practical management concern. The aim was to get an early operational sense of whether a commonly available pain-relief product might also help with overnight itching, while keeping the bedside routine straightforward. The six-night schedule was identical for all participants: no treatment on nights one and two, aspirin (900 mg) on the third and fourth nights, and then no treatment again on the fifth and sixth nights. Each night, two kinds of information were collected: scratching activity measured by a limb movement meter and, the following morning, the patient’s own rating of itching on a 10 cm linear analogue scale. For each patient, readings were averaged within each two-day period, and the paper by Daly and Shuster (1986) reported the summaries in this table as means (SE). The authors noted that itch and scratch varied both between patients and within the same patient over time, but that neither measure showed a consistent shift during the aspirin period. As the service considers whether such a pilot should shape future practice, some clinicians have also pointed to practical concerns such as the fixed ordering of nights, awareness of treatment, and possible changes simply from being observed repeatedly.
input.question: Based on the way this six-night pilot was organised, how strong is the study setup as evidence about whether aspirin itself changed itching or scratching, and what features of the arrangement should make decision-makers cautious when interpreting the results in this table?

input.background: A small exploratory clinical service review followed 13 people with chronic skin conditions whose night-time itching remained a management concern. The team wanted an early read on whether adding aspirin at 900 mg might make any practical difference to symptom burden. The schedule was fixed in sequence rather than tailored: no added medication on nights one and two, aspirin on nights three and four, and again no added medication on nights five and six. Each morning, patients marked how troublesome the itch had felt on a 10 cm line, while overnight scratching activity had been captured using a limb-movement device. For reporting purposes, each patient’s nightly records were condensed into three two-night summaries, and Table 1 shows the published averages with standard errors for the periods before treatment, during treatment, and after treatment. The authors’ narrative conclusion was that patients varied both from one another and from night to night, yet there was no clear overall shift in either itching or scratching while aspirin was being given.
input.question: If you were asked to review this pilot write-up for a clinical audience, explain how the investigators appear to have reached their conclusion from Table 1, and then comment on how the evidence should really have been handled before making a claim about whether aspirin changed itch severity or night-time scratching in these same 13 patients.

input.background: A dermatology team ran a small exploratory ward-based review involving 13 people with longstanding itchy skin conditions to see whether a commonly used analgesic might have any practical value for night-time symptoms. The schedule was fixed: no active product was used on nights one and two, aspirin 900 mg was given on nights three and four, and no active product was used again on nights five and six. Each night, scratching activity was tracked with a limb-movement device, and each patient also gave a next-morning rating of itch on a 10 cm line. For reporting purposes, each person’s nightly observations were combined into three two-night summaries: before treatment, during treatment, and after treatment. The published paper presented the group results in the table as mean values with values in parentheses, and commented that symptom levels varied both between patients and within the same patient over time, with no clear pattern of change during the aspirin period.
input.question: Senior clinicians then wrote that, because this review did not show an effect of oral aspirin, they could rule out the possibility that therapeutic doses of aspirin act centrally on pruritis. Looking only at what was actually done and reported here, explain why that business-like conclusion goes further than the study evidence can support.

linear_analogue_scale.description: Patient-reported itch assessment on a 10 cm linear analogue scale, averaged over each two-day period (before, during, and after aspirin treatment). The answer notes that the data show some improvement and discusses the width of confidence intervals.

nocturnal_limb_movements.description: Nocturnal limb movements measured by a limb movement meter, averaged over each two-day period (before, during, and after aspirin treatment). The answer references the observed data showing some improvement and discusses the inadequacy of the sample size.

sample_size.description: Number of patients in the study. The answer explicitly references this as a 'small study' to argue that the authors' conclusion of excluding an aspirin effect is incorrect.

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A renal-diabetes care team is reviewing an early internal evidence package before deciding whether to position captopril more prominently in treatment guidance for insulin-dependent diabetic patients with nephropathy who also present with elevated systolic blood pressure. The records in the table track each patient’s systolic reading at intake and again after 1 week, with patients assigned to either captopril or placebo. In the original write-up, the investigators looked separately within each arm at how readings moved over the week. Because the captopril arm showed a clear within-arm drop while the placebo arm did not, they argued that captopril should be viewed as a valuable new option for this patient segment. Clinical leadership wants to know whether that line of reasoning is solid enough for a treatment claim, especially given the small study, routine week-to-week fluctuation in blood pressure, and the practical need to distinguish a true treatment advantage from ordinary variation.
input.question: Based on the patient readings in the table and the way the original write-up framed the result, what is problematic about the investigators’ approach and about the conclusion they drew regarding captopril’s value relative to placebo?

input.background: A clinical development team is revisiting results from a small kidney-complication study in insulin-dependent diabetic patients to prepare internal messaging for a blood-pressure treatment candidate. Table 1 lists each patient’s systolic blood pressure at enrolment and again after one week, with patients having been assigned to either captopril or a look-alike inactive regimen. An earlier write-up focused on whether readings moved noticeably within each arm on its own and, based on that presentation, promoted captopril as a promising option for hypertensive patients in this population. Before that message is reused in medical and market-access discussions, the team wants to check whether the claim is really supported when the two arms are assessed against each other rather than narrated separately. Keep in mind that short-term blood-pressure movement can also reflect ordinary week-to-week fluctuation, regression toward usual levels, and the fact that the two arms do not have the same number of patients.
input.question: Using the patient records in Table 1, provide the appropriate assessment of whether captopril shows a genuine one-week benefit for systolic blood pressure beyond what would be expected from the comparison arm, and state what can reasonably be concluded about its value for treating hypertension in insulin-dependent diabetics with nephropathy.

input.background: A regional transfusion service is stress-checking a niche inventory scenario for an upcoming hospital support window. In its donor base, the share of people with blood group B is 0.08. Operations is considering a routine collection run in which 1 pint is drawn from each of 100 unrelated donors, but the immediate concern is not total volume; it is whether the run could leave the network with an unusually thin amount of type B stock for short-notice requests. Other issues such as routing, shelf-life coordination, and ward-level demand forecasting are being discussed separately, but for this review the team wants to focus only on the chance of a very low type B yield from that 100-donor run.
input.question: For this 100-donor collection plan, what is the overall chance that the service ends up with fewer than 3 pints of blood group B?

p_blood_group_B.description: The probability that a single donor has blood group B.

n_donors.description: The number of unrelated blood donors (sample size), each providing one pint of blood.

input.background: A medical affairs team is comparing two external research summaries before deciding how strongly to position a product claim in internal briefing materials. One summary highlights a headline result reported as P<0.001, while the other highlights a result reported as P=0.02. Some nontechnical stakeholders have started treating the first study as if it automatically demonstrated a bigger real-world benefit than the second. However, the evidence review group has noted that such headline figures can be influenced by factors other than the practical size of the underlying difference, including how the work was set up, how much information was collected, and how variable the observations were. The team wants a short explanation for executives, consistent with the discussion in section 16.3.6.
input.question: Why would it be unsafe for the team to conclude, solely from seeing P<0.001 in one study and P=0.02 in another, that the first study established a stronger underlying effect than the second?

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A team reviewing evidence from two otherwise matching investigations has been challenged by a striking mismatch in the headline results: one report highlights a finding described as P < 0.001, while the other presents P = 0.2. Leadership wants to understand how two efforts aimed at the same underlying business question could end up sending such different signals to decision-makers. In internal discussions, people have mentioned execution scale, natural case-to-case fluctuation, and the tendency for smaller initiatives to show more erratic swings in what gets observed, even when the underlying situation is not meaningfully different.
input.question: When comparing studies run at different scales, how does the number of cases included shape the size and stability of the observed effects, and how can that help explain why one study reported P < 0.001 while another reported P = 0.2?

study_size.description: The size of the studies (large vs. small), which is the factor examined for its effect on observed effects and P-values.

observed_effects.description: The observed effects from the studies, which tend to be closer together when studies are large and more variable when studies are small.

P_values.description: The P-values obtained from the two identical studies, which vary as a function of study size. The large discrepancy between the two values is the phenomenon being explained.

input.background: A maternity unit is preparing a brief note for staff after an unusually busy stretch in which six births were recorded one after another in the same labour ward during a single day. Historically, the share of baby boys in this setting is taken to be 0.52. For a communications example, the team wants to compare a few specific boy/girl orderings across these six consecutive deliveries, where B denotes a boy and G denotes a girl. The interest is in the exact recorded order, not just the total number of boys or girls, even though clinicians know many operational factors in the ward may feel important when people discuss such runs informally.
input.question: Among the following exact six-birth patterns for that day’s consecutive deliveries—GBGBGB, BBBGGG, and GBBBBB—which ordering would be expected to occur most often, and which would be expected to occur least often?

P_boy.description: The probability of a baby being a boy, used to determine which sequence is most/least likely.

Sequence.description: The three candidate sequences of boys (B) and girls (G) for six consecutive births, among which the most and least likely are to be identified.

input.background: A national apparel brand is reviewing how its adult sizing strategy aligns with the body profiles seen in its customer base. In an internal reference summary, the typical stature recorded for adult men is 179.1 cm with a spread of 5.84 cm, while for adult women the corresponding figures are 171.7 cm and 5.75 cm. For planning purposes, the sizing team is willing to treat the height pattern within each sex as following the usual bell-shaped profile. Although merchandising leaders have also raised issues such as regional preferences, footwear, and fit tolerance, the immediate task is limited to this reference summary.
input.question: If the company uses the average adult male height as a benchmark, what share of adult women would be expected to be taller than that benchmark?

men_height.description: Adult men's height distribution in cm.

women_height.description: Adult women's height distribution in cm.

input.background: A consumer apparel company is reviewing sizing strategy for a new unisex product line and wants to understand who makes up the very tall end of its adult customer base. Internal reference figures indicate that adult male height is centered at 179.1 cm with a spread of 5.84 cm, while adult female height is centered at 171.7 cm with a spread of 5.75 cm. For planning purposes, the team is willing to treat height patterns within each sex as following the usual bell-shaped profile. The market mix under consideration is 60% female overall. Although merchandising staff have also raised questions about regional differences, footwear preferences, and self-reported versus measured stature, management wants this pass to rely only on these summary benchmarks.
input.question: For adults who are above 182.9 cm (six feet), what share should the sizing team expect to be women?

men_height.description: Heights of adult men in the population, normally distributed with given mean and standard deviation.

women_height.description: Heights of adult women in the population, normally distributed with given mean and standard deviation.

proportion_female.description: Proportion of adults that are female, used in the Bayes' theorem calculation.

height_threshold.description: Height threshold (182.9 cm / six feet) used to determine the proportion of adults taller than this value who are women.

input.background: A public health planning team is reviewing long-run female mortality patterns in England and Wales using the historical figures shown in the table from the Office of Population Censuses and Surveys Mortality Statistics. At first glance, the archive seems to tell two different stories at once: within every listed age band, the annual number of deaths per 1000 women was markedly lower in 1983 than in 1931-5, yet the headline figure for women taken together does not move at all. Senior stakeholders are concerned that this could be misread in briefing notes as evidence that half a century of gains in survival somehow failed to improve the overall picture. The team suspects that broad shifts in who makes up the female population across age bands may matter, especially given longer life expectancy and the growing share of women living into older ages, but they want the explanation framed clearly for a nontechnical audience using only the figures already provided.
input.question: If you were preparing a short policy briefing based on the table, how would you explain to decision-makers why the overall annual death rate per 1000 women of all ages stayed at 11.4 even though every age-specific rate became lower?

Age.description: Age groups of females in England and Wales, used to illustrate how the age structure of the population affects the overall death rate.

Death_rate_1931_5.description: Annual death rates per 1000 females in 1931-5 for each age group and all ages combined. Compared with 1983 rates to show age-specific declines counterbalanced by changed age structure.

Death_rate_1983.description: Annual death rates per 1000 females in 1983 for each age group and all ages combined. Compared with 1931-5 rates to show age-specific declines counterbalanced by changed age structure.

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A public dental-health team is revisiting a published summary from Carmichael et al. (1989) while preparing a briefing on whether long-term exposure to fluoridated water may be linked to differences in severe tooth damage among young children across socioeconomic groups. The summary is organised by social class and reports the share of five-year-olds with five or more decayed, missing, or filled teeth (% dmft), shown separately for children who had lived continuously either in a fluoridated area or in a nearby area without fluoridation. Some staff have suggested applying the usual chi-squared significance check to this breakdown so they can present a formal comparison between the two areas, but others are concerned that the way the information is reported may not line up cleanly with what that procedure expects.
input.question: Given the way the results are presented, is it reasonable to use a chi-squared test to compare % dmft by social class in the fluoridated and non-fluoridated areas?

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A clinical review team is revisiting the patient records reported by Ayesh et al. (1987) for 65 people with rheumatoid arthritis who received sodium aurothiomalate (SA). For each patient, the file shows age, the accumulated amount of SA received, and the sulphoxidation index (SI), a laboratory measure linked to how well the body converts an organic divalent alkyl sulphide into its sulphoxide form. To support a discussion about treatment tolerance, the records in the table overleaf are already split into 28 patients who did not experience major adverse reactions and 37 who did. Some SI entries appear as ">80.0", reflecting the way the laboratory result was recorded rather than an exact reading. Clinicians are mainly interested in whether the SI readings in the two patient sets appear concentrated in a narrow band or whether a smaller number of patients sit far away from the bulk of the group.
input.question: If you were preparing a simple side-by-side display of how often different SI ranges occur for the two patient groups in the table overleaf, what practical issue would you run into from the recorded SI values, and what overall pattern would you say each group's SI values follows?

SI_without_adverse_reactions.description: Sulphoxidation index (SI) values for the 28 patients without major adverse reactions. Some values are right-censored (>80.0). The answer discusses the difficulty of drawing histograms and the skewed shape of the distribution of SI in this group.

SI_with_adverse_reactions.description: Sulphoxidation index (SI) values for the 37 patients with major adverse reactions. Some values are right-censored (>80.0). The answer discusses the difficulty of drawing histograms and the skewed shape of the distribution of SI in this group.

input.background: An obstetric care team is reviewing bedside blood-pressure practice after noticing that the cuff reading and the intra-arterial reading do not always line up for the same patient encounter. For 50 pregnant women, systolic pressure was taken in the same arm by both approaches at essentially the same time, and body weight and upper-arm circumference were recorded as part of the routine assessment; age was also available from the clinical record. The team is less concerned with isolated case anecdotes than with whether certain maternal characteristics systematically go with larger gaps between the two readings, since that would affect how staff interpret ward measurements and equipment choice in day-to-day care.
input.question: Using these records, assess whether the size and direction of the cuff-versus-direct systolic reading gap appear to vary in any meaningful way with a woman’s weight, arm circumference, or age.

Diff (I-D).description: Difference between indirect and direct systolic blood pressure measurements (I-D), used as the dependent variable in the correlation and regression analysis.

Weight (kg).description: Body weight of the pregnant women in kilograms, used as an independent variable in correlation and regression analysis with Diff (I-D).

Arm circumference (cm).description: Arm circumference of the pregnant women in centimeters, used as an independent variable in correlation analysis with Diff (I-D).

Age.description: Age of the pregnant women, used as an independent variable in correlation analysis with Diff (I-D).

input.background: A field medicine team reviewing a rapid-acclimatization trek in East Africa is reassessing hormone-monitoring records from 15 expedition members after the group moved quickly to 4300 m. For each person, plasma aldosterone was checked at 09:00 at the staging location and then again on the following two mornings at high altitude. The log also includes each climber’s acute mountain sickness (AMS) score, which the clinical staff used as a parallel indicator of how uncomfortable the ascent became, although several operational factors besides symptoms may have influenced individual readings. Management wants a concise summary of how the morning aldosterone profile shifted across the three scheduled check points.
input.question: Using the measurements provided, compare the plasma aldosterone readings across the three scheduled days and determine which day-to-day comparisons show a clear difference that is unlikely to be due to routine subject-to-subject fluctuation alone.

input.question: Using the records in the table, give a 95% range of plausible values for the average within-person change in plasma aldosterone between Day 1 at low altitude and Day 2 at high altitude.

input.background: Following external criticism of a two-period comparison of bran biscuits and placebo biscuits used in the dietary management of patients with irritable bowel syndrome, the lead author defended the write-up by saying that this kind of patient study almost inevitably produces result ranges that straddle no difference, spread out substantially, and point in opposite directions at once. He suggested that, because the signals from this sort of crossover exercise are usually so imprecise, the whole way the findings were summarised is not really suitable for decision-making and will tend to generate outputs that are too ambiguous to matter. The debate has since been taken up more broadly by clinicians and editors, alongside side issues such as patient adherence, washout concerns, symptom volatility, and how much certainty small diet studies can realistically deliver.
input.question: From the standpoint of sound evidence appraisal, is it reasonable to claim that because the reported result range is broad and runs across both improvement and worsening, the analysis itself is unsuitable and the findings are therefore too vague to be meaningful?

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A women’s health outreach team is preparing briefing material for small-group counseling sessions and wants to avoid overstating how unusual certain patterns would be in a group this size. Their reference note treats each pregnancy as having the same 0.15 chance of ending in miscarriage, and the probability listing in the table summarizes what can happen when looking at groups of 10 pregnant women. Staff have also mentioned that public reactions are often driven by visible clusters rather than by the underlying baseline risk, so leadership wants a clear way to discuss how rarely very concentrated outcomes should be expected in such a session.
input.question: Using the table and the 15% benchmark, what is the chance that in a group of 10 pregnant women, more than half of them would experience a miscarriage?

p.description: Probability that a single pregnancy ends in miscarriage.

n.description: Number of pregnant women in the group.

threshold.description: Threshold defining the requested event: more than half of the 10 women experience a miscarriage, i.e. the miscarriage count is greater than 5.

input.background: A workplace health review team is preparing a briefing on concerns that have periodically surfaced around employees who regularly use video display terminals. For context, the team is working from a commonly cited baseline in which 15% of all pregnancies end in miscarriage, and it has a reference lookup for what different totals out of 10 pregnancies would look like under ordinary conditions. The current discussion is not about proving harm, but about helping compliance staff judge whether the number of unusual-looking local patterns they see across many user groups is more than what routine background experience would already generate. Because the review spans many employers, there is also interest in avoiding overreaction to rare events that can still appear when the network is large enough.
input.question: Suppose there are 20000 groups of video display terminal users, each large enough that 10 women in the group become pregnant within a year. If a group is flagged as a "cluster" when 6 or more of those 10 pregnancies end in miscarriage, how many such flagged groups should be expected over one year if terminal use does not increase miscarriage risk?

number_of_groups.description: The number of groups of video display terminal users large enough for ten women to become pregnant in one year.

probability.description: Original table probabilities for six through ten miscarriages.

input.background: A school health team is considering a limited screening check when there is concern that a contagious condition may already be circulating on campus. Based on prior expectations, if the condition is truly present in the school population, roughly 10% of children would be affected. Because pulling too many students out of class is disruptive and resource intensive, administrators want to know the smallest spot-check that would still give strong reassurance that an active issue would not be missed. Assume the concern is specifically about whether at least one affected child would be found in the group selected for testing if the condition is indeed in the school.
input.question: What is the minimum number of children the team should test so that the chance of identifying the condition, if it is present in the school, is 0.95 (95%)?

infection_rate.description: The probability that a child tests positive (infection spread rate), given as 10%. In the answer, the complement 0.9 (probability of a child being negative) is derived from this value.

target_probability.description: The desired probability of detecting the infection if it is present. In the answer, the complement 0.05 (probability of all children testing negative) is used to solve for the required sample size.

output.category: Minimum Sample Size Required to Achieve a Specified Probability

input.background: A public-sector workforce planning team is reviewing how changes in the physical profile of the adult male population may have affected the size of the potential entry pool for uniformed service roles over a 25 year span. Internal records note that the average adult male height moved from 175.8 cm to 179.1 cm during that period, while the spread around that average remained 5.84 cm. One long-standing screening rule for male applicants to the police force is a minimum standing height of 172 cm. input.background: A clinical operations lead is reviewing a bedside blood-pressure capture rule proposed for routine subject visits. For each subject, staff would record three readings during the same sitting, under the working assumption that the person’s underlying blood pressure is not actually shifting over that brief interval. The proposed workflow says the first two readings define an expected band, and the third reading would be flagged as untrustworthy and removed from consideration whenever it falls outside that band rather than within it. The team argues this rule is simple to train, though some clinicians are concerned it may reject too many final readings regardless of how noisy the device tends to be.
input.question: For one subject, how often would this workflow end up rejecting the third blood-pressure reading because it does not fall between the first two? Please determine the chance of that happening, noting that the result should not depend on the overall spread of the measurement error.

input.background: A genetic counseling service in Britain is preparing guidance for families discussing inherited conditions. Counselors explain that, for any one child born to such a couple, the chance that the child will be born with cystic fibrosis is 1 in 4. Families often ask for this information to be translated into what it means for a small number of future births, even though each pregnancy is considered on its own.
input.question: For a couple where both parents are carriers, what is the chance that their first two children will both be unaffected by cystic fibrosis?

input.background: A regional public health planning team in Lothian has been reviewing how household spending pressure may have affected drinking behaviour across the turn of the decade. In 1978–79, 1007 residents were originally contacted, including 608 men and 399 women, and asked about their alcohol use during the previous seven days. By 1981, duties and brewers’ prices had pushed alcohol prices upward faster than the broader cost of living for the first time in more than 30 years. A return exercise in 1981–82 was then organised around the 676 people classified internally as ‘regular drinkers’ based on the first round, rather than the full original pool. Over the three-year period, alcohol prices increased by 61%, while the retail price index increased by 52%. Average earnings edged up slightly more than the retail price index, but unemployment in the Edinburgh area also rose sharply. Of the 676 regular drinkers, 463 (69%) were contacted again, while 213 were not reached for reasons such as being untraceable, moving away, refusal, illness, or death. The project team highlighted lower alcohol use and fewer related problems among the 463 people seen again, and linked that pattern to alcohol becoming less affordable relative to income, although operational choices around whom to revisit have been questioned.
input.question: If the practical aim was to understand whether people were cutting back their alcohol intake, was it a sound decision to leave out everyone who had said in the first round that they had not been drinking?

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A public health planning team in the Lothian region has been revisiting an alcohol-use panel first assembled in 1978–79, when 1007 residents were contacted, including 608 men and 399 women, and asked about what they had consumed during the previous seven days. By 1981–82, the team chose to revisit only the 676 people originally classified as regular drinkers. This follow-up took place after a period of notable market and economic change: over the three years, alcohol prices had risen by 61%, compared with a 52% rise in the retail price index; average earnings had increased only slightly more than the retail price index; and unemployment in the Edinburgh area had climbed sharply. Of those 676 regular drinkers, 463 (69%) were interviewed again, while 213 were not, for a mixture of operational and personal reasons, including being untraceable, having left the region, refusal, illness, or death. The project write-up highlights lower alcohol consumption and fewer related problems among the 463 people seen again, and presents these changes in the context of alcohol becoming more expensive relative to income. Senior reviewers now want to know how securely that story can be carried into policy discussion, given the way the follow-up was actually completed.
input.question: For the 1981–82 revisit of the 676 regular drinkers, what share of the intended follow-up group was successfully interviewed again? Based on the reasons the other 213 were not included, in what practical ways might the missing group differ from the 463 who were seen again? Given that management wants to link the observed reduction in drinking and adverse effects to the changing affordability of alcohol, how should the incomplete follow-up shape the credibility of that interpretation?

regular_drinkers_total.description: Total number of 'regular drinkers' eligible for the follow-up survey in 1981–82.

re_interviewed.description: Number of regular drinkers successfully re-interviewed in the second survey.

non_respondents.description: Number of regular drinkers who were not re-interviewed in the second survey due to various reasons (untraceable, left region, refusal, illness, death).

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A regional public-health planning team in Lothian has been using community drinking figures to support messaging around affordability and harm reduction. The original fieldwork in 1978–79 covered a random sample of 1007 residents, comprising 608 men and 399 women, and asked about alcohol use over the previous seven days. After 1981 brought the first period in more than 30 years in which taxation and brewers' prices pushed alcohol prices up faster than the retail price index, the team revisited the issue in 1981–82. That later exercise focused on 676 people classified internally as 'regular drinkers' because they had reported drinking in the first round. Across the three-year span, alcohol prices increased by 61% and the retail price index by 52%; average earnings moved only slightly ahead of the retail price index, while unemployment in the Edinburgh area rose sharply. Of the 676 regular drinkers, 463 (69%) were reached again, while 213 were not, for reasons including being untraceable, having left the region, refusal, illness, or death. Internal commentary highlighted lower consumption and fewer adverse consequences among the 463 who were re-contacted, and linked that pattern to alcohol becoming less affordable relative to income. However, programme managers also know that drinking behaviour can fluctuate with calendar effects, holidays, weather, pay cycles, and other routine pressures that are not always obvious in headline summaries.
input.question: If leadership wants to treat the apparent reduction among the 463 re-interviewed subjects as evidence supporting the affordability explanation, how much concern should they have that the two field exercises were not run at exactly the same point in the year?

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A public-health policy team in the Lothian region was reviewing whether consumer price changes might have altered drinking patterns during a period of economic strain. In 1978–79, they had interviewed 1007 local residents, made up of 608 men and 399 women, about what they had consumed over the previous seven days. After major price pressure hit the drinks market in 1981—when taxation changes and brewers' price increases pushed alcohol prices up faster than the retail price index for the first time in more than 30 years—the team went back in 1981–82 to revisit those who had identified themselves as ongoing drinkers in the first round. That follow-up effort targeted 676 such 'regular drinkers'. Over the three years, alcohol prices had risen by 61%, while the retail price index had risen by 52%. Average earnings had gone up only slightly more than the retail price index, and at the same time unemployment in the Edinburgh area had climbed sharply. In the end, only 463 of the 676 people (69%) were interviewed again; the remaining 213 were not, for reasons including being untraceable, moving away, refusal, illness, or death. The write-up highlighted that the 463 people reached the second time around appeared to be drinking less and reporting fewer related problems, and it linked that pattern to the worsening affordability of alcohol.
input.question: From a decision-making standpoint, is it sound for the authors to treat the lower alcohol consumption seen among the 463 people who were interviewed again as evidence that the increase in excise duty on alcohol was the reason for the change?

output.category: Identification of Statistical Fallacies and Biases

input.background: A regional public health team in Lothian is reviewing legacy findings from a community drinking study to decide how much weight to give them in policy discussions. In 1978–79, 1007 residents were contacted, including 608 men and 399 women, and asked about their drinking over the previous seven days. Around the time of the later review, the market had shifted noticeably: by 1981, higher taxation and brewers’ prices meant alcohol prices had begun rising faster than the retail price index for the first time in more than 30 years. A second round of contact in 1981–82 focused only on the 676 people classified internally as 'regular drinkers' from the first round. Over the three-year period, alcohol prices increased by 61%, while the retail price index increased by 52%. Average earnings rose a little more than the retail price index, but unemployment in the Edinburgh area also climbed sharply. Of those 676 regular drinkers, only 463 (69%) were reached and interviewed again; the other 213 were lost for a range of operational reasons, including being untraceable, moving away, refusing, being too ill, or having died. The published write-up highlighted lower drinking levels and fewer related problems among the 463 people who were interviewed again, and linked that pattern to alcohol becoming more expensive relative to income. Senior staff now want to know whether that conclusion can safely be carried over to the wider group the follow-up was meant to speak for, given the way the second-round group was actually assembled.
input.question: If the department is using the 463 people interviewed again as the basis for a broader message about what happened to the original regular drinkers, is that group a sound stand-in for the full 676, or is there a risk that the follow-up picture is tilted by who could and could not be brought back into the study?

input.background: A sports publishing group is reviewing a well-known archival project based on professional baseball records. In that project, researchers pulled birth and death information from an encyclopaedia for 1472 players listed as right-handed and 236 listed as left-handed, with the aim of comparing how long players from the two groups appeared to live. input.background: A pediatric emergency care team reviewed the reporting choices used in a trial comparing two immediate treatment pathways for children arriving with acute asthma: a single dose of prednisolone versus a look-alike inactive treatment. In the trial, 73 children were assigned to the placebo pathway and 67 to the prednisolone pathway. The published paper highlighted an early throughput outcome of practical interest to clinicians and hospital managers: 2 children in the placebo arm were sent home after the first assessment, compared with 20 in the prednisolone arm. The article reported this as 3% for placebo (95% interval -1 to 6%) and 30% for prednisolone (19 to 41%), with an extremely small reported significance level, and the methods note says that this figure came from Fisher's exact test. Some staff have questioned whether that reporting choice was mainly driven by convention, by the small number of early discharges in one arm, or by something else about the 2-by-2 summary itself.
input.question: Given these trial counts and the way the early discharge outcome is split across the two treatment arms, was it a sensible choice to base the comparison on Fisher's exact test rather than the Chi squared test?

The records in the table group students by whether they are boys or girls and then place them into rounded half-hour bands according to time spent in bed. Staff are discussing whether the two groups appear to follow the same overall bedtime pattern, since even small shifts across the shorter- and longer-duration bands could affect how sleep guidance is framed for this age group. The figures available are only the grouped counts shown in the table, and the rounding convention was to move reported times up to the next half hour.
input.question: Using the table, assess whether boys and girls show a materially different distribution across the time-spent-in-bed categories, or whether the observed pattern is broadly similar between the two groups.

Boys.description: Number of 14-year-old boys in each category of time spent in bed (≤7.0, 7.5, 8.0, 8.5, 9.0, 9.5, 10.0, >10.0 hours). This variable and 'Girls' represent frequency counts for the same time-in-bed categories, split by gender.

Girls.description: Number of 14-year-old girls in each category of time spent in bed (≤7.0, 7.5, 8.0, 8.5, 9.0, 9.5, 10.0, >10.0 hours). This variable and 'Boys' represent frequency counts for the same time-in-bed categories, split by gender.
